title: How to Reconcile One Provider Bill With Two EOBs
excerpt: Determine whether the explanations of benefits replace each other or cover separate lines, then reconcile both with the provider bill.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Reconcile One Provider Bill With Two EOBs
metaDescription: Determine whether the explanations of benefits replace each other or cover separate lines, then reconcile both with the provider bill.
content:
A clinic sends one statement, but your health plan shows two explanations of benefits, or EOBs. Before you add the patient amounts, decide why there are two notices. One might replace an earlier decision. They might describe two services on the same account. They could also come from different insurers that processed the same service in sequence.

## Match the scope of each notice

Lay out the bill and the two EOBs. Record the patient, provider, service date, service description, claim reference and processing date. Start with a particular charge on the bill, then find the line that represents it on each notice. Use the itemized version if the bill shows only the current account total. CMS explains the main fields on an EOB and separately identifies the account information and payments on a bill. [CMS explanation of benefits guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [CMS medical bill guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

If the same plan processed both, ask which decision is active for the line and whether one voided or replaced the other. If two plans appear, identify which processed first and whether the second notice reflects that payment. If two distinct visits appear, keep a separate subtotal for each visit.

## Assign a row to each service

For an illustration, the first EOB assigns $80 for a May 4 visit. The second assigns $50 for the same visit after a correction. The plan confirms the $50 decision replaced the $80 decision. Use $50 as the current responsibility for that line. A separate $20 charge for May 11 on its own EOB may belong in the account total, subject to credits already posted.

Put the active amount next to the provider's current charge and any amount you paid. Ask the billing office to confirm that its ledger uses the same decisions. The [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) can help lay out those amounts by line.

If you cannot match a charge to either EOB, keep it on a separate row and ask for the payer's claim reference or the date the provider sent the claim. That row remains open while you reconcile the charges with confirmed references.

If the provider sent a correction, [check how the corrected claim changed your share](/articles/patient-responsibility-changed-corrected-claim). If two plans handled the same service, [trace the primary payment through the secondary EOB](/articles/secondary-eob-primary-insurance-payment).

title: Your Patient Share Changed After the Provider Corrected the Claim
excerpt: Compare the original and corrected claim decisions, identify what changed on the affected line and confirm the provider's updated balance.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Patient Share Changed After the Provider Corrected the Claim
metaDescription: Compare the original and corrected claim decisions, identify what changed on the affected line and confirm the provider's updated balance.
content:
The insurer initially assigns you $65 for a visit. The provider corrects the claim, and a new explanation of benefits, or EOB, shows $115. Ask what changed in the submitted claim and what changed when the plan processed it. A new amount can reflect a different code, units, service date or payment decision, depending on the record.

## Separate the provider's submission from the insurer's decision

Get the original and corrected EOBs. Ask the billing office for the date it sent the correction, the original reference, the replacement reference if available and a description of the change. Ask the insurer which version it accepted and whether it decided all the affected lines. UnitedHealthcare's administrative guide is one example of a payer instructing providers to submit a corrected claim as a replacement with the original reference. Use your own plan's identifiers and procedure. [UnitedHealthcare provider guide on claim corrections](https://www.uhcprovider.com/en/resource-library/edi/edi-quick-tips-claims.html)

Mark the lines that changed. Compare the service information, allowed amount, plan payment and patient responsibility. Check whether the plan's explanation distinguishes a deductible, copayment, coinsurance or an amount assigned for another reason. CMS explains how the patient amount on an EOB relates to the provider's bill and payments already made. [CMS EOB guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

## Reconcile what you actually paid

Suppose the old notice assigns $65 and the new active notice assigns $115. You paid $40 after the first bill. If that payment remains credited to the same service and there are no other changes, the current amount still due on that line would be $75. If the provider's new statement shows the full $115, ask where the $40 posted and request an updated ledger.

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) to put the active decision beside the payment record. If the corrected submission is still under review, note that status and ask for the expected update. If you disagree with the decision itself, ask the plan for the review or appeal instructions on the current notice.

Keep the earlier payment receipt even if the provider reissued the bill under a new number. Ask the billing office to confirm where the original payment is credited before comparing the revised totals.

If both notices keep the same number, [confirm which revision remains active](/articles/two-revised-eobs-same-claim-number). If the difference is in the deductible, [compare the deductible with the bill and plan ledger](/articles/eob-deductible-differs-after-reprocessing).

title: The Hospital Bill Says Insurance Pending After the EOB Says Processed
excerpt: Compare statement and processing dates, then ask whether the hospital received and posted the insurer's determination for that claim.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Hospital Bill Says Insurance Pending After the EOB Says Processed
metaDescription: Compare statement and processing dates, then ask whether the hospital received and posted the insurer's determination for that claim.
content:
The plan portal says a claim was processed. The hospital statement still has an insurance-pending line. Put a date on each status. The plan's decision and the hospital's posting of that decision are separate events, and an older statement may have been issued before either the payment or the explanation reached the billing office.

## Match the claim before checking timing

Write down the hospital account and the insurer's claim reference. Match the patient, dates of service and billing entity. A hospital visit can produce separate hospital and professional claims. Confirm that the EOB you found is the one the hospital is waiting on. CMS distinguishes the plan's explanation from the provider's request for payment. [CMS EOB guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [CMS guide to reading a medical bill](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

Check the statement date and the plan's processing date. Ask the insurer whether it issued a payment, applied the line to your responsibility, denied it or processed it for another payer. Ask how the result was sent. The hospital can check whether it received the remittance and attached it to your account. For covered electronic payments, CMS describes how providers can use matching trace information to associate an electronic funds transfer with its remittance advice. [CMS guidance on matching payment and remittance](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/burden-reduction/administrative-simplification/operating-rules/eft-remittance-advice)

## Ask what is still pending

Imagine the hospital cut a statement on June 5. The plan processed the claim June 7 and the hospital posted it June 12. A June 5 statement would still reflect the earlier status. If the June 18 statement also shows pending, ask which claim remains open, whether a secondary carrier is involved and when the updated patient balance will be available.

Request the date and amount of any posted insurer payment and a current statement. If a payment deadline appears, ask the billing office what amount it expects while the posting is being resolved and record the response. The [Insurance Claim Follow-Up Email Builder](/tools/claim-follow-up-composer) can help organize those dates and the two reference numbers.

If the plan sent a reversal and a replacement, [request both entries and track the posting sequence](/articles/insurer-reversal-replacement-eob-accident). If the payment was sent to you, [check its payee and what the provider actually received](/articles/eob-payment-to-patient-provider-balance).

title: Your EOB Deductible and Provider Bill Differ After Reprocessing
excerpt: Verify how much of the active EOB went toward the deductible and how the provider applied prior payments to the same service.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your EOB Deductible and Provider Bill Differ After Reprocessing
metaDescription: Verify how much of the active EOB went toward the deductible and how the provider applied prior payments to the same service.
content:
A reprocessed explanation of benefits assigns $100 to the deductible. The provider shows a different balance. Look first at the difference between the deductible portion and the total current patient share. A provider's statement may combine that share with other patient amounts, prior credits or separate services.

## Locate the deductible on the active claim

Ask the plan to confirm the active determination, service date, claim line and amount assigned to the deductible. Identify any other cost-sharing amounts on the same line. Ask what happened to the deductible entry from the earlier determination, particularly if the plan reversed it. HealthCare.gov explains the deductible and notes that different plan designs can have separate deductibles or cover certain services before the deductible is met. [HealthCare.gov deductible definition](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/deductible/)

Keep the plan's deductible tracker separate from the individual claim. The tracker may show the balance for the year or for a family, while the EOB assigns a specific amount for one service. If the plan reprocessed several claims, ask how it adjusted the running totals and which policy period the service belongs to.

## Reconcile the bill line with the current patient amount

Suppose the active EOB lists $100 deductible and $40 coinsurance, for $140 patient responsibility. You already paid $25 to the provider for that encounter. If that credit is still on the account, the unpaid share in this example is $115. If the statement reads $215, ask whether the provider added the deductible twice or included another charge. Request a line-by-line explanation instead of relying on the label on the bill.

CMS explains that an EOB's patient balance may include amounts the patient has already paid. Ask the billing office for the posted payments, applied credits and current balance for that service. [CMS EOB guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [CMS medical bill guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

## Send the question with the exact amounts

Put the active EOB amounts and the provider's itemized balance into the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler). If the difference began with a provider correction, [compare the two claim decisions and the changes to each line](/articles/patient-responsibility-changed-corrected-claim). If the number is on an installment portal, [check which charges the payment plan actually covers](/articles/medical-payment-plan-balance-differs-eob).

title: How to Match an EOB Claim Number With a Radiology Bill
excerpt: Match the scan date, billing entity and component first, then ask the insurer and radiology office to confirm the claim reference.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Match an EOB Claim Number With a Radiology Bill
metaDescription: Match the scan date, billing entity and component first, then ask the insurer and radiology office to confirm the claim reference.
content:
A radiology bill lists an account number and a health plan notice lists a claim number. Those identifiers can describe the same work in two different systems. Start with the service and who billed it. A single scan may lead to a facility charge and a separate charge for the clinician's interpretation.

## Find the exact billing entity

Record the date, the facility, the exam description and the name on the itemized bill. Ask the billing office for the billing provider, any provider identifier it can share, the code or component billed and the payer claim reference returned on the remittance. Ask the insurer to search by date and billing entity if the claim number is unavailable. CMS identifies the provider, service description and claim reference as fields to check on an EOB. [CMS guide to EOB fields](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

Some radiology services have professional and technical components. CMS's Medicare manual describes component billing and modifiers for eligible services. If a bill refers to an interpretation or a technical component, ask which was billed and use the coding details the provider gives you. Plan rules and claim presentation can vary. [CMS Medicare radiology billing manual](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/clm104c13.pdf)

## Check the amount only after the match

For example, the insurer shows a $45 patient amount on an imaging center claim. A separate $35 bill comes from the radiologist who read the scan. Both may share the scan date. Ask whether the $35 bill corresponds to a different claim and which EOB explains that amount. The identical date gives you a starting point for the search.

Record the link as “radiology account R14 corresponds to plan claim 8124,” with the name and date of the confirmation. Then compare the EOB's patient amount with any payments or credits on that account. Keep the facility and interpretation in separate rows.

When a second bill lists the same imaging description, ask for the service code and billing entity for both entries. A match on the date and exam is a starting point. The component, provider and payer reference complete the comparison.

## Send a short matching request

Use the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) to list the account, scan date and identifiers you need. For a statement sent by a billing company, [verify the provider behind the account](/articles/eob-no-provider-name-billing-company-statement). If one invoice spans several dates, [reconcile each line before totaling them](/articles/reconcile-therapy-invoice-multiple-service-dates).

title: Your Bill Shows a Copay After the EOB Says You Owe Zero
excerpt: Verify that the zero-dollar insurance decision covers the same provider and service, then ask where the copay charge came from.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Bill Shows a Copay After the EOB Says You Owe Zero
metaDescription: Verify that the zero-dollar insurance decision covers the same provider and service, then ask where the copay charge came from.
content:
A portal shows a $30 copay while the insurer's explanation of benefits, or EOB, shows $0 for the visit. Ask the provider to match its charge to the current plan decision for the exact service. A check-in amount, an earlier statement and a finalized claim can reflect different stages of the account.

## Find the service behind the copay

Compare the patient, provider, date, description and claim reference. If the statement includes more than one service, identify the specific line showing $30. Ask whether the charge was entered at check-in, carried forward from an earlier visit, or applied after the plan's decision. If the insurer has issued multiple EOBs, verify which is active.

HealthCare.gov describes a copayment as a fixed amount for a covered service under the plan's terms. CMS explains where to find the patient balance on the EOB and how to compare it with the provider bill. Ask the plan how the copay terms applied to the claim in question if the notice is unclear. [HealthCare.gov copayment definition](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/co-payment/) · [CMS guide to EOBs](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

## Ask what happened to a payment already made

Suppose you paid $30 at check-in and the active EOB assigns zero for that visit. Ask the billing office whether the payment remains on that account, was applied to another charge or is eligible for a credit or refund. Keep the receipt and request a dated statement showing the transaction. If you never paid the charge, ask the office to reconcile the remaining $30 with the active claim decision and show the current amount due.

If the provider says a different service generated the charge, ask for the date, code or description, and its own insurance decision if there is one. Record the explanation separately instead of using the zero balance from the first claim to resolve both charges.

## Document the correction

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) to compare the charge, current plan amount and provider's ledger. If the receipt was credited to another visit, [trace the payment by transaction and service date](/articles/copay-credited-wrong-service-date). If the bill describes a service the plan treated as bundled, [check the reason and the responsibility assigned to that line](/articles/eob-bundled-service-separate-provider-bill).

title: An EOB Adjustment Appears as a Charge on the Revised Bill
excerpt: Trace the provider's debit and credit entries, then ask which part of the insurance adjustment is included in the balance due.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: An EOB Adjustment Appears as a Charge on the Revised Bill
metaDescription: Trace the provider's debit and credit entries, then ask which part of the insurance adjustment is included in the balance due.
content:
The insurance notice shows an adjustment. The revised provider statement lists the same amount as a positive charge. Ask the billing office whether that amount is an adjustment reversal, an informational entry or a new charge added to the patient balance. A label can mean different things in an insurer's explanation and the provider's ledger.

## Trace the entries in posting order

Request the itemized bill and an account history for the affected service. Record the original charge, the allowed amount if shown, insurer payment, patient share, provider adjustment and any later reversal. Put each entry beside its posting date, description and sign. Ask the billing office how it represents credits and which entries affect the amount due.

CMS's Medicare remittance guidance describes group codes that assign responsibility for adjustments. For example, CO identifies a contractual obligation and PR identifies patient responsibility in that setting. Your EOB and the billing office's own posting explanation are the records to compare for your plan. [CMS payment and remittance advice guide](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/electronic-billing/health-care-payment-remittance-advice)

## Check the balance after the whole sequence

For an example, the original charge is $300, the plan allows $120, pays $90 and assigns $30 to the patient. A $180 contractual adjustment accounts for the difference between charge and allowed amount. If a later statement shows $180 as a debit, ask which original entry it reversed and whether a replacement adjustment posted. Compare the net patient amount at the end of the sequence with the active EOB. [CMS guide to allowed charges and the patient balance](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

Ask for a dated ledger with each reversal and replacement matched to the relevant claim. If the provider still expects payment, ask which active plan decision or charge explains the amount and request an updated statement.

If the statement shows only the new debit, request the earlier transaction and its offset on the same page. Comparing both entries makes it easier to see whether the original adjustment has been reversed and how the replacement changes the running balance.

## Record what remains due

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) for the current amounts and retain the intermediate entries as supporting records. For an entire claim that was reversed and reissued, [pair the notices with the provider's postings](/articles/insurer-reversal-replacement-eob-accident). For a separate charge the plan treated as included in another service, [review the bundled service decision](/articles/eob-bundled-service-separate-provider-bill).

title: How to Compare a Secondary EOB With the Primary Payment
excerpt: Follow the same service through both plans and check how the secondary insurer used the primary plan's payment and adjustments.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Compare a Secondary EOB With the Primary Payment
metaDescription: Follow the same service through both plans and check how the secondary insurer used the primary plan's payment and adjustments.
content:
Your primary plan paid part of a bill. The secondary plan issued its own explanation of benefits, or EOB. Start with the same date and service line on both notices. The useful question is how the secondary plan accounted for the first payment when it reached its own decision.

## Identify the order and the matching line

Record the provider, service date, primary claim number and secondary claim number. Ask both plans which coverage was primary for that service and whether the second plan received the first EOB or an electronic crossover. If the first plan has since reprocessed the claim, ask which version the secondary plan used.

Medicare's coordination guide explains the primary and secondary payer sequence for people with Medicare and other coverage. The order and benefits vary with the type of coverage and the circumstances. For two other plans, ask for the coordination rules that govern your claim. [Medicare's coordination of benefits guide](https://www.medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/coordination/who-pays-first)

## Track the amount each plan actually assigned

On the primary notice, record the allowed amount, payment and responsibility. On the secondary notice, find the reported primary payment, any secondary adjustment, the secondary payment and the final amount assigned to you if shown. If the secondary notice records a different primary payment, ask the billing office which primary decision it submitted.

For example, the primary plan pays $100 and lists $50 in patient responsibility. If the secondary plan accounts for that $100 and pays $30 against the eligible remainder, a provider ledger reflecting both payments might show $20 still due for that line. Verify the applicable amounts before treating that example as your bill. CMS's EOB guide explains how plan payments and the patient balance are presented. [CMS guide to reading an EOB](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

## Get the provider's current balance

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) with the current notices and the provider's posted credits. Ask whether both decisions were applied to the same account and whether a payment you made earlier is still credited. Save the date each office confirmed the result.

If the two notices could belong to different services, [classify the EOBs before comparing the totals](/articles/reconcile-one-provider-bill-two-eobs). If the primary plan revised the same reference twice, [verify which decision the secondary payer received](/articles/two-revised-eobs-same-claim-number).

title: The Provider Sent a Refund After the Insurer Revised Your EOB
excerpt: Match the refund to the payment, claim line and ledger credit that created it, then verify the remaining balance.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Provider Sent a Refund After the Insurer Revised Your EOB
metaDescription: Match the refund to the payment, claim line and ledger credit that created it, then verify the remaining balance.
content:
A check or card credit arrives from your medical provider after insurance reprocesses a claim. Match it to the original payment before adjusting your records. It may reflect a corrected patient share, a duplicate payment or a credit on a different service. The refund notice and the provider's transaction history can establish what it covers.

## Locate the credit that led to the refund

Gather the revised explanation of benefits, or EOB, the earlier statement, your receipt and the notice or bank entry for the refund. Compare the service date and account number on the receipt with the refund reference. Ask the billing office to name the payment it returned, the service affected and the date it posted the refund. CMS's sample EOB explains why the assigned patient balance can include an amount you already paid. [CMS sample explanation of benefits](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/11819-sample-explanation-benefits-508.pdf)

If the refund covered only part of the credit, ask for an itemization showing what happened to the difference. It might have been applied to another open account or still be available as a credit. Confirm which amount was returned to you and which amount, if any, was returned to an insurer.

## Compare the figures as transactions

Suppose you paid $200 for a visit and the current EOB assigns $110 to you. Your ledger shows a $90 patient credit after the insurer's revision. You receive $60 back. Ask the provider to show what it did with the remaining $30. If the office transferred it, record the receiving account and request confirmation it posted there. If it remains on the original account, ask for the current statement showing it.

For medical and billing records held by covered providers and health plans, HHS explains how to request copies and ask for amendments if information is incorrect. The right of access is subject to the applicable rules and exceptions. [HHS guide to medical and billing records](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-individuals/medical-records/index.html)

## Keep the refund trace with the bill

Use the [Claim Expense and Receipt Tracker](/tools/receipt-coverage-map) to pair the receipt, credit and refund. Record whether the funds arrived or are still expected. If the credit went to a different service date, [check how the payment was allocated](/articles/copay-credited-wrong-service-date). If a settlement statement uses an outstanding refund in its math, [separate the expected money from the receipts already posted](/articles/settlement-statement-provider-refund-not-received).

title: How to Reconcile Several Therapy Dates on One Invoice With the EOB
excerpt: Match each appointment to a claim line, confirm its units and patient share, and check how payments posted across the invoice.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Reconcile Several Therapy Dates on One Invoice With the EOB
metaDescription: Match each appointment to a claim line, confirm its units and patient share, and check how payments posted across the invoice.
content:
A physical therapy office bills a month's visits together. Your explanation of benefits, or EOB, has a separate line for each date and may show more than one service on some dates. Build the reconciliation visit by visit before you compare the invoice total.

## Use the dates and codes together

Request the provider's itemized statement for the invoice period. List each visit, its service description or code where available, the units billed and any payment you made that day. Match the entry to the date, provider and line on the insurance notice. If one date appears on two claims, ask whether they cover different services or whether one replaces the other.

CMS's institutional billing training gives an example of how line-item service dates are reported for Medicare outpatient bills and inpatient Part B bills. For your therapy invoice, ask the provider how its billing system maps appointments and services to the claims the insurer received. [CMS institutional billing guidance on line dates](https://www.cms.gov/outreach-and-education/mln/wbt/mln7388180-mln-wbt-1450/1450/lesson05/16/index.html)

## Compare the visits before adding them

For an illustration, the current EOBs assign $25 for May 6, $25 for May 13 and $60 for May 20. The three active amounts total $110 before any credits. If the office statement lists $135, look for the extra $25 as its own line. It may come from a prior visit, a duplicate entry or another service. Verify the relevant dates, line references and amounts with the office.

If you paid $25 at the first visit, check where that receipt posted. CMS distinguishes the insurer's patient balance from the provider's record of payments and the amount currently due. [CMS EOB guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [CMS medical bill guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

## Ask the office to tie the invoice to the claim history

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) to compare the active responsibility and posted credits for each visit. If you have an invoice line without a matching EOB, ask for its claim reference and current status. Ask for a corrected itemization if a line is duplicated.

If your statement combines separate imaging charges, [match the facility and interpretation claims by component](/articles/match-radiology-bill-eob-claim-number). If two notices appear to apply to one invoice line, [work out whether they replace each other](/articles/reconcile-one-provider-bill-two-eobs).

title: The EOB Shows Payment to You but the Provider Balance Stayed the Same
excerpt: Check who received the insurer's payment and whether the provider's account shows how that payment should be applied.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The EOB Shows Payment to You but the Provider Balance Stayed the Same
metaDescription: Check who received the insurer's payment and whether the provider's account shows how that payment should be applied.
content:
An explanation of benefits, or EOB, shows a payment to the patient or subscriber. Your provider still shows a balance. Ask the insurer who the payee was and whether the payment was issued or delivered. Then ask the billing office how it expects to apply that money to the specific service.

## Check the payee and payment status

Record the claim reference, provider, service date, amount, payee and payment date. Ask the insurer whether it issued a check or electronic payment, where it was sent and whether it was returned, stopped or reissued. If you filed a claim yourself, compare the submission and reimbursement instructions. CMS's sample EOB identifies the payee separately from the provider and patient balance fields. [CMS sample explanation of benefits](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/11819-sample-explanation-benefits-508.pdf)

For Medicare services, how the provider participates and whether it accepts assignment affects the way payment is handled. Medicare's guide explains the differences between providers that accept assignment, non-participating providers and providers that have opted out. For a private plan, confirm the payee and terms directly with that plan. [Medicare guide to provider assignment](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs/provider-accept-Medicare)

## Work out the provider's current expected amount

Imagine an out-of-network claim shows a $180 payment made to you. The office's itemized bill still shows $260 because its ledger records only payments it received. Ask how much of the bill the provider expects after any applicable adjustments, which service the payment relates to and how it will credit any payment you send. Save the receipt and the new balance once it posts.

If you already paid the office, compare the date and amount of that payment with the plan reimbursement. Ask the billing office and plan to explain a discrepancy before forwarding a duplicate payment. CMS's bill guide shows how provider payments and the current balance appear on a statement. [CMS medical bill guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

## Track delivery and posting separately

Use the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) to record who confirmed the payee, what was received and what posted to the provider's account. If the carrier sent payment to the office and the bill still says pending, [check the timing of the hospital posting](/articles/hospital-insurance-pending-eob-processed). If the payment came from a second insurer, [reconcile it with the primary payment first](/articles/secondary-eob-primary-insurance-payment).

title: Your Accident Bill Was Processed Under the Wrong Plan Member
excerpt: Check the patient and subscriber fields, then ask the provider and insurer to correct the claim and confirm the resulting balance.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Accident Bill Was Processed Under the Wrong Plan Member
metaDescription: Check the patient and subscriber fields, then ask the provider and insurer to correct the claim and confirm the resulting balance.
content:
A plan notice uses the wrong name for care you received after an accident. First check whether the displayed name is the patient or the policy subscriber. A dependent can receive care under a subscriber's plan. The issue to resolve is whether the claim identifies the person who actually received the service and the correct coverage for that person.

## Match the patient details through a secure channel

Compare your itemized bill, coverage card and explanation of benefits, or EOB. Confirm the patient name and service date with the provider. Ask the insurer to verify the member identifier, patient field and relevant plan coverage using its secure portal or a verified contact number. Keep sensitive identifiers in the approved channel. CMS's sample EOB lists patient and subscriber as separate fields. [CMS sample explanation of benefits](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/11819-sample-explanation-benefits-508.pdf)

Ask which record introduced the mismatch. If the provider sent a claim with the wrong member details, ask for the correction date and claim reference. If the provider used the correct details and the payer associated the claim with a different person, ask the payer to explain its correction process. Confirm how each office will address any amount already paid, adjustments and account balances.

## Confirm the claim now belongs to the right person

For example, the clinic's account lists the dependent who attended the appointment. The EOB uses the subscriber as the patient. Ask for the corrected plan notice and then check whether the provider posted the new result to the dependent's account. If the insurer requests identity verification, follow its official process.

HHS explains the right to request a change when a covered provider's or plan's medical or billing records contain incorrect information. The office can explain which formal amendment process, if any, applies to the document at issue. [HHS guidance on medical and billing record corrections](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-individuals/medical-records/index.html)

Ask both organizations which reference to use for the correction and save it beside the disputed notice. If the plan changes the reference, record how it links the old record to the corrected decision.

## Record the corrected references

Use the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) for the office, date and status of each correction. If the correction changes the amount owed, [compare the original and corrected claim decisions](/articles/patient-responsibility-changed-corrected-claim). If the issuer of the statement is also unclear, [verify the billing company and underlying provider](/articles/eob-no-provider-name-billing-company-statement).

title: The Provider Moved Your Balance to a New Account After EOB Reprocessing
excerpt: Trace the transfer out of the original account and into the receiving account, then confirm which balance remains payable.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Provider Moved Your Balance to a New Account After EOB Reprocessing
metaDescription: Trace the transfer out of the original account and into the receiving account, then confirm which balance remains payable.
content:
The provider reprocesses a bill and opens a new account number. The old and new screens both show a balance. Ask for the transaction that connects them. The useful records are the transfer out, the transfer in and the current ledger entries that explain whether any amount appears twice.

## Ask what moved and why

Gather the older statement, the revised explanation of benefits, or EOB, and the latest statement. Record the old and new account numbers, service date, billing entity, active claim reference and each statement date. Ask whether the provider moved the full account or specific lines, and request the transfer date, amount and reason for each. CMS's medical bill guide explains why the account identifier and current balance are useful when asking about a statement. [CMS guide to reading a medical bill](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

Ask how the provider handled payments you made before the move. Request the amount posted on the original account, the amount carried to the new account and any other transfers or refunds. Keep both ledgers until you can match the entries.

## Reconcile the same obligation across two accounts

For an example, the first account held $180 after insurance. The provider transfers $120 to the new account after a revised decision and removes the remaining $60. Verify the $120 transfer out, its entry on the new account and the $60 adjustment. If an earlier statement still displays $180, ask the provider to issue dated balances for both accounts.

If a covered provider holds billing and payment records about you, HHS explains the right to access those records, subject to applicable exceptions. If a covered debt collector contacts you, CFPB explains the validation information it generally must provide, including itemization of payments and credits. Match the collector's reference to the provider's accounting. [HHS right of access to billing and payment records](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/does-an-individuals-right-under-hipaa/index.html) · [CFPB debt validation guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-information-does-a-debt-collector-have-to-give-me-about-the-debt-en-331/)

## Keep one record of the amount still due

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) with the active EOB and both ledgers. Ask the billing office to confirm in writing which account receives future payments. If you had an installment agreement, [reconcile the plan's balance with the transferred charges](/articles/medical-payment-plan-balance-differs-eob). If the insurer reversed a claim before the move, [track the reversal and replacement postings](/articles/insurer-reversal-replacement-eob-accident).

title: Your Copay Was Credited to the Wrong Service Date
excerpt: Match the receipt to the service date it was collected for and ask the billing office to move the credit to the correct encounter.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Copay Was Credited to the Wrong Service Date
metaDescription: Match the receipt to the service date it was collected for and ask the billing office to move the credit to the correct encounter.
content:
Two visits appear on the same provider account. You paid a copay at the first one, but the statement credits it to the second. Start with the receipt and the ledger. The issue is where the payment was applied, even if the combined account balance looks plausible.

## Locate the payment and the visit it was meant for

Find the receipt, card or bank record and any appointment confirmation. Record the transaction date, amount, receipt number and service date. A payment posted later may carry a different date from the visit. Ask the office to show both the transaction and the encounter it credited. CMS's medical bill guide identifies the service date, account number and payments as useful fields to compare. [CMS guide to reading your medical bill](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

Check the active explanation of benefits, or EOB, for each encounter. Write down the patient responsibility and any other posted payments. If both visits had similar amounts, use the receipt and the office's posting record to identify which service the payment was for.

## Compare the balances before and after the correction

For an illustration, the July 2 visit assigns $30 and the July 9 visit assigns $50. You paid $30 on July 2. The statement shows July 2 unpaid and $20 still due for July 9 because the $30 credit was applied there. If the credit is moved to the first visit, the balance for July 2 should become zero and the $50 July 9 balance would remain, assuming no other entries. The overall amount would still be $50.

Ask the billing office to confirm which date it corrected and to issue an updated statement. If the available medical or billing record itself is inaccurate, HHS explains the process for requesting an amendment from a covered provider or plan. [HHS guide to medical and billing records](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-individuals/medical-records/index.html)

## Save the updated record by date

Use the [Claim Expense and Receipt Tracker](/tools/receipt-coverage-map) to pair the payment receipt with the corrected encounter. If the plan's latest decision assigns zero to the visit, [ask what happened to the original copay charge](/articles/provider-copay-eob-zero-owed). If a credit resulted in a refund, [trace the amount returned and any balance left as a credit](/articles/provider-refund-after-revised-eob).

title: The EOB Omits the Provider Name but a Billing Company Sent a Statement
excerpt: Verify the underlying medical provider and claim before paying a statement from a third-party billing company.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The EOB Omits the Provider Name but a Billing Company Sent a Statement
metaDescription: Verify the underlying medical provider and claim before paying a statement from a third-party billing company.
content:
A company you do not recognize sent a medical statement, and the explanation of benefits, or EOB, does not display the treating provider's name. Establish who performed the service, which entity submitted the claim and who is authorized to receive payment. Those roles can belong to different organizations.

## Identify the service through a verified contact

Use a phone number or portal you already know for the facility or provider where you received care. Give the service date, general description and statement reference through its approved channel. Ask whether the company handles its billing and which provider or group the company represents for that account. Ask the insurer to look up the billing entity and provider identifier tied to the claim reference.

CMS's EOB guide explains the provider and claim details typically shown on a notice. If the office supplies a National Provider Identifier, the CMS registry can help you check the name associated with it. The registry helps identify the provider. Confirm the specific billing relationship and payment instructions with the provider directly. [CMS EOB guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [CMS NPI Registry](https://npiregistry.cms.hhs.gov/search)

## Match the account to the insurer's claim

Suppose you visited a hospital imaging department. A statement arrives from a billing company for a radiology group. Ask the hospital whether that group read the scan and ask the insurer which claim shows the professional component. Record the name on the bill, the group, service date and claim number that the insurer confirms. A match to the hospital claim alone may account for only the facility's part of the visit.

If the provider cannot identify the statement, ask the billing company for an itemized copy and the billing provider name. Use secure channels for personal or insurance information. Once you confirm the connection, compare the active EOB amount, posted payments and current balance.

Ask the verified provider where it wants payments directed. Keep that instruction with the statement, especially if the envelope, online payment page and plan notice show different names.

## Record the verified payee and reference

Use the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) to track who verified the account and when. For separate imaging bills, [match each component with its own claim](/articles/match-radiology-bill-eob-claim-number). If the notice also names the wrong patient, [check the patient and subscriber fields with the plan](/articles/accident-bill-processed-wrong-plan-member).

title: Two Revised EOBs Have the Same Claim Number. Which One Applies?
excerpt: Use the insurer's processing history and active claim decision to identify the correct version when both notices show the same reference.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Two Revised EOBs Have the Same Claim Number. Which One Applies?
metaDescription: Use the insurer's processing history and active claim decision to identify the correct version when both notices show the same reference.
content:
Two revised explanations of benefits, or EOBs, share the same claim number. One assigns $72 and the other assigns $49. Use the insurer's claim history to establish which version applies. The reference alone may identify the claim while leaving the sequence of decisions open.

## Compare the notices as versions of the same record

Save both notices with their issue dates and any processing or revision dates shown. Record the patient, service dates, provider and line descriptions. Compare the amounts and explanation codes. Ask the insurer to confirm the status of each decision for those lines, whether it reversed or replaced an earlier decision and whether another adjustment is pending.

CMS's EOB guide explains how the claim number identifies the claim and where the patient amount appears. UnitedHealthcare's provider guide gives one example of a corrected claim that references the original. The insurer can tell you which identifiers or dates distinguish the specific versions on your account. [CMS guide to EOB fields](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [UnitedHealthcare corrected claim guidance](https://www.uhcprovider.com/en/resource-library/edi/edi-quick-tips-claims.html)

## Ask for the active amount for each line

For example, one notice is dated July 8 and the other July 12. The plan confirms the July 12 document is a copy of an older determination regenerated for delivery, while the July 8 decision is the active reprocessing result. Ask it to state the active amount and the date of that decision in writing. If each notice covers different lines, mark the active status on a line-by-line basis.

Ask the provider whether it received the same decision and when it posted it. Compare your payments and credits against that posting. Save the insurer's confirmation beside the copy you use for reconciliation so a later reviewer can follow your choice.

Ask which date refers to processing and which refers to printing or delivery if the notices use a single label. Note the name of the person who confirmed those dates. That gives you a basis to check another regenerated copy if the portal posts one later.

## File both versions and mark the active one

Use the [claim statement comparison tool](/tools/statement-version-comparator) to record what changed. If a provider submission triggered the revision, [compare the original claim with the correction](/articles/patient-responsibility-changed-corrected-claim). If you find a reversal alongside the two versions, [trace it through the remittance and provider's ledger](/articles/insurer-reversal-replacement-eob-accident).

title: Your Medical Payment Plan Balance Differs From the EOB
excerpt: Compare the plan's starting amount, installments, insurance adjustments and remaining principal with the active responsibility on the EOB.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Medical Payment Plan Balance Differs From the EOB
metaDescription: Compare the plan's starting amount, installments, insurance adjustments and remaining principal with the active responsibility on the EOB.
content:
You set up monthly payments when a clinic billed $600. Insurance later reprocessed the claim, and the new explanation of benefits, or EOB, assigns $360. Ask the provider and whoever holds the installment agreement how the reduction and payments were posted. The installment portal may track a different balance from the provider ledger.

## Identify who holds the agreement and which charges it covers

Find the signed agreement, its starting balance, the included services and the payee for each installment. Ask whether the arrangement is with the provider or an outside financing company. A provider ledger can show a bill paid by financing while the financing company still tracks a balance. CFPB discusses medical payment options and the need to identify any fees or financing terms before comparing amounts. [CFPB guide to medical bills and payment options](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-should-i-know-about-medical-credit-cards-and-payment-plans-for-medical-bills-en-1827/)

Then match the active EOB to the services in the agreement. Note any installment already posted, insurer payment or provider adjustment. If the arrangement covers more than one account, request an itemization by service or account. CMS explains that the patient amount on an EOB may include amounts already paid. [CMS explanation of benefits guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

## Run the comparison with the same starting point

In an example, a provider-managed plan started at $600. Three $75 payments reduced it to $375 before insurance reprocessing. If the updated responsibility for the same services is $360 and all $225 paid is credited there, the unpaid amount for those services is $135. Ask whether the installment record reflects that change and whether the remaining payment schedule will be updated.

With third-party financing, ask who receives an adjustment or refund and when the financing balance will reflect it. Keep interest, fees and unrelated services separate from the medical balance. Request the written current principal and the next payment information from the agreement holder.

## Keep the agreement and reconciliation together

Use the [Medical Bill Payment Plan Calculator](/tools/medical-payment-plan-model) to compare the schedule after the provider or lender confirms the current numbers. If an account was moved, [verify both sides of the transfer](/articles/provider-balance-transferred-after-eob-reprocessing). If the discrepancy is in the deductible assigned to a service, [compare the reprocessed EOB with the provider ledger](/articles/eob-deductible-differs-after-reprocessing).

title: The EOB Says a Service Was Bundled but the Provider Billed It Separately
excerpt: Confirm which service the plan bundled, what amount it assigned to you and why the provider's separate balance appeared.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The EOB Says a Service Was Bundled but the Provider Billed It Separately
metaDescription: Confirm which service the plan bundled, what amount it assigned to you and why the provider's separate balance appeared.
content:
A health plan lists a service as included in another procedure. The provider statement still requests a separate payment for the line. Compare the exact claim and the provider's coding and posting record. The amount a plan declines to pay separately and the amount it assigns to the patient are different fields.

## Locate the bundled line and the service it was combined with

Write down the provider, service date, claim reference, line description and adjustment reason. Ask the plan which other line it treated as including the service and how it assigned responsibility for the denied or adjusted amount. Ask whether the current decision applies to the entity that sent the bill. A facility and a professional group can each bill related work.

CMS's National Correct Coding Initiative describes Medicare edits that can prevent separate payment for certain code pairs under defined conditions. The edit and plan rules that apply to your claim should come from the payer. Medicare's remittance guidance also explains how group codes describe who is assigned a financial obligation in that program. [CMS procedure-to-procedure edits](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/national-correct-coding-initiative-ncci-edits/medicare-ncci-procedure-procedure-ptp-edits) · [CMS Medicare remittance guidance](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/electronic-billing/health-care-payment-remittance-advice)

## Ask why the charge is still on the bill

For an illustration, the EOB shows a $40 patient amount for a procedure and a second line with zero patient responsibility because it was included in the first. The provider asks for $40 plus $75 for the second service. Ask it to reconcile the $75 with the decision, confirm whether it posted the adjustment, and identify the billing basis for any amount it still expects.

Request a new itemized statement if the provider updates the claim. If the payer says the line was processed under a different provider or benefit, ask it to confirm the reference and any new responsibility. CMS's consumer EOB guide explains which fields to match with the bill. [CMS explanation of benefits guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

## Save the answer with the specific service line

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) to compare the active plan amount with what the billing office requests. If an adjustment appears as a positive charge, [track its debit and credit entries](/articles/eob-adjustment-appears-as-charge). If a copay remains after the decision assigns zero, [reconcile the charge with the current notice](/articles/provider-copay-eob-zero-owed).

title: How to Document an Insurance Reversal and Replacement EOB After an Accident
excerpt: Record the original decision, the reversal and the replacement separately, then verify which entries posted to the provider's account.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Document an Insurance Reversal and Replacement EOB After an Accident
metaDescription: Record the original decision, the reversal and the replacement separately, then verify which entries posted to the provider's account.
content:
The insurer reverses a claim after an accident and later issues a replacement explanation of benefits, or EOB. Treat the three events as separate entries. A reversal can undo the prior decision before the new determination reaches the provider. The amount currently due depends on the active decision and the posted ledger.

## Ask for the sequence from the insurer

Request the original and replacement references, processing dates and service lines, and ask which decision the reversal canceled. Record whether the new decision is final or a correction is still pending. Keep the earlier notices and the portal's current status. X12 describes a reversal and correction as separate entries in the standard remittance format, with one entry reversing the original and another showing the correction. [X12 guidance on electronic claim reversals and corrections](https://x12.org/resources/requests-for-interpretation/rfi-1733-835-reversals-and-corrections)

Ask the provider for the ledger entries tied to each insurer decision. Record the payment, contractual adjustment and patient responsibility as separate fields. Ask whether the carrier issued a payment, recovered an amount or netted it against another payment to the provider. A remittance record can help the billing office identify the transaction it posted. [CMS payment and remittance advice guide](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coding-billing/electronic-billing/health-care-payment-remittance-advice)

## Calculate the remaining balance from the active decision

Suppose the original decision shows the plan paying $120 and assigning $40 to the patient. The reversal cancels those amounts. The replacement shows the plan paying $90 and assigning $60. The active patient share in that illustration is $60, before credits from payments you already made. If you paid the original $40 and it remains posted to that service, ask the provider to confirm the remaining $20.

If only the reversal appears in the ledger, ask the office to check whether the replacement remittance arrived and whether it will issue a fresh statement. Save its response and the date.

When the insurer and provider use different references, ask each to identify the transaction date and service line. Keep the pair of references together so you can match the corrected notice to the updated account.

## Label the final version and the unresolved steps

Use the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) to record processing and posting as separate dates. If the insurer kept the same claim number, [confirm which revision is active](/articles/two-revised-eobs-same-claim-number). If the hospital still says the claim is pending, [ask which decision has reached its billing system](/articles/hospital-insurance-pending-eob-processed).

title: A New Adjuster Asked for Records You Already Submitted
excerpt: Show the earlier delivery, confirm what the new adjuster can see, and resend only the records needed through an approved channel.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A New Adjuster Asked for Records You Already Submitted
metaDescription: Show the earlier delivery, confirm what the new adjuster can see, and resend only the records needed through an approved channel.
content:
A new adjuster asks for the same photos or records you sent last week. Start with the receipt from your first submission. Give the new adjuster a way to find the documents and make it easy to identify anything the insurer still needs. A second submission can be useful when you label it as a copy and retain the earlier delivery history.

## Give the adjuster enough information to locate the first upload

Find the prior email or portal confirmation. Record the claim number, recipient, date, confirmation reference and the attachment names. Confirm the correct insurer contact before sharing files, particularly if the packet includes medical information. Use the insurer's secure portal or another channel the carrier confirms.

Washington requires claim files to contain enough detail to reconstruct relevant events and dates. The NAIC's auto claim guide also explains how to document the loss and follow up with the assigned adjuster. Keep your own delivery record so you can identify a specific submission during a handoff. [Washington claim-file documentation rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-340&full=true) · [NAIC guide to filing an auto claim](https://content.naic.org/article/what-you-should-know-about-filing-auto-claim)

## Send a request the adjuster can answer in one reply

A message might read, “On June 12 I uploaded the repair estimate dated June 10 and six passenger-side photos to claim 1234. The portal gave confirmation R57. Could you confirm which files are visible on your side and tell me which ones you need again?” If a file is genuinely missing, resend it and reference the first delivery in the message.

If the new adjuster actually needs a newer document, label it with the version or date. For example, send a revised estimate dated June 20 as a new version and state that the June 10 estimate was the earlier submission. Keep both if they explain why the amount changed.

## Record the handoff and the reply

Use the [Insurance Claim Follow-Up Email Builder](/tools/claim-follow-up-composer) to summarize the prior delivery and identify the action needed. Save any new confirmation alongside the old one. If the same file keeps being requested, [keep a log of each resend and acknowledgment](/articles/track-repeated-insurer-attachment-requests). If the new adjuster also lacks notes about prior decisions, [rebuild the handoff from the dated record](/articles/new-adjuster-missing-claim-notes).

title: How to Confirm a Spoken Policy Limit With the Adjuster in Writing
excerpt: Ask the insurer to identify the coverage, limit type and policy documents that support the dollar amount mentioned on the call.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Confirm a Spoken Policy Limit With the Adjuster in Writing
metaDescription: Ask the insurer to identify the coverage, limit type and policy documents that support the dollar amount mentioned on the call.
content:
The adjuster says “the limit is $50,000.” Follow up with a written request for the coverage and exact limit that statement refers to. A per-person bodily injury limit, a per-accident limit, a property damage limit and a proposed settlement amount describe different things. The claim number alone may not identify which one you discussed.

## Describe what you heard and request the underlying detail

Record the call date, adjuster and exact figure you understood. Ask which policy and coverage the figure belongs to, whether it is per person or per accident, and whether the carrier is describing the policy's stated limit or the amount currently available. Ask for the relevant declarations, coverage document or formal disclosure when available.

State insurance rules can give a claimant a formal way to ask. Florida Statutes § 627.4137, for example, describes a written request for a sworn statement from an insurer that does or may provide liability coverage and includes the limits of known policies in the required information. Use the rule that applies to your claim. [Florida liability coverage disclosure statute](https://www.leg.state.fl.us/Statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0600-0699%2F0627%2FSections%2F0627.4137.html)

## Keep a limit separate from an offer or a payment

For example, the adjuster mentions $50,000 on a call about bodily injury. Your follow-up can ask, “Was that the per-person bodily injury limit on the applicable policy, the amount you are offering on my claim, or a different figure? Please identify the coverage and confirm the limit in writing.” If other claims share the coverage, ask how the insurer distinguishes the policy limit from what it says is available.

The Texas Department of Insurance's consumer guide explains separate auto coverages and policy limits. Use the actual policy and confirmation to record what applies in your case. [Texas Department of Insurance auto insurance guide](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/pubs/consumer/cb020.html)

If the reply gives a single figure, ask the insurer to identify the unit. For bodily injury, a limit tied to one person can differ from the total available for the accident. Record each figure with the insurer's label and keep an offer or payment on its own line.

## Keep the written record with the call note

Use the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) to record the original conversation and the insurer's reply as separate entries. If the insurer also mentioned a cutoff for responding, [ask it to confirm the offer's expiration date](/articles/insurance-offer-expires-no-date-in-letter). If a check arrived with an unclear description, [verify the coverage associated with the payment](/articles/ask-adjuster-which-coverage-check-pays).

title: The Adjuster Says the Offer Expires but the Letter Has No Date
excerpt: Get the active offer's exact response deadline, time zone, terms and method of acceptance in writing before relying on it.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Adjuster Says the Offer Expires but the Letter Has No Date
metaDescription: Get the active offer's exact response deadline, time zone, terms and method of acceptance in writing before relying on it.
content:
An adjuster says an offer expires soon, but the letter gives no date. Ask which offer version is active and when a response must reach the insurer. An offer deadline, a policy deadline and a deadline to sue belong on separate lines in your record.

## Request the specific cutoff and the document that sets it

Write down when the adjuster mentioned expiration and which letter or figure the call concerned. Ask for the calendar date, local time and time zone. Ask whether the insurer requires a response, signed release or another document by that time, and how it measures receipt. Request the full current offer and any proposed release together.

A follow-up might say, “Your November 4 letter offers $8,000. On November 6 you mentioned a deadline. Please confirm the exact date, time and time zone for this version, the response method and any documents you require by then.” If you need more time to review, ask whether the insurer will agree to an extension and save any written confirmation.

## Track legal and policy dates on a separate timeline

Washington's claim settlement rule addresses written notice to certain unrepresented claimants when an applicable statute of limitations or policy or contract time limit may affect their rights during negotiations. It also addresses statements about the effect of a time limit for completing a third-party release or form. Check the rules and policy for your own claim. [Washington claim settlement standards](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-380)

California's code illustrates how filing periods depend on the claim. It has separate provisions for personal injury and for professional negligence by a health care provider. Track any applicable legal filing date separately from the deadline to accept the offer. Confirm both dates promptly when either is uncertain. [California personal injury filing provision](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-ccp/part-2/title-2/chapter-3/section-335-1/) · [California health care negligence filing provision](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-ccp/part-2/title-2/chapter-3/section-340-5/)

If the insurer gives you a new date after you ask for more time, save the confirmation and the version of the offer it covers. Ask which time zone applies if the offer closes at a stated hour.

## Save the date with the version you received

Use the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner) to record the deadline once the insurer confirms it. If the offer exists only in a phone call, [capture the amount, scope and proposed release terms](/articles/record-spoken-settlement-offer-before-release). If the adjuster described the amount as a policy limit, [request a separate written confirmation of the limit](/articles/confirm-adjuster-policy-limit-in-writing).

title: What to Say When an Adjuster Asks About a Speed You Did Not See
excerpt: Describe the motion and landmarks you actually observed, identify any estimate as such and separate the posted limit from actual speed.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: What to Say When an Adjuster Asks About a Speed You Did Not See
metaDescription: Describe the motion and landmarks you actually observed, identify any estimate as such and separate the posted limit from actual speed.
content:
The adjuster asks how fast another car was going. You saw it enter the intersection but could not measure its speed. Say what you observed and where your observation began. Explain the limits of your view, then provide the details you can support.

## Describe the observation in sequence

Give your location, line of sight, the direction of travel and the first point where you saw the vehicle. Note whether a parked car or another obstacle blocked the earlier approach. Separate what you saw from what you heard from another witness or later read in a report. The National Institute of Justice's eyewitness evidence guide describes collecting and recording a witness's recollection. That distinction helps keep an insurance account clear too. [NIJ guide to eyewitness evidence](https://ojp.gov/library/publications/eyewitness-evidence-guide-law-enforcement)

A response could be, “I saw the blue car enter the intersection from the east when I was stopped at the line. A van blocked my view of the approach. I couldn't determine its speed. I saw it pass the crosswalk before the impact.” If you can describe an interval or landmark without measuring speed, give the detail and identify it as an observation.

## Identify the source of any number

If you know the posted limit, label it as the limit. If an officer or expert estimated speed, give the source and the date of the estimate. A dashcam recording can preserve what happened and may support a later analysis if timing and other inputs are verified. NHTSA's Model Minimum Uniform Crash Criteria illustrates how crash data distinguish separate facts and how reporting fields can vary by jurisdiction. [NHTSA crash data guidance](https://www.nhtsa.gov/traffic-records/model-minimum-uniform-crash-criteria)

If the adjuster repeats a number you did not give, ask them to note the correction and identify the source. Preserve your original account and the relevant photo or recording without changing it.

## Keep the observation with the supporting evidence

Use the [accident witness questions tool](/tools/witness-interview-planner) to organize position, visibility and sequence. If a dispute turns on what fact the carrier accepts, [ask it to identify the disputed facts and supporting records](/articles/ask-insurer-disputed-accident-facts). If a transcript adds a number you didn't say, [check exactly what a correction form would certify](/articles/before-signing-recorded-statement-correction).

title: How to Correct an Approximate Date in a Recorded Accident Statement
excerpt: Identify the original statement, explain what changed about the date, and ask the insurer to attach the clarification to the file.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Correct an Approximate Date in a Recorded Accident Statement
metaDescription: Identify the original statement, explain what changed about the date, and ask the insurer to attach the clarification to the file.
content:
During a recorded call you said the accident happened “around May 12.” Later you found a dated record showing May 10. Send a focused clarification with the source and the date of the call. Keeping the original estimate and the corrected information together lets the adjuster understand why the dates differ.

## Identify the statement and the source of the new date

Locate the claim number, date of the recording and the question or passage you want to clarify. Request a copy or relevant excerpt if available. Identify the contemporaneous record that supports the date, such as a police report, dispatch record or original photo. Keep the original file and note where it came from. NIST's digital evidence guidance explains the value of preserving files and recording how they were obtained. [NIST digital evidence preservation guidance](https://www.nist.gov/publications/digital-evidence-preservation-considerations-evidence-handlers)

A notice might say, “On the June 3 recorded call I estimated the accident date as May 12 because I was speaking from memory. The police report dated May 10 identifies the collision as occurring on May 10. Please add this clarification and the attached report to the statement record.” Give a date range instead if the evidence only narrows the timing.

## Ask the insurer to show where it applied the correction

Ask for acknowledgment that the note was added and whether the claim's loss date field needs an update. If the date affects the coverage period, a deadline or the link to another record, ask the adjuster to confirm the active date used in the decision. Washington's claim-file rule illustrates why records should allow relevant events and dates to be reconstructed. For eligible first-party requests, it also describes access to certain statements and other records, subject to exceptions. [Washington claim-file documentation rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-340&full=true)

Keep the date of your correction and the loss date in separate fields. If a second document repeats the earlier date, identify that document in the same message and ask how the insurer will associate your clarification with it.

## Preserve both versions and the supporting document

Use the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) to record the date of the accident, the statement and the correction separately. If the insurer asks you to sign a correction, [check which version it would certify](/articles/before-signing-recorded-statement-correction). If the issue came from the adjuster's written recap, [compare the recap with your contemporaneous notes](/articles/compare-adjuster-recap-original-call-notes).

title: How to Ask Which Insurance Coverage a Check Was Paid Under
excerpt: Match the check number to the payer's claim and coverage line, then ask which amount it pays and what remains unresolved.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Ask Which Insurance Coverage a Check Was Paid Under
metaDescription: Match the check number to the payer's claim and coverage line, then ask which amount it pays and what remains unresolved.
content:
An insurer sends a check with the claim number but a generic description. Ask the adjuster to identify which coverage and loss it pays. One accident may involve separate payments for vehicle damage, bodily injury or medical expenses. The check number and a written explanation are useful for following the payment through the claim file.

## Match the check to the payment record

Record the insurer, claim number, check or transaction number, issue date, amount and payee. Ask for the payment explanation or itemization. Have the adjuster identify the coverage, bills or repairs included, any deductible or adjustment, and whether the payment is partial or final for that item. Ask for any documents the insurer says accompany the check.

Texas's auto insurance guide distinguishes liability, collision, medical payments, personal injury protection and uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage. California's auto claim guide describes why some checks may also name a lender or repair facility. Review the specific policy and payment record for your claim. [Texas auto coverage guide](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/pubs/consumer/cb020.html) · [California auto claim guide](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/105-type/95-guides/01-auto/hadaccident.cfm)

## Ask one question that resolves the ambiguity

For example, a $1,400 check arrives after you sent both a repair estimate and medical bills. A message can say, “Please confirm whether check 318 for $1,400 is for vehicle damage or another coverage. Which claim line does it pay, and is there a remaining amount under that coverage?” Keep the actual check or image and the response in the same record.

If a release or full-settlement wording appears on or with the payment, check what it covers before accepting any terms. Confirm the status of other pending payments separately.

Compare the amount with the estimate or benefit statement after you have identified the coverage. Ask for an itemization if the check pays more than one line or includes a deductible adjustment. If it is payable to you and a repair shop or lender, confirm what both payees need to do.

## Record the check on the correct line

Use the [Insurance Claim Cash Flow Planner](/tools/claim-cashflow-calendar) to track when each payment was issued and received. If the adjuster mentioned a policy limit while discussing it, [confirm the limit and coverage in writing](/articles/confirm-adjuster-policy-limit-in-writing). If the payment identifies a different car, [verify the vehicle and claim reference](/articles/adjuster-claim-number-wrong-vehicle). If a fee applies to only one part of a settlement, [allocate the fee using the signed agreement and payment references](/articles/calculate-settlement-fee-one-coverage-payment).

title: The Adjuster Asked for Your Full Medical History for One Injury Date
excerpt: Ask which records, providers and dates the adjuster needs and review the scope of any authorization before signing it.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Adjuster Asked for Your Full Medical History for One Injury Date
metaDescription: Ask which records, providers and dates the adjuster needs and review the scope of any authorization before signing it.
content:
You reported an injury from one accident, and the adjuster asks for a release covering your full medical history. Ask which part of the claim the insurer is evaluating and which records it needs to do so. The practical issue is the scope of the request and how it relates to the actual injury and policy.

## Get the request and form together

Ask the adjuster to identify the injury, provider, date range and type of record requested. For example, it may be seeking the emergency visit, follow-up treatment or earlier care for the same area of the body. Request the actual form and a written explanation of any policy requirement and deadline it is relying on.

When a covered health provider needs a HIPAA authorization to disclose information, the federal rule lists elements that include a meaningful description of the information, who may disclose and receive it, the purpose and an expiration date or event.
