Compare those fields with the insurer's stated request. HHS explains how an authorization permits specified disclosures. [45 CFR § 164.508](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-E/section-164.508) · [HHS guide to authorization](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/what-is-the-difference-between-consent-and-authorization/index.html)

## Check whether a narrower packet answers the question

For an illustration, the carrier says it needs the emergency department note from June 9 and the orthopedist's follow-up note. The form names all providers over ten years. Ask whether those two records, a specified date range or a narrower authorization would meet the request. If the carrier says it needs additional records, ask which issue they would address.

Keep copies of any records sent and the signed version of any authorization. If the insurer treats signing as a condition of benefits, or if litigation or sensitive information is involved, get case-specific advice about scope and any response deadline.

Ask the adjuster which recipient will receive the records and how the files should be delivered. Use the verified secure upload route when the records include sensitive details, and keep a dated confirmation for the claim file.

## Keep an index of the records and recipients

Use the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) to list the providers and dates under discussion. If the insurer also asks to speak to your employer, [clarify which wage and schedule details it wants](/articles/adjuster-employer-interview-missed-work). If a billing record identifies the wrong member, [verify the patient fields with the provider and plan](/articles/accident-bill-processed-wrong-plan-member).

title: What to Do When a New Adjuster Has Missing Claim Notes
excerpt: Rebuild the claim handoff with dated records, then ask the new adjuster to confirm which decisions and follow-ups are still active.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: What to Do When a New Adjuster Has Missing Claim Notes
metaDescription: Rebuild the claim handoff with dated records, then ask the new adjuster to confirm which decisions and follow-ups are still active.
content:
The new adjuster can see your claim number but cannot find an earlier approval or a promise to call back. Send a brief handoff that separates the actions you can prove from the ones you still need the insurer to confirm. The most useful handoff gives the new adjuster an exact place to look and one decision to make.

## Reconstruct the events that affect the next decision

Make a three-column record with the date, the action and the evidence for it. For instance, June 4 was the original inspection, June 10 was the shop's supplement upload and June 12 was the former adjuster's call. Attach the inspection report or confirmation if you have it. Describe an oral promise as a dated recollection, and identify any decision you received by email as written.

In Washington, insurers' claim files must contain enough detail to reconstruct relevant events and dates. The rule also gives insureds access to portions of their first-party claim file at reasonable intervals, subject to exceptions for certain records or information. Ask the insurer what records it can provide for your claim and which version of a document is active. [Washington claim-file documentation rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-340&full=true)

## Ask for confirmation at the point where work stopped

In a hypothetical repair claim, the shop's $780 supplement has a delivery receipt and the former adjuster said it was being reviewed. You could write, “The shop sent supplement S2 on June 10, confirmation R173. On June 12 I was told it was under review. Can you confirm that S2 is in the file and tell me its current status and who will handle the next decision?” Add the repair shop's contact only when it helps the reviewer take that step.

If the missing note involved an approval, ask for the approved estimate or amount. If it involved a deadline, confirm the date separately. The NAIC recommends gathering dated records of communications if you need to escalate an insurance complaint. [NAIC complaint documentation guide](https://content.naic.org/consumer/how-to-file-complaint)

## Save the replacement handoff beside the original records

Use the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) to connect each event to its receipt, letter or call note. When the issue is a missing attachment, [give the new adjuster the original upload reference](/articles/new-adjuster-asks-for-already-submitted-records). If the new recap changes a decision, [compare it with your contemporaneous notes](/articles/compare-adjuster-recap-original-call-notes) before updating your timeline.

title: How to Follow Up on a Repair Supplement With No Response
excerpt: Find the shop’s delivery record, confirm the insurer received the correct revision, and ask for a decision or inspection date.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Follow Up on a Repair Supplement With No Response
metaDescription: Find the shop’s delivery record, confirm the insurer received the correct revision, and ask for a decision or inspection date.
content:
Your repair shop found more damage, sent a revised estimate and is waiting for the insurer to respond. Ask the shop for a copy of the exact supplement and its delivery record. Then direct your follow-up at the current reviewer and ask which item is holding up a decision.

## Find the revision the insurer should be reviewing

A supplement is a revised repair request that can include additional damage, parts or labor identified after the first estimate. Record the revision number and submission date. Ask the shop whether the amount shown is the new total or the increase over the approved estimate. Texas's insurance department explains that a shop can send a new estimate for additional repairs and that the insurer pays for the extra work if it agrees with the estimate. [Texas Department of Insurance auto claims guide](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/tips/what-to-do-after-a-wreck.html)

Check the attachment list for teardown photos, parts prices and labor notes. Ask the shop whether it is waiting to order parts, continue work or schedule a reinspection. That helps you explain the practical consequence of the delay.

## Give the reviewer one specific request

Suppose the first estimate is $2,460 and revision S2 adds $640 for a damaged bracket and related labor. You could write, “Shop B submitted supplement S2 on June 10 under claim 4218. Please confirm it is assigned to a reviewer. Can you tell us when to expect an itemized response, or give the shop a date for reinspection?” Include the delivery confirmation if you have it.

California's auto claims regulation has separate provisions for insurer inspections or reinspections in response to a supplement and for requests for photos or estimates. Check the provision that applies to your claim and use the actual date the insurer received the request. [California supplemental estimate standards](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-2695.8)

## Track the decision by line item

Ask for the approved amount and the items still open if the insurer accepts only part of the revision. Confirm the instructions for the shop in writing and save the new estimate alongside the earlier one. When a supplement is delayed by a missing image, [ask which photos the adjuster reviewed](/articles/photos-insurer-used-for-damage-estimate). If several documents remain outstanding, [send a short status list with an owner for each](/articles/missing-documents-insurance-claim-follow-up). Use the [auto repair estimate comparison tool](/tools/repair-quote-comparator) to align matching parts and labor across estimates.

title: How to Ask Which Photos the Insurer Used for a Repair Estimate
excerpt: Match the estimate to specific photos and damage areas, then ask the adjuster how to submit any missing views for review.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Ask Which Photos the Insurer Used for a Repair Estimate
metaDescription: Match the estimate to specific photos and damage areas, then ask the adjuster how to submit any missing views for review.
content:
You sent photos of your damaged car, but the estimate skips a panel that appears damaged in one of them. Ask the adjuster which files were used for that part of the estimate. A file name or a photo index gives you a better way to locate the gap than sending the entire album again.

## Tie your question to the estimate line

Write down the claim number, estimate date, vehicle and damage area. Identify the adjacent line or part if the affected item is missing. Keep any wide views that orient the reader, close-ups that show the damage and later shop photos taken after disassembly. Texas's insurance regulator recommends documenting accident damage and vehicle identifiers with photos when you can safely do so. [Texas Department of Insurance photo guidance](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/tips/what-to-do-after-a-wreck.html)

Ask whether the estimate was based on your upload, an appraiser's inspection, photos from the shop or a combination. In Washington, an insured's right to request portions of a first-party claim file at reasonable intervals can include photographs, subject to the rule's disclosure exceptions. [Washington claim-file access rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-340&full=true)

## Show where the two records diverge

In a hypothetical rear impact, estimate E1 lists the bumper cover. Your wide view shows which corner was hit, and a shop close-up labeled S2-04 shows a cracked retainer visible after disassembly. You could write, “Which photos support the bumper line on E1? Can you confirm whether S2-04 was available to the reviewer and whether the shop should submit that retainer on a supplement?”

Preserve the original photos and use copies for arrows or crops. Label any image that shows the vehicle after a panel was removed so the reviewer can place it in sequence. Ask the shop to identify the part and whether the added damage affects its estimate.

## Turn the answer into a specific next step

Record whether the reviewer confirms the image was received, confirms it was considered or wants a different angle. Use the [Accident Photo Checklist](/tools/photo-documentation-planner) to record the view, part and filename. If the shop already sent its supplement, [follow up on the exact revision in the queue](/articles/follow-up-no-response-repair-supplement). If the insurer says the damage is unrelated to the loss, [ask which fact or evidence supports that conclusion](/articles/ask-insurer-disputed-accident-facts).

title: The Adjuster Said Your Claim Was Denied but the Portal Is Open
excerpt: Ask for the written decision and check exactly which coverage, repair or payment it affects while the portal still shows the file as open.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Adjuster Said Your Claim Was Denied but the Portal Is Open
metaDescription: Ask for the written decision and check exactly which coverage, repair or payment it affects while the portal still shows the file as open.
content:
An adjuster says your claim was denied. When you log in, the portal still says “open.” Ask the insurer to identify the coverage, expense or request it decided and to give you the dated decision. A portal can show a status for the whole file while the phone conversation concerns one part of it.

## Find out what the denial covers

Write down who called, when they called and the wording you remember. Use the policy and claim number to ask whether the decision concerns coverage, responsibility for the accident, one item on an estimate or another part of the claim. If property damage and rental are both under review, ask for the status of each.

California's fair claims regulation requires written denials or rejections of covered first-party claims with the applicable factual and legal bases, and addresses written denials, rejections or disputes over liability or damages for third-party claims. The regulation contains specific exceptions and qualifications. Washington has its own standards for first-party acceptance and denial, including written denials in the circumstances described in its rule. [California denial standards](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-2695.7) · [Washington claim settlement standards](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-380)

## Ask for the record you can act on

For example, an adjuster says “that was denied” after discussing a rental charge. The portal still displays a property-damage claim and an inspection appointment. You could write, “On July 8 I understood that the June 22 rental charge was denied. Please confirm whether the decision applies to that charge, the entire rental benefit or any other portion of claim 2719. Please send the dated decision and identify the provision or facts you relied on.”

Ask how to provide additional information or request review, and record any deadlines the insurer identifies. If a deadline is uncertain, check the policy, the dated correspondence and the applicable rules independently of the portal display. Save a dated screenshot of the status if it explains the mismatch.

## Keep a record of the answer

Use the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) for the call, the portal status and the eventual written response. If the insurer's decision relies on a point of disagreement about the crash, [ask the reviewer to identify the specific fact it disputes](/articles/ask-insurer-disputed-accident-facts). If the call came from a new adjuster, [rebuild the handoff from the earlier records](/articles/new-adjuster-missing-claim-notes).

title: How to Compare an Adjuster’s Call Recap With Your Notes
excerpt: Compare the written recap with your dated notes, identify material differences, and send the insurer a correction it can verify.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Compare an Adjuster’s Call Recap With Your Notes
metaDescription: Compare the written recap with your dated notes, identify material differences, and send the insurer a correction it can verify.
content:
You took notes during a call, then received an adjuster's recap that describes a different decision. Compare the two versions while the details are fresh. Focus on differences that could change an amount, a deadline, what you agreed to do or how the insurer understands the facts.

## Identify the speaker and the exact difference

Keep the original notes, the recap and the call date. For each issue, compare the recap's exact words, what you recorded at the time and any document that supports your recollection. Mark whether your notes contain a direct quote or a paraphrase. If the call had several people, identify who said what as accurately as you can.

For example, a recap says, “You agreed the shop would absorb the difference.” Your notes say you agreed to ask the shop to compare rates. The shop's later email can establish that it reviewed the rates, even if it cannot establish what the adjuster said. Keep both facts visible. Washington's claim-file rule describes the level of documentation needed to reconstruct relevant events and dates in insurer files. [Washington claim-file documentation rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-340&full=true)

## Correct the action the recap assigns to you

You could write, “In the July 8 recap, the second paragraph says I agreed the shop would absorb the difference. My notes show I agreed to ask for a rate breakdown. The shop sent that breakdown on July 9. Please confirm how you recorded my response and whether the additional labor charge is still under review.”

If an oral exchange cannot be verified, say which part you remember and ask for the version the insurer used. The NAIC recommends keeping dates, times and written records of insurer communications if you need to raise the issue with a regulator. [NAIC guide to documenting a complaint](https://content.naic.org/consumer/how-to-file-complaint)

## Keep both records linked to the follow-up

The [claim statement comparison tool](/tools/statement-version-comparator) can help you place the recap and your notes side by side. Keep the sent correction and any acknowledgment with both originals. For a date in a recorded statement, [attach the record that supports the corrected date](/articles/correct-date-recorded-accident-statement). If the insurer sends a transcript correction for signature, [check exactly what the signature would confirm](/articles/before-signing-recorded-statement-correction).

title: What to Ask Before Signing a Recorded Statement Correction
excerpt: Check whether the form confirms a transcript edit, adopts the full statement, or includes a separate agreement before you sign it.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: What to Ask Before Signing a Recorded Statement Correction
metaDescription: Check whether the form confirms a transcript edit, adopts the full statement, or includes a separate agreement before you sign it.
content:
An insurer sends you a correction page after you flag an error in a recorded statement. Read the language next to the signature and ask for the full version the insurer would keep. A page that identifies one correction can also refer to other pages or contain additional terms.

## Identify the exact text covered by the signature

Ask for the original transcript, the corrected page and, if available, the corresponding audio excerpt. Record the recording date, page, line and question. Say whether the transcript captured the wrong word or whether you gave an answer that you now need to clarify. Those are different entries in a record.

For example, the transcript might say “I saw him cross before I moved” when the recording says “I saw him cross after I moved.” In another case, the transcript may be accurate but a timestamp gives you a better date. The first question is whether the transcript matches the audio. The second is how the insurer attaches your later clarification to the original answer. Washington's first-party claim-file rule gives eligible insureds a route to ask for statements and related records, subject to its exceptions. [Washington claim-file access rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-340&full=true)

## Ask what the rest of the form does

Read the document as a whole, including referenced pages. If it refers to a certification, authorization or release, ask the insurer to specify its effect and whether the correction can be made on a separate form. California Civil Code § 1641 provides an example of a state rule that reads the parts of a contract together. For a form affecting substantive rights, confirm the applicable law and wording before signing. [California rule on reading a contract as a whole](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-civ/division-3/part-2/title-3/section-1641/)

A request might read, “Please confirm whether the signature applies only to the change on page 3, line 12, or to the complete statement and any attached terms. Please send the complete corrected version you intend to keep.”

## Save the version that actually goes into the file

Use the [claim statement comparison tool](/tools/statement-version-comparator) to mark the changed words. Save the signed copy, attachments and delivery confirmation together if you send it. For a factual date correction, [link the supporting record to the specific answer](/articles/correct-date-recorded-accident-statement). If the issue began with a recap rather than a transcript, [compare the recap against your original notes](/articles/compare-adjuster-recap-original-call-notes).

title: How to List Missing Documents in an Insurance Claim Follow-Up
excerpt: Send a short status list that distinguishes documents you owe, uploads awaiting confirmation, and records someone else must provide.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to List Missing Documents in an Insurance Claim Follow-Up
metaDescription: Send a short status list that distinguishes documents you owe, uploads awaiting confirmation, and records someone else must provide.
content:
An adjuster says documents are missing, but several people have been sending files. Turn the request into a status list with a separate entry for each record. Identify who has it, when it moved and the action that will get it to the reviewer.

## Give each document an owner and a status

Use the document name, service or issue date, sender, delivery reference and current status. A document can be ready to send, sent with delivery confirmed, sent with receipt pending, or still being prepared by someone else. Ask the insurer to distinguish a missing attachment from a file it received but could not open or use.

Keep the list in the body of your message. Reference an approved upload location for sensitive attachments and keep the full identifiers in the insurer's secure channel. The NAIC's complaint guide recommends gathering bills, records and a dated record of communications. Those same records make it easier to answer a follow-up request before escalation. [NAIC complaint documentation checklist](https://content.naic.org/consumer/how-to-file-complaint)

## Write the next action into the message

Suppose a claim needs three items. Your message could say, “Claim 5231. The July 9 repair estimate was uploaded on July 10, receipt Q42. Please confirm it opens. The July 12 supplemental photos are with the repair shop, which expects to upload them Friday. Please confirm whether you need the June 28 invoice or the June 28 payment receipt so I can send the right file.”

If the missing item is holding up only one part of the claim, ask the adjuster to name that part. In Washington, a claims communication that reasonably calls for a response is subject to the applicable reply standard under WAC 284-30-360. The rule distinguishes individual policies from group contracts. [Washington claims communication standard](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=284-30-360&full=true)

## Close each item when you have a receipt or decision

Add the insurer's answer beside the item it addresses. Use the [Insurance Claim Follow-Up Email Builder](/tools/claim-follow-up-composer) to draft the next request from the remaining entries. If the same attachment appears on another missing list, [link each resend to the original receipt](/articles/track-repeated-insurer-attachment-requests). For a revised estimate that is already in the insurer's queue, [ask for its review or inspection date](/articles/follow-up-no-response-repair-supplement).

title: The Adjuster Gave You a Claim Number for the Wrong Vehicle
excerpt: Verify the claim and vehicle through the insurer, then check where existing photos, estimates and payments were recorded before resending anything.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Adjuster Gave You a Claim Number for the Wrong Vehicle
metaDescription: Verify the claim and vehicle through the insurer, then check where existing photos, estimates and payments were recorded before resending anything.
content:
The adjuster gives you a claim number, but the portal shows a different vehicle. Pause the transfer of documents and confirm the correct file with the insurer through a known phone number or its official portal. Ask whether the number is attached to the wrong vehicle or whether one accident is being tracked under multiple file references.

## Match the claim to the vehicle and loss

Have your policy number, loss date and the vehicle's year, make and model ready. Compare the last digits of the vehicle identification number with the estimate and insurance documents. Send the full identifier only through the insurer's approved channel if it needs it. Texas's regulator recommends gathering identifying information and documenting each vehicle after a crash. [Texas Department of Insurance accident checklist](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/tips/what-to-do-after-a-wreck.html)

Ask the insurer to confirm the active file reference for each affected vehicle and coverage. Use contact details from your policy or the carrier's official site if the unexpected number arrived by email or text. The FTC advises using a phone number or website you know is genuine when checking an unexpected message. [FTC guide to verifying unexpected messages](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-avoid-scam)

## Ask what happens to the records already sent

For example, you own two gray cars and an estimate for the hatchback appears under the sedan's reference. You could write, “Please confirm the active claim number for the July 3 loss involving the 2021 hatchback. Estimate E7 and four photos were uploaded under the number I was given. Can you confirm which file holds those records and tell me whether you can associate them with the correct vehicle?”

If a payment has already been issued, ask the insurer to verify the vehicle, coverage and payment reference before you act on it. If you see information that belongs to another person, report the mismatch using a verified contact and avoid forwarding the other person's documents.

## Save the old and new references as separate entries

Record the confirmed claim number, the correction date and what the insurer says it moved. Keep your earlier delivery receipt with the corrected record in the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger). If the mix-up followed a transfer to a new reviewer, [reconstruct the prior claim notes](/articles/new-adjuster-missing-claim-notes). If a check has an unclear purpose, [ask which coverage it was issued under](/articles/ask-adjuster-which-coverage-check-pays).

title: How to Track Repeated Requests to Resend a Claim Attachment
excerpt: Connect each resend to the original file and delivery record, then ask the insurer whether it can open and associate the attachment.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Track Repeated Requests to Resend a Claim Attachment
metaDescription: Connect each resend to the original file and delivery record, then ask the insurer whether it can open and associate the attachment.
content:
The insurer asks for the same attachment a third time. Find your first confirmation and send a dated record that distinguishes delivery, successful opening and assignment to the claim. Each of those can fail at a different point. Your next message should help the insurer tell you which one happened.

## Keep a receipt for each transfer

Create one row per attempt with the date, channel, recipient, file name, version and confirmation number. If a portal lists the upload, keep a screenshot showing its status and date. Record a rejection notice or file-size error beside the attempt. For a sensitive document, use the verified secure route the insurer gives you.

NIST's guidance on digital evidence describes preserving files and documenting their origin and handling. In an ordinary claim, keeping the file you actually sent and its delivery receipt gives you a stable record to compare with later copies. The NAIC also recommends retaining the correspondence and dates when documenting a complaint. [NIST guidance on digital evidence preservation](https://www.nist.gov/publications/digital-evidence-preservation-considerations-evidence-handlers) · [NAIC complaint preparation guide](https://content.naic.org/consumer/how-to-file-complaint)

## Ask which step needs to be repeated

Here is a hypothetical example. The first portal upload of Invoice-June12.pdf gave receipt U18. A second upload gave U44. The adjuster can see U44 but says the attachment is password protected. Instead of uploading the same copy again, confirm an approved way to provide a readable version. Keep it under a distinct filename and note which earlier upload it replaces.

You could ask, “Can you confirm whether Invoice-June12.pdf was received, opens successfully and is attached to the June 12 service under claim 3149? The upload references are U18 and U44. Please tell me if a different format or upload route is needed.”

When a third party sent the file, ask that sender for its receipt. Give the reviewer the sender's name and submission date so it can search under the right account or contact.

## Mark the issue closed when the reviewer confirms the file

Use the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) to record the insurer's response and which version is active. If someone else took over the file, [use the original receipt to orient the new adjuster](/articles/new-adjuster-asks-for-already-submitted-records). If the insurer is missing several different records, [send one status list for all open documents](/articles/missing-documents-insurance-claim-follow-up) and attach only the files it has identified.

title: How to Ask an Insurer Which Accident Facts It Disputes
excerpt: Ask the insurer to identify the specific fact behind its decision so you can provide evidence that answers that point.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Ask an Insurer Which Accident Facts It Disputes
metaDescription: Ask the insurer to identify the specific fact behind its decision so you can provide evidence that answers that point.
content:
An insurer says it disputes liability or disagrees with your version of the accident. Ask it to name the exact fact in question and explain how that fact affects its position. A disagreement about which lane a car occupied calls for a different response from a disagreement about when the damage happened.

## Turn a broad objection into a question you can verify

Separate three issues. Ask what the insurer believes happened, what records it relied on, and what decision followed. If its decision covers several issues, ask for an itemized response. Describe any evidence you have by name and date so the adjuster can identify it in the claim file.

California's fair claims rule addresses written notices for third-party disputes over liability or damages and factual and legal grounds for first-party denials. Washington's unfair claims practices rule includes standards for reasonable investigation and for explaining the policy basis in relation to the facts or applicable law when denying a claim or offering a compromise settlement. Which standard applies depends on the claim and jurisdiction. [California fair claims standard](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/10-CCR-2695.7) · [Washington unfair claims practices rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-330)

## Send the evidence that answers the question

Suppose the insurer says it cannot confirm where the impact happened. You might write, “Is the issue the lane I occupied before contact, the point where the vehicles touched, or the place the cars stopped afterward? The scene diagram and the two photos taken before the cars moved are in upload R32. Please confirm which fact is disputed and whether you have reviewed those records.”

If the insurer identifies a conflicting statement, ask for the substance and what records it can provide. Describe which facts your evidence directly shows. A photo of the final position, for example, can support where a vehicle stopped. An earlier position may need a separate record or analysis.

## Build a response that mirrors the dispute

Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to put the disputed fact beside the record that addresses it. Keep dates and references so the reviewer can find the originals. If the dispute concerns speed you could not see, [state where your observations begin and end](/articles/adjuster-asks-speed-you-did-not-see). If the decision was communicated by phone, [request the written decision and the coverage it affects](/articles/adjuster-verbal-denial-claim-portal-open).

title: How to Record a Spoken Settlement Offer Before Seeing the Release
excerpt: Document the amount, coverage and conditions you heard, then request the complete written offer and release so you can review their scope.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Record a Spoken Settlement Offer Before Seeing the Release
metaDescription: Document the amount, coverage and conditions you heard, then request the complete written offer and release so you can review their scope.
content:
An adjuster names a dollar amount by phone and says paperwork will follow. Record what you heard and ask for the exact written terms. The amount, the scope of the release and the process for payment each need their own confirmation.

## Record the offer while the call is fresh

Write down the date, name of the person who made the offer, insurer, claim number, coverage and stated amount. Mark whether the figure was described as gross or as a payment after a deduction. Note any deadline, named payee or condition the adjuster mentioned, and keep track of which points still need confirmation.

A hypothetical note might say, “On July 15 the adjuster mentioned $4,600 to resolve the property-damage claim. They said paperwork would follow. I still need to confirm who would sign, which claim or coverage would be released, and how payment would be issued.” Use a dated record if you later need to show what was communicated. The NAIC recommends keeping insurer correspondence and call dates for complaints. [NAIC guide to documenting claim communications](https://content.naic.org/consumer/how-to-file-complaint)

## Ask for the full terms and supporting documents

You could reply, “Please send the complete written offer and proposed release, including all attachments. Please identify which claim and coverage the $4,600 applies to, the parties and claims named in the release, and any deadline or payment conditions.”

Read the proposed release together with any definitions and incorporated pages. California's Civil Code provides an example of a state contract interpretation rule that reads provisions together. If prior words or actions might have legal consequences, record them accurately and get advice on the applicable law. [California rule on reading the contract as a whole](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-civ/division-3/part-2/title-3/section-1641/)

## Record changes from the spoken to the written version

Keep the first note when the written terms arrive. Put the new amount, affected coverage and conditions in a second entry with the written date. If a term differs, ask which version the insurer intends to offer and request the correction in writing. Use the [Insurance Settlement Offer Tracker](/tools/offer-progression-log) to track each version. If the insurer mentioned an expiration without a date, [ask for the exact time and terms of the offer](/articles/insurance-offer-expires-no-date-in-letter). For multiple coverage payments, [check which payment enters the fee calculation](/articles/calculate-settlement-fee-one-coverage-payment).

title: What to Ask Before an Adjuster Interviews Your Employer
excerpt: Identify the dates and wage facts the adjuster needs, then confirm who will respond and what any permission to contact your employer covers.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: What to Ask Before an Adjuster Interviews Your Employer
metaDescription: Identify the dates and wage facts the adjuster needs, then confirm who will respond and what any permission to contact your employer covers.
content:
An insurance adjuster wants to interview your employer about missed work. Ask which dates and facts the reviewer needs to verify. A payroll question about hours paid calls for different information from a question about work restrictions or a return-to-work schedule.

## Identify which employment records answer the request

Ask whether the insurer needs dates absent, hours scheduled, hours worked, pay rate, payroll amounts or the use of paid leave. Ask whether a signed verification from payroll or human resources would answer the request and whether the insurer has a form. Identify the person who can verify each field.

The federal recordkeeping regulation lists the hours and wage data employers generally maintain for employees covered by that part of the FLSA rules. California's lost-earnings jury instruction is an example of the distinction between establishing earnings lost to date and establishing reasonably certain future lost earnings. Use the records that match the question in your claim. [Federal wage and hour recordkeeping rule](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-V/subchapter-A/part-516/subpart-A/section-516.2) · [California lost-earnings jury instruction](https://www.justia.com/trials-litigation/docs/caci/3900/3903c/)

## Read any permission form and define the scope

For example, you missed 18 scheduled hours over three days. Your timecard shows eight hours were charged to paid leave, while ten hours were unpaid. Ask payroll to confirm both entries. Ask the adjuster if the request covers those three dates or a longer period needed to establish your usual schedule. If the employer also holds health-related information, separate the wage records from any request for clinical information. HHS explains how HIPAA generally treats employment records and disclosures by covered health providers differently. [HHS guidance on employers and health information](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-individuals/employers-health-information-workplace/index.html)

You could write, “Please list the dates, the wage fields you need and who will contact payroll. Can the employer answer in writing using our timecards and pay stubs? Please send the proposed authorization so I can review the recipient, scope and duration.”

## Save the verification and reconcile it with payroll

Use the [Hourly Lost Wages Calculator](/tools/hourly-lost-work-calculator) to organize the hours and pay inputs, then compare them with the employer's reply and the pay period. If the request also includes medical files, [identify the scope of the medical authorization separately](/articles/adjuster-requests-full-medical-history). If the insurer questions why the absence was included, [ask which fact it wants verified](/articles/ask-insurer-disputed-accident-facts).

title: Why a Filing Fee Was Deducted From Only One Settlement Payment
excerpt: Trace the filing fee to its receipt and check how it was allocated across payments and reflected in the attorney fee calculation.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Why a Filing Fee Was Deducted From Only One Settlement Payment
metaDescription: Trace the filing fee to its receipt and check how it was allocated across payments and reflected in the attorney fee calculation.
content:
Your case settled through two payments. The first settlement statement deducts the full court filing fee, while the second has no filing fee line. Check the actual cost and how it was assigned before comparing the checks. A single cost can be collected from one payment while still belonging to the case as a whole.

## Trace the charge from the court receipt to the statement

Find the receipt or cost ledger entry. Record the court, filing date, amount, case number and who paid it. Ask the firm to show whether it advanced the charge and whether the other disbursement contains any amount for the same receipt under a combined costs line.

The State Bar of California identifies filing fees as a type of litigation cost and describes questions about whether a client pays costs directly or reimburses costs the attorney advanced. California Business and Professions Code § 6147 also addresses what covered contingency agreements must say about how costs and disbursements affect the fee and recovery. [California State Bar guide to costs](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/public/legal-resources/working-attorney/what-expect-regarding-fees-and-billing) · [California contingency fee statute](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-bpc/division-3/chapter-4/article-8-5/section-6147/)

## Check the deduction and the fee base separately

Consider a hypothetical $12,000 first payment and $8,000 second payment. The firm advanced a $435 filing fee and recovers it from the first payment. The total case cost for that receipt is $435. With attorney fees left out of this example, the amounts after that cost are $11,565 and $8,000. Together they equal $19,565.

The calculation of the attorney fee is a separate check. If the agreement uses costs to adjust the fee base, ask which payment or total was used, and have the firm show the arithmetic. If the disbursements show a shared or prorated cost, compare the sum of the allocations with the invoice. Keep a clear reference from each portion back to the single underlying receipt.

## Ask for a reconciliation you can keep

Request both itemized statements and the reference showing the amount collected against the receipt. Use the [Settlement Deduction Questions](/tools/deduction-question-builder) to list the cost, supporting document and remaining question. If you paid the filing fee yourself, [separate prepaid costs from sums reimbursed at closing](/articles/calculate-settlement-net-costs-already-paid). If only one coverage payment is subject to the contingency fee, [check the scope of that fee separately](/articles/calculate-settlement-fee-one-coverage-payment).

title: A Provider Balance Remains After a Settlement Lien Was Resolved
excerpt: Match the lien satisfaction to the provider’s itemized bill to see which charges it covered and why another balance appears.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Provider Balance Remains After a Settlement Lien Was Resolved
metaDescription: Match the lien satisfaction to the provider’s itemized bill to see which charges it covered and why another balance appears.
content:
Your closing statement says a medical lien was resolved, yet it also lists an unpaid provider balance. Compare the lien paperwork with the itemized bill by account and date of service. The entries could reflect different services, a posting delay, or the same balance appearing twice. The documents should show which explanation fits.

## Identify the obligation each document describes

Start with the lien notice, payoff agreement or release, proof of payment and current provider statement. Write down the provider name, account number, services and dates covered by the resolution. Ask whether the document satisfies the lien against the recovery, resolves the underlying account as well, or covers only the listed lines. Compare the text with the release and the provider's current ledger.

California Civil Code § 3045.1 is an example of a statute covering eligible hospital liens against damages recovered in qualifying cases. The California Supreme Court in Parnell addressed the connection between that lien and an underlying debt in the circumstances of that case. Confirm which law or agreement governs the actual claim. [California hospital lien statute](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-civ/division-3/part-4/title-14/chapter-4/section-3045-1/) · [Parnell v. Adventist Health](https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/parnell-v-adventist-health-33509/)

## Ask for the balance by service date

In a hypothetical example, the $2,100 payment satisfied an agreement for the hospital's May 12 emergency department account. The closing statement also shows $260 for a May 12 radiology interpretation with a different billing entity. Ask whether that is a separate professional bill and request the matching notice from the insurer if applicable. If the $260 instead refers to the same hospital account covered by the agreement, ask where the payoff and any adjustment were posted. CMS explains how to check the provider, service and payments on a bill. [CMS guide to reading a medical bill](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

## Keep the payoff and residual balance on different rows

Record what was paid, what was written off and what remains claimed. Ask who is expecting the residual payment and whether any sum is being held for it. Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) if the insurer processed the services. If a balance was waived, [record the waiver separately from the payoff](/articles/track-waived-medical-charges-separate-repayment). If a disputed amount is in trust, [request a breakdown of what was released and what remains held](/articles/disputed-lien-held-in-trust-partial-disbursement).

title: How to Reconcile a Settlement Check With Your Trust Ledger
excerpt: Match the insurer’s payment, attorney fees, case costs, liens and any holdback to your client ledger and final disbursement.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Reconcile a Settlement Check With Your Trust Ledger
metaDescription: Match the insurer’s payment, attorney fees, case costs, liens and any holdback to your client ledger and final disbursement.
content:
Your settlement check is smaller than the gross payment on the insurer's letter. Ask for the client-specific trust accounting and compare it with the settlement statement. The statement explains the intended split. The ledger shows the dated transactions and the funds that remain on hold.

## Identify the deposits that funded your case

Record each payer, gross amount, payment reference and date the money reached the firm. Keep different coverages on different rows. Ask the firm to explain any deposit that is still pending, a credit paid directly to you, or a payment that went to another authorized payee.

California's professional conduct rules require lawyers to keep records of funds and property held under Rule 1.15 and to provide appropriate written accountings. The State Bar's trust accounting handbook includes examples and explains recordkeeping practices. Ask for the accounting that applies to your case and the rules that govern it. [California Rule 1.15](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/rules/rules-professional-conduct/current-rules-professional-conduct/chapter-1-lawyer-client-relationship) · [California State Bar client trust accounting handbook](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/maintaining-compliance/client-trust-accounting-iolta/client-trust-accounting-handbook)

## Compare each distribution with the money that moved

Consider a hypothetical $30,000 deposit. The ledger records $9,000 to the firm for its fee, $450 in reimbursed case costs, $2,550 paid to a health plan, $16,000 paid to the client and $2,000 still held for a separate disputed item. The distributions total $28,000. The remaining $2,000 reconciles the ledger to the deposit. For this example, the client's check is $16,000 and the possible future payment depends on how the held funds are resolved.

Check the fee against the agreement and each reimbursement against the supporting invoice or payoff. If a line was labeled payable in the closing statement but has no transaction yet, ask when it was scheduled and whether the remaining funds include it. If a provider received funds directly from the insurer, ask where the payment appears in the overall settlement accounting.

## Ask about one unexplained difference at a time

Use the [Net Settlement Calculator](/tools/settlement-net-waterfall) to lay out the gross amount and each actual deduction. Keep held funds and estimated entries clearly labeled. If part of the proceeds remains in trust, [identify the disputed amount and what will release it](/articles/disputed-lien-held-in-trust-partial-disbursement). If a cost looks like it was previously paid, [trace the original payment before subtracting it again](/articles/calculate-settlement-net-costs-already-paid).

title: How to Calculate a Settlement Fee on One Coverage Payment
excerpt: Separate the coverage payments, verify which amount the fee agreement uses, and calculate the attorney fee and net on distinct lines.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Calculate a Settlement Fee on One Coverage Payment
metaDescription: Separate the coverage payments, verify which amount the fee agreement uses, and calculate the attorney fee and net on distinct lines.
content:
Your insurer issued one payment under collision and another under injury coverage. If the attorney fee applies to only one of those amounts, list each payment separately and identify the fee base from the signed agreement. The fact that the payments concern one accident is only one part of that review.

## Match the scope of the agreement to the payment

Collect the engagement agreement and any amendments, the insurer's payment notices and the settlement statement. Note each coverage, payer and payee. Ask which agreement provision applies to the payment and whether the percentage is calculated before or after allowable costs. Keep a cost charged to the case separate from the percentage calculation.

ABA Model Rule 1.5 describes how a written contingency fee agreement should explain the calculation, expenses and whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee is calculated. Check the rule adopted in your jurisdiction. The California State Bar's consumer guide explains how to review that distinction in a fee agreement. [ABA Model Rule 1.5 on fees](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/professional_responsibility/publications/model_rules_of_professional_conduct/rule_1_5_fees/) · [California State Bar guide to fee agreements](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/public/legal-resources/working-attorney/what-expect-regarding-fees-and-billing)

## Work the calculation one payment at a time

Here is a hypothetical example. A $6,000 collision payment is outside the scope of the fee agreement and a $20,000 injury payment is subject to a 30% fee on gross proceeds. The fee is $6,000, calculated on the $20,000 only. If the injury payment also covers $500 in agreed case costs and $2,500 in a separate repayment, that payment contributes $11,000 to the client's net. With the $6,000 collision payment, the total net from the two payments is $17,000.

If the agreement instead calculates the fee after the $500 cost, the fee on $19,500 would be $5,850. Keep the underlying payment amounts fixed so you can see which difference comes from the fee clause. Ask the firm to identify any allocation rule or other term that changes the inputs.

## Check what actually reached each payee

Use the [Net Settlement Calculator](/tools/settlement-net-waterfall) for each payment, then compare the figures with the combined settlement statement. If the coverage on a check is unclear, [request the insurer's payment description](/articles/ask-adjuster-which-coverage-check-pays). If a filing fee was collected from one payment, [trace the cost and fee base separately](/articles/filing-fee-deducted-one-settlement-payment).

title: How to Compare Two Repayment Estimates While a Demand Is Pending
excerpt: Put both estimates on the same timeline, identify added or disputed charges, and model how the final demand could change your net.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Compare Two Repayment Estimates While a Demand Is Pending
metaDescription: Put both estimates on the same timeline, identify added or disputed charges, and model how the final demand could change your net.
content:
Two documents show different amounts that might be repaid out of a settlement. Before comparing the totals, identify who issued each figure, what period it covers and which stage of the process it represents. The difference can come from new charges, an accepted dispute, a formula for recovery costs, or two documents covering separate obligations.

## Compare the same obligation on both documents

Record the issuing entity, reference number, statement date, last service or payment date covered, and the services listed. Put increases and reductions on different rows. Ask which lines were added, removed or changed and whether the changes are final or pending review.

For Medicare recovery from a beneficiary, CMS says a conditional payment letter reports an interim amount and explains how to dispute unrelated items. The Benefits Coordination & Recovery Center typically issues a recovery demand after receiving and processing settlement information. A separate pre-settlement process is available in eligible cases and has its own steps. [CMS Medicare recovery process](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process) · [CMS demand calculation options](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/demand-calculation-options)

## Reconcile the difference before running a net estimate

Suppose the first hypothetical letter shows $4,800 and the updated one shows $5,200. The new letter adds an $850 therapy payment and removes a $450 unrelated item after a dispute. Those changes explain the $400 increase. Track any request still outstanding separately, along with a date to check for the response.

Ask whether either total reflects any applicable deduction for fees and expenses. The Medicare recovery formula in 42 CFR § 411.37 addresses qualifying procurement costs in defined situations. For another payer, use the plan terms and applicable law for that obligation. Compare estimates that use the same assumptions before deciding what the change means. [Federal rule on Medicare recovery and procurement costs](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-411/subpart-B/section-411.37)

## Keep the estimates as separate scenarios

Use the [net settlement offer comparison tool](/tools/offer-net-comparison) to compare the same gross recovery with each possible deduction, labeling the results as estimates. Replace the figure when an authorized final demand or payoff arrives. If your settlement statement already shows a reserve, [check who approved the estimate and how the difference will be released](/articles/settlement-statement-lists-estimated-lien). For background, [see how Medicare repayment was disputed in a real settlement case](/articles/a-125000-crash-settlement-and-medicares-repayment-demand).

title: How to Spot a Vendor Fee Listed Twice on a Settlement Statement
excerpt: Trace each vendor charge to its invoice and payee, then check whether a lien reduction changes the payoff or adds a separate cost.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Spot a Vendor Fee Listed Twice on a Settlement Statement
metaDescription: Trace each vendor charge to its invoice and payee, then check whether a lien reduction changes the payoff or adds a separate cost.
content:
A vendor appears under both case costs and a lien reduction on your settlement statement. Ask the firm to match each line to a document and a cash movement. A reduction changes the amount payable to a claimant, while a vendor invoice may represent a separate cost for work performed. A duplicate can arise when the same invoice is subtracted in both places.

## Ask what each line represents

Find the vendor name, invoice number, service date, amount and person who paid. Ask whether the vendor gathered medical records, provided a negotiation service or did other work. Then find the lienholder's written payoff and any document that explains the reduction. Match those to the settlement statement.

The State Bar of California separates attorney fees from case expenses and recommends checking what the client pays directly or reimburses. In Medicare cases, federal rules describe how eligible procurement costs can affect the amount Medicare recovers. Those rules concern the recovery calculation. Ask the firm how it accounted for any invoice separately. [California State Bar guide to case costs](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/public/legal-resources/working-attorney/what-expect-regarding-fees-and-billing) · [Federal Medicare procurement cost rule](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-411/subpart-B/section-411.37)

## Test for a duplicate with the net calculation

Suppose a hypothetical original lien was $6,000, the written payoff is $4,500 and a vendor charged $300 under a separate agreement. The $1,500 reduction explains the change to the lien. The two outgoing amounts, if owed and paid from the settlement, are $4,500 to the lienholder and $300 to the vendor. Together they reduce the proceeds by $4,800. If the statement subtracts the same $300 again as a lien-reduction charge, ask the preparer to identify the second invoice or correct the arithmetic.

Sometimes similar charges have different invoice numbers or cover different work. Ask for both records and check whether one was already paid by the client or another party. A payee, reference and date make the distinction easier to verify than a category name.

## Ask for an itemized correction if the invoice repeats

Use the [Duplicate Settlement Deduction Checker](/tools/deduction-overlap-checker) to compare invoice IDs and overlapping entries. Then verify the result against the underlying paperwork. If the difference is a write-off, [record it as a separate reduction alongside cash actually paid](/articles/track-waived-medical-charges-separate-repayment). If the same invoice was partly prepaid, [trace the prepaid portion to its receipt](/articles/calculate-settlement-net-costs-already-paid).

title: How to Track Waived Medical Charges Separately From Repayment
excerpt: Record the original charge, the amount the provider agreed to waive, and the cash actually paid so the settlement statement reconciles.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Track Waived Medical Charges Separately From Repayment
metaDescription: Record the original charge, the amount the provider agreed to waive, and the cash actually paid so the settlement statement reconciles.
content:
Your provider agreed to reduce a bill before your settlement was paid. Record the reduction as a change to the balance and the payoff as a separate movement of money. The closing statement should show the amount actually paid from your proceeds and the records supporting any remaining balance.

## Distinguish the provider’s adjustment from the payer’s recovery

Ask for the latest itemized bill, any applicable explanation of benefits, and the written waiver or payoff agreement. Identify the service dates and account covered. Ask when the waiver takes effect, whether it depends on a payment by a certain date, and what record will show that the account was resolved. CMS's bill guide shows the difference between charges, payments and the amount currently due. [CMS guide to reading a medical bill](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

If a health plan or Medicare seeks repayment for services it covered, keep that demand on its own row with its own payee and supporting record. CMS explains how Medicare tracks conditional payments and issues a demand when applicable. A provider's write-off may affect its bill while the separate repayment process concerns funds another entity paid. [CMS Medicare recovery process](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process)

## Use the ledger to identify how much cash left the settlement

In a hypothetical example, a provider asserts a $3,000 balance. A signed agreement waives $1,200 once the provider receives $1,800 by the specified date. After payment and posting, the account statement would show the $1,800 cash payment and the $1,200 adjustment. For the settlement cash ledger, the outgoing amount is $1,800. Keep the written reduction with the bill so the full $3,000 is accounted for.

If the next bill still shows $1,200, ask whether the payoff was posted to the correct account and whether the condition for applying the waiver was satisfied. Ask for a revised statement or a written explanation of a separate amount still being claimed.

## Reconcile the bill and the disbursement side by side

Use the [medical bill and EOB comparison tool](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler) for the provider account and the [Net Settlement Calculator](/tools/settlement-net-waterfall) for the actual payment. If another bill remains after the lien was resolved, [match the written resolution to the service dates and accounts](/articles/unpaid-provider-balance-after-lien-resolved). If a refund is expected after posting, [check who receives it and when it can appear in the settlement accounting](/articles/settlement-statement-provider-refund-not-received).

title: How to Calculate Settlement Net When You Already Paid Some Costs
excerpt: Separate expenses you paid earlier from costs the firm advanced, then reconcile the closing check and your total net as two different figures.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Calculate Settlement Net When You Already Paid Some Costs
metaDescription: Separate expenses you paid earlier from costs the firm advanced, then reconcile the closing check and your total net as two different figures.
content:
Some case costs were paid from your own account before the settlement arrived. Identify those costs before comparing the closing statement with the check. The amount due at closing and your overall proceeds after expenses answer different questions.

## Find who paid each invoice and whether a reimbursement is due

For each cost, write down the vendor, invoice number, total billed, amount you paid and amount the firm or another party paid. Keep the receipts and any credit or reimbursement on the same record. Ask the firm which remaining amounts will be charged to the proceeds and whether any sum will be paid back to you.

The State Bar of California explains that clients may pay costs directly or reimburse amounts advanced by their lawyer. It also recommends confirming whether costs affect the base used for a contingency fee. ABA Model Rule 1.5 describes how a covered fee agreement specifies expenses and the order of the fee calculation. Refer to the agreement and local rule for your case. [California State Bar guide to case costs](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/public/legal-resources/working-attorney/what-expect-regarding-fees-and-billing) · [ABA Model Rule 1.5 on contingency fees](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/professional_responsibility/publications/model_rules_of_professional_conduct/rule_1_5_fees/)

## Compute the closing check and the full cost separately

In a hypothetical example, the gross settlement is $25,000 and the fee is $7,500. You paid $180 for records before settlement and the firm advanced a $420 filing cost. Assume the agreed fee is calculated on gross and the prior $180 remains your expense. The check after the fee and the $420 reimbursement is $17,080. Your net after also accounting for the $180 you spent earlier is $16,900.

If the closing statement lists $600 as total case costs, ask for the breakdown of what was already paid and what will be withheld now. If the agreement or an adjustment reimburses your earlier payment, track that reimbursement as a separate credit and verify who receives it.

## Make each receipt reconcile once

Use the [Net Settlement Calculator](/tools/settlement-net-waterfall) with only the agreed inputs for the check you are modeling. Keep earlier out-of-pocket spending on its own line when comparing the broader result. For a fee charged against one payment, [separate the percentage calculation from cost allocation](/articles/calculate-settlement-fee-one-coverage-payment). If the same invoice appears twice on the statement, [compare the vendor records and payees](/articles/duplicate-vendor-fees-settlement-statement).

title: A Provider Refund Appears in Your Settlement Before It Arrives
excerpt: Trace the expected refund to the person who will receive it and ask how the amount will be shown after it is actually posted.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Provider Refund Appears in Your Settlement Before It Arrives
metaDescription: Trace the expected refund to the person who will receive it and ask how the amount will be shown after it is actually posted.
content:
Your settlement breakdown includes a provider refund you have yet to receive. Ask whether the entry is an expected credit, an actual deposit or a number used to estimate a future balance. Identify who is supposed to receive the money and where it will be recorded when it arrives.

## Find the transaction the provider is reversing

Gather the original receipt, the revised explanation of benefits if there is one, and any refund confirmation. Ask the provider to give the amount, payee, method, issue date and transaction reference. Verify whether a card refund goes to the original card, whether a check is being mailed, or whether the provider made a credit within its own account.

CMS explains how an EOB's patient balance can include amounts already paid, and how a provider statement records the payments and adjustments on that account. Match the entries to the account that generated the original payment. [CMS explanation of benefits guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [CMS guide to medical bill transactions](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

## Reconcile the current amount and the expected credit

Suppose you previously paid $600 and the provider agrees to return $250 to your original card. The refund has been approved but has yet to post. If the provider is paying you directly, record the $250 separately from the funds the firm has received. Ask the firm what its statement means if the refund appears on a line that affects the check. If the provider plans to pay the firm, ask for the client ledger entry after the deposit and an explanation of who receives the resulting credit.

California's professional conduct rules include requirements for recordkeeping and accounting for funds lawyers hold. Use the current client accounting to compare a pending provider promise with an actual receipt in trust. [California Rule 1.15 on handling funds](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/rules/rules-professional-conduct/current-rules-professional-conduct/chapter-1-lawyer-client-relationship)

## Update the reconciliation when the refund posts

Use the [Insurance Claim Cash Flow Planner](/tools/claim-cashflow-calendar) to record the expected date, then enter the posting date and actual payee. If the provider reduced the bill without issuing cash, [compare the write-off and actual payoff on separate rows](/articles/track-waived-medical-charges-separate-repayment). If an amount moved through the firm, [match the deposit and disbursement to the trust ledger](/articles/reconcile-settlement-check-client-trust-ledger).

title: How to Check a Disputed Lien Still Held in Trust
excerpt: Reconcile the partial payment and the exact amount held, then ask what will resolve the dispute and trigger a final accounting.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Check a Disputed Lien Still Held in Trust
metaDescription: Reconcile the partial payment and the exact amount held, then ask what will resolve the dispute and trigger a final accounting.
content:
You received part of your settlement while a lien or repayment claim is still disputed. Ask for the amount actually held for that issue and the accounting for everything already distributed. Then identify the event that will determine how the remaining money is paid.

## Identify the dispute and the amount held for it

Ask for the claimant's name, account or reference, amount requested, amount disputed and amount reserved. Find out whether the dispute concerns the services listed, the amount claimed or the entity entitled to payment. Ask who is handling it and what documents are still needed.

ABA Model Rule 1.15 describes keeping property that is subject to competing interests separate until the dispute is resolved and distributing portions that are undisputed. California Rule 1.15 has its own provisions on accounting and prompt distribution of undisputed funds to the entitled person. Check the rule and facts that apply where your lawyer practices. [ABA Model Rule 1.15 on disputed property](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/professional_responsibility/publications/model_rules_of_professional_conduct/rule_1_15_safekeeping_property/) · [California Rule 1.15 on undisputed funds](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/rules/rules-professional-conduct/current-rules-professional-conduct/chapter-1-lawyer-client-relationship)

## Ask for the three amounts that reconcile the settlement

Consider a hypothetical $32,000 deposit. The firm pays $10,000 in agreed fees and costs, sends you $19,000 and holds $3,000 for the disputed claim. Those three amounts total $32,000. If the dispute resolves for $2,250 and the remaining $750 is due to you, the final accounting should show both distributions and the resulting zero balance for this example.

Ask whether any other sum is separately held. For each item, request the date it was reserved and the record needed to resolve it, such as a written payoff, withdrawal of a demand or an agreement on the disputed services. Ask when you will get the updated statement after funds are released.

## Treat the current payment and future disbursement as separate entries

Use the [Net Settlement Calculator](/tools/settlement-net-waterfall) to model the current payment and different possible outcomes for the holdback. Keep the assumptions visible until the dispute is resolved. For the amounts that have already moved, [match the check to the client ledger](/articles/reconcile-settlement-check-client-trust-ledger). If the hold is based on a preliminary number, [ask where the lien estimate came from and when it will be replaced](/articles/settlement-statement-lists-estimated-lien).

title: What to Ask When a Settlement Statement Lists a Lien Estimate
excerpt: Identify the source and date of the estimated lien, then find out whether the amount is a projection, a reserve, or a payment awaiting confirmation.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: What to Ask When a Settlement Statement Lists a Lien Estimate
metaDescription: Identify the source and date of the estimated lien, then find out whether the amount is a projection, a reserve, or a payment awaiting confirmation.
content:
A settlement statement labels a lien as “estimated.” Ask who produced the figure, what document supports it and whether it will affect the check you are about to receive. An amount in a projection, a sum held in trust and money already sent to a claimant belong on different lines.

## Ask what the estimate is based on

Record the creditor or plan, account number, issue date, services included and the amount shown. Ask whether the preparer used an interim notice, a proposed payoff, or a calculation made by the firm. If it comes from Medicare, identify whether you are looking at a conditional payment letter or a demand. CMS describes the interim amount, the process for disputing unrelated items and how the recovery demand is issued. [CMS guide to conditional payments and recovery](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process)

Ask if the figure is already net of any approved reductions. Obtain a copy of the notice or explanation used so you can compare the next version on the same basis. If more than one entity has a claim, identify the support for each estimate.

## Ask whether the estimate changes what you receive now

For example, a preliminary statement lists an estimated $4,900 and the firm confirms it held that amount for a single unresolved item. If the authorized payoff later comes in at $3,750 and there are no other claims to that reserve, the difference to account for is $1,150. Ask the firm to show the amount paid, the date and the disposition of the difference. California Rule 1.15 addresses written accountings and prompt distribution of undisputed funds the client or other person is entitled to receive. [California trust accounting rule](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/rules/rules-professional-conduct/current-rules-professional-conduct/chapter-1-lawyer-client-relationship)

A question for the firm could read, “What document supports the $4,900 estimate, how much is actually held, and when will the updated statement show the final payment and any difference?”

## Replace the estimate only when the status changes

Use the [Settlement Deduction Questions](/tools/deduction-question-builder) to track the estimate, the amount held and the evidence you still need. If you have competing interim figures, [compare them line by line](/articles/compare-repayment-estimates-pending-demand). If the firm has sent a partial check, [reconcile it with the actual amount reserved for the dispute](/articles/disputed-lien-held-in-trust-partial-disbursement).

title: How to Compare Claimants’ Gross Settlements With Shared Case Costs
excerpt: Check each claimant’s gross allocation and the basis for shared costs, then reconcile each person’s net to the same total expense.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Compare Claimants’ Gross Settlements With Shared Case Costs
metaDescription: Check each claimant’s gross allocation and the basis for shared costs, then reconcile each person’s net to the same total expense.
content:
Several people settled claims from the same case and one invoice was shared. Begin with each claimant's gross amount and then trace the basis for dividing that invoice. The gross shares, fees and individual costs can differ even when everyone is affected by the same shared expense.

## Identify each allocation before comparing net payments

Use the settlement breakdown, applicable fee agreements and cost ledger. Separate each person's gross share, individually assigned costs and fees. Put genuinely shared costs in a separate group with the underlying invoice and the allocation rule used. Ask which agreement, written approval or other authority supplies that rule for the case.

California Rule 1.8.7 addresses aggregate settlements by a lawyer representing multiple clients. It generally requires each client's informed written consent, with disclosure of the claims involved and each person's participation, and excludes class action settlements subject to court approval. ABA Model Rule 1.8(g) provides a related model rule. Applicable obligations depend on the jurisdiction and representation. [California rule on aggregate settlements](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/rules/rules-professional-conduct/current-rules-professional-conduct/chapter-1-lawyer-client-relationship) · [ABA Model Rule 1.8(g)](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/professional_responsibility/publications/model_rules_of_professional_conduct/rule_1_8_current_clients_specific_rules/)

## Compare the outcomes with a shared invoice

Suppose two hypothetical gross shares are $36,000 and $24,000 and one expert invoice totals $1,200. If the approved allocation is proportional to gross proceeds, the shares are 60% and 40%, so the costs are $720 and $480. If the applicable arrangement divides the invoice equally, each share is $600. Both approaches reconcile to $1,200. The $120 shift for each person comes from the allocation rule, and the example leaves other deductions aside.

Then check whether the fee on each share uses gross proceeds or a base after eligible costs. Ask for the calculation before comparing individual checks. If one person advanced the expert's bill, find the reimbursement entry and check whether the allocation reflects that advance.

## Reconcile the separate statements to the shared total

Use the [Pro Rata Allocation Calculator](/tools/shared-limit-allocation-model) to organize gross shares when there is a shared pool, then compare the cost allocations with the actual invoices. If one cost was withheld from just one payment, [trace that cost back to the receipt](/articles/filing-fee-deducted-one-settlement-payment). If the firm disbursed the payments through trust, [compare the relevant transactions with each client's accounting](/articles/reconcile-settlement-check-client-trust-ledger).

title: When Your Dashcam Clock Disagrees With the 911 Call Time
excerpt: Match a shared event to both recordings, estimate the clock offset, and keep the impact, call and dispatch times separate.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: When Your Dashcam Clock Disagrees With the 911 Call Time
metaDescription: Match a shared event to both recordings, estimate the clock offset, and keep the impact, call and dispatch times separate.
content:
Your dashcam stamps the impact at 6:14:10 p.m. A dispatch record puts the first call later. Both times may be useful. First identify the event each timestamp describes. A crash, the start of a phone call, the call being answered and a unit being dispatched can all happen at different moments.

## Ask what each time means

Save the dashcam file in its original format and note whether the time appears on the image, in the file information or in the viewer. Write down the displayed time zone and any device setting you can verify. Keep the original display in your notes even after you estimate a correction.

Ask the agency that holds the 911 records which times it records and how it labels them. Depending on the system, the useful records may include call audio, computer-aided dispatch entries and a description of the fields. Include the address, local date, time window and incident number when making the request. Anne Arundel County, Maryland, publishes an example of an agency-specific request process. [Anne Arundel County 911 records instructions](https://www.aacounty.org/police-department/central-records/obtaining-911-call-records)

## Compare the clocks using the same event

Suppose the dashcam audio records a speakerphone connection at 6:14:32 p.m. and the agency confirms that its 6:15:14 p.m. entry marks that same connection. The agency clock in that example is 42 seconds ahead of the dashcam. Applying that offset to the dashcam's 6:14:10 impact gives an estimated agency-clock time of 6:14:52. State which event you matched and label the result an estimate.

If the agency's entry actually marks when the caller dialed or when a dispatcher opened the incident, that subtraction would mix different events. Seek another shared cue or leave the offset unresolved. When possible, test the offset against a second event. SWGDE's video acquisition guidance recommends documenting a recorder's time against a reference clock and recording the difference. [SWGDE digital recorder acquisition guidance](https://www.swgde.org/documents/published-complete-listing/17-v-002-1-4/)

## Share the raw and adjusted times together

Keep a row for each event with the source, original timestamp, time zone, meaning of the field and estimated corrected time. Attach the excerpt that explains each field. Use the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) to keep the record of the impact distinct from the record of the call.

If you still need a clean working file, see [how to verify a dashcam copy and preserve the original card](/articles/verify-dashcam-copy-preserve-memory-card). When the second clock comes from a truck module, see [how to interpret separate triggered events in a truck download](/articles/truck-event-data-two-triggers-same-ignition-count).

title: How to Verify a Dashcam Copy While Preserving the Original Card
excerpt: Preserve the dashcam card, verify the working file by checksum, and document the difference between a clip and a forensic image.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Verify a Dashcam Copy While Preserving the Original Card
