metaDescription: Preserve the dashcam card, verify the working file by checksum, and document the difference between a clip and a forensic image.
content:
A dashcam clip can be useful evidence, and the original card may hold earlier or later segments and information about how those files were stored. Preserve both if possible. Decide whether you need a verified copy of a visible clip or a forensic acquisition of the whole card. The two give you different records.

## Protect the card before making a working copy

Record the camera model, the card's label and capacity, when you received it and who handled it. Keep the card out of a dashcam that might record over older files. If the contents are disputed, the card is damaged or you need deleted files, ask a digital evidence examiner to acquire the card. A qualified examiner can document a read-only workflow, including write-blocking where appropriate. NIST's preservation guidance discusses storage media, preserving integrity and recording handling. [NIST digital evidence preservation guide](https://www.nist.gov/publications/digital-evidence-preservation-considerations-evidence-handlers)

Treat an export already obtained as its own record. Save the original export as received. Make a second copy for playback and note who supplied the export, how it was obtained and whether it came from the card, the dashcam application or a messaging service. When a camera provides several short segments, keep the adjacent files and their original names so the sequence can be checked.

## Compare copies of the same file

Calculate a SHA-256 checksum for the preserved export and for the working copy. If the two hashes match, that is evidence that these files contain the same bytes. Record the file name, size, date of the check and both values. The [SHA-256 File Checksum Tool](/tools/evidence-file-fingerprints) can make that comparison without putting a private video on a public file-sharing site.

An exported MP4 and a card image serve different purposes. The MP4 contains one playable file. A forensic image can preserve the card's broader contents and storage structure, depending on how it was acquired. Two files that look the same during playback can have different hashes after conversion. Keep converted or annotated clips under distinct names and document their relationship to the source. [SWGDE digital forensic video analysis practices](https://www.swgde.org/documents/published-complete-listing/18-v-001-2-0/)

## Preserve the sequence as well as the footage

Imagine the app shares only the minute containing impact. An earlier segment might show when the camera's clock changed, and a later one might contain a 911 call. Save any segment index and original export instructions alongside the clip you intend to share. For the next step, see [how to reconcile a dashcam time with a 911 record](/articles/dashcam-clock-different-from-911-call-time) and [what to request in a native video export](/articles/request-native-crash-video-frame-timing).

title: The Insurer Used a Comparable Car That Had Already Sold
excerpt: Verify when the comparable was actually available, what price the report used, and which valuation rule applies to your total loss.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Insurer Used a Comparable Car That Had Already Sold
metaDescription: Verify when the comparable was actually available, what price the report used, and which valuation rule applies to your total loss.
content:
You call the dealer named on a total-loss report and learn that the car sold weeks earlier. The useful follow-up is to find out when it was actually offered, what price the insurer used and how the listing was used. A vehicle offered as a replacement and a historical market observation serve different roles.

## Get the dates that sit behind the row

Request the complete valuation report and identify the vehicle by VIN or stock number. Record the loss date, the valuation's effective date and the listing capture date. Ask the dealer to confirm when the car was available, when it sold or was removed and which price the dealer advertised. Ask the insurer whether the price shown is a listing amount, a reported sale amount or an adjusted value from the valuation vendor.

If the dealer confirms only that the car is gone today, ask a narrower question about its status on the date shown in the report. Preserve the written response and any original listing that still exists. A reused photo or a reposted ad can make the capture date look current after the actual availability ended.

## Check the valuation method and market window

In Washington, an insurer using the replacement method must offer a comparable motor vehicle available for inspection within a reasonable distance. Cash valuations use a different framework. Washington's total-loss rule allows certain historical comparables, including vehicles available within 90 calendar days of the loss in the rule's itemized settlement requirements. The rule separately addresses the data a computerized source must use. [Washington total-loss settlement rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-391)

Consider a Washington loss on November 1. A car the dealer sold on October 20 could still be relevant to a cash valuation if the data and the vehicle meet the applicable criteria. A January sale from before that November loss raises a different question. Ask the insurer which observation it used and where it fits in the stated market window. Washington's valuation-report rule describes details the claimant can use to verify the listed vehicles and adjustments. [Washington valuation-report requirements](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-392)

## Request the correction that the evidence supports

Send the VIN, the challenged row, the dealer's dated response and any better comparables with their availability and price. Ask the insurer to confirm the data, explain why it qualifies or provide an itemized revised valuation. The [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) can pair each disputed entry with its source.

If the report uses a different effective date, read [how to check the date in a total-loss appraisal](/articles/appraisal-award-valuation-date-total-loss). If your rental cutoff depends on the settlement timeline, keep it separate using [the total-loss rental guide](/articles/total-loss-rental-before-settlement-check).

title: Your Total-Loss Offer Arrived Before the Check. When Does the Rental End?
excerpt: Confirm the rental benefit, payment dispatch date and return deadline before the rental company starts billing you directly.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Total-Loss Offer Arrived Before the Check. When Does the Rental End?
metaDescription: Confirm the rental benefit, payment dispatch date and return deadline before the rental company starts billing you directly.
content:
The insurer emails a total-loss offer on Monday. The check has yet to arrive, and the rental company calls about a return date. Ask the carrier to identify the event that ends its payment for the rental. An offer, acceptance, dispatch of the settlement, receipt of the check and exhaustion of your rental benefit can occur on different days.

## Find the dates and the balance of the benefit

Get the rental authorization, daily limit, total limit and the amount used so far. Ask whether the authorization comes from your own rental reimbursement coverage or from someone else's liability carrier. Ask which policy language or claim rule the carrier is using and the date and time the rental company has been told to stop direct billing.

If there is a settlement payment, request the date it was sent, the delivery method and the payee. A check naming a lender can reach a different recipient than you expected. Record the time the rental company expects the vehicle back and its daily charge after the authorization ends.

## Apply the rule that matches your claim

Washington's rule effective October 18, 2026 addresses first-party claims where the amount of loss has been agreed and rental coverage is available. It provides for use of the rental coverage through the shorter period of seven calendar days after payment is sent to the claimant or until the coverage is exhausted. The Washington insurance regulator explains the update for consumers. [WAC 284-30-391(7)](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-391) · [Washington insurance regulator's rule summary](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/about-us/news/2026/quicker-responses-more-transparency-consumers-added-claims-process)

For an illustration under those conditions, assume the carrier sends the payment on November 10 and the rental coverage has four eligible days left. Exhaustion may come before the seven-day point, regardless of when you open the mail. Ask the carrier to state the covered return deadline in writing. California's consumer guide separately emphasizes the terms of the purchased rental coverage. Use the policy and rules for your own claim. [California auto claim guide](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/105-type/95-guides/01-auto/upload/Accident-What-Next-w-05-27-21-Web-Only.pdf)

## Put the possible out-of-pocket days on a calendar

If the insurer and rental company give different dates, ask them to confirm the same cutoff and who will pay for each day. Use the [Rental Budget Stress Test](/tools/rental-budget-stress-test) to compare the cost of returning the vehicle on the confirmed date with any extra days you would pay for. Enter the rental firm's actual daily price and fees.

If the check went to an old lender, see [how to track a misdirected total-loss payment](/articles/total-loss-check-old-lienholder-after-refinance). If you are still evaluating the offer, review [how to verify a comparable the dealer has already sold](/articles/total-loss-comparable-car-sold-before-valuation).

title: An Underinsured Motorist Claim After Two Drivers Paid
excerpt: Reconcile both liability payments, identify any policy election, and ask the UIM insurer to show how it calculated the credit.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: An Underinsured Motorist Claim After Two Drivers Paid
metaDescription: Reconcile both liability payments, identify any policy election, and ask the UIM insurer to show how it calculated the credit.
content:
Two insurers pay after a multi-vehicle crash. Your underinsured motorist carrier then lists a credit on its worksheet. To check it, follow each dollar to the driver, coverage and injury or property claim it resolved. Then ask which law and policy provision the carrier used to decide whether that amount counts toward a credit.

## Build the payment record by driver

For each insurer, keep the declarations or written limits information if available, the offer, signed release and payment confirmation. Record the driver, insurer, claim number, amount, payee, date and coverage. Flag any amount paid to another claimant from the same limits. Label bodily injury, property damage and medical payments separately.

In an example, Driver A's carrier pays $22,000 for bodily injury. Driver B's carrier pays $12,000 for bodily injury and issues a separate $4,000 property check. Your record should show $34,000 in bodily injury proceeds and a separate $4,000 property payment. If a worksheet shows $38,000 on one injury credit line, ask the adjuster to explain the allocation and reconcile it to the documents.

## Find the rule on the policy that responds

Virginia provides one example of why the policy election matters. Its statute generally provides for UIM payment without a credit for the applicable liability coverage available for payment, subject to an election signed by a named insured to reduce UIM payments. The same statute defines available liability coverage by reference to coverage applicable to the injured person's claim after payments on other claims from the same occurrence. Ask for the actual endorsement and any election the insurer relies on. [Virginia Code § 38.2-2206](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title38.2/chapter22/section38.2-2206/) · [Virginia's statutory election notice](https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title38.2/chapter22/section38.2-2202/)

Ask the insurer to show the applicable injury or property limit, the basis for each credit and the order of calculation if more than one UIM policy is involved. If the payment was shared with other injured people, request the record supporting the amount allocated to you. Check any policy consent or notice requirements before signing a release that could affect another claim.

## Ask for a worksheet you can reproduce

Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to connect each credit on the worksheet to a payment document or policy provision. Keep the final calculation and the carrier's earlier versions. The amount recoverable depends on the coverage, damages and governing law.

If coverage itself is disputed because you were using a fleet car, start with [the fleet-car regular-use guide](/articles/regular-use-exclusion-on-call-fleet-car). If a liability release has a mismatched date, review [the draft release before relying on it](/articles/settlement-release-wrong-crash-date).

title: A Fleet Car Was Assigned Only During On-Call Weeks. Does Regular Use Apply?
excerpt: Compare the policy language with the actual fleet assignment, key access and restrictions during and between on-call rotations.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Fleet Car Was Assigned Only During On-Call Weeks. Does Regular Use Apply?
metaDescription: Compare the policy language with the actual fleet assignment, key access and restrictions during and between on-call rotations.
content:
An insurer invokes a regular-use exclusion after a crash in a work car. You drove the fleet vehicle during one on-call week each month. Document how the assignment actually worked. Frequency matters to the factual record, and access between trips can be just as important when the policy speaks of a vehicle furnished or available for regular use.

## Describe access as precisely as mileage

Start with the exclusion, definitions and coverage endorsement in force on the crash date. Note whether it refers to a specific vehicle, a vehicle regularly used, or vehicles furnished or available for regular use. Check the VIN and which coverage the insurer is reviewing.

Ask the employer for the on-call calendar, fleet checkout logs, key records, rules for taking the car home and permission to use it outside work. A rotating assignment could involve one permanently assigned car with restricted use, or a different car that the driver can only obtain for a specific shift. Document who could approve an exception and whether the worker actually kept the keys off rotation.

## Compare the pattern with the decision the insurer cites

In *Rush v. Erie Insurance Exchange*, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld the regular-use exclusion against a challenge under Pennsylvania's motor vehicle insurance law. The case involved a detective using an employer-owned police vehicle. Read the opinion alongside the language of your endorsement and the facts about your own access. Pennsylvania's statute separately describes the state's rules for offering uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage. [Pennsylvania Supreme Court opinion in Rush](https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/2024/77-map-2022.html) · [75 Pa.C.S. § 1731](https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/LI/CT/HTM/75/00.017.031.000..HTM)

For an example, a technician takes a car home Monday through Sunday during a recurring rotation and returns the keys at the end of that week. Put the calendar and key receipt together. If the insurer describes the car as continuously available, ask it to identify the records supporting access between rotations. If it relies on repeated access during each assigned week, ask for the part of the endorsement that applies to that pattern.

## Send the comparison with the claim number

A short request can identify the exclusion, state the documented limits on access and ask whether the insurer disputes those facts or interprets the policy differently. Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to attach the policy, schedule and key record to the corresponding points.

For the complete background to the Pennsylvania case, read [how the work-car policy dispute arose](/articles/can-your-auto-policy-cover-a-crash-in-a-work-car). If coverage applies and the dispute instead concerns liability payments, see [how to check a UIM credit after two drivers pay](/articles/underinsured-motorist-credit-two-driver-payments).

title: A Lyft Crash After Ride Acceptance and Before Pickup
excerpt: Ask for the trip status at impact and line up the acceptance, cancellation and crash times before comparing insurance coverage.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Lyft Crash After Ride Acceptance and Before Pickup
metaDescription: Ask for the trip status at impact and line up the acceptance, cancellation and crash times before comparing insurance coverage.
content:
A Lyft driver has accepted a request and is on the way to the passenger when a crash occurs. The record that matters for coverage is the trip's status at impact. A map screenshot can establish the route shown on a phone. A timestamped trip history can show when the status changed.

## Request the state changes around the crash

Collect the trip reference, account or vehicle identifier and an incident time window. Ask Lyft or the claim handler for the available records showing when the ride was offered, accepted, canceled or reassigned, and when any pickup was recorded. Ask which entries reflect server time, which reflect device time, and what time zone the export uses. Save the confirmation screen or trip history you already have with its source.

Lyft describes different insurance arrangements while waiting for a request and while en route to pick up a rider or on a ride. Its materials discuss coverage conditions and state variation. Ask for the applicable certificate or policy and the exact claim decision for the driver, passenger or other person involved. [Lyft's driver insurance resources](https://www.lyft.com/driver/insurance)

## Compare the crash with the acceptance and cancellation

For example, an August trip record shows acceptance at 23:51:04 UTC. A synchronized California crash record reports 4:51:18 p.m. Pacific daylight time, which is 23:51:18 UTC. The two timestamps put the reported impact 14 seconds after acceptance. A cancellation at 23:52:10 UTC would be later. If the crash time is approximate, record the uncertainty instead of treating a rounded time as exact.

California's Public Utilities Commission calls the interval from accepted match to pickup Period 2. It lists primary commercial insurance requirements for Periods 2 and 3 and describes separate requirements for other stages or coverages. Use the applicable state and policy terms to determine which coverage responds and for what loss. [CPUC rideshare insurance requirements](https://www.cpuc.ca.gov/regulatory-services/licensing/transportation-licensing-and-analysis-branch/transportation-network-companies/tnc-insurance-requirements)

## Send the event history in one time zone

Use the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) to keep the source timestamps, converted times and coverage decision together. Ask the claim handler to identify the trip state it used at impact and the record supporting it. Include a copy of the trip confirmation and the crash record.

If the crash time comes from a dashcam and the recording differs from a dispatch record, [compare the clocks using a shared event](/articles/dashcam-clock-different-from-911-call-time). If two liability carriers have paid and an additional policy is in dispute, see [how to organize payments for a UIM review](/articles/underinsured-motorist-credit-two-driver-payments).

title: Two Truck Event Records Show the Same Ignition Count
excerpt: Compare each trigger, timestamp and recording window before treating a shared ignition count as evidence about the crash sequence.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Two Truck Event Records Show the Same Ignition Count
metaDescription: Compare each trigger, timestamp and recording window before treating a shared ignition count as evidence about the crash sequence.
content:
A truck download has two event entries, and both show the same ignition count. First check which field the number represents. A count sampled at an event and a count reported at download can answer different questions. The meaning depends on the recorder, software and data definition.

## Identify what produced each entry

Ask the examiner for the module type, software version, native download and data dictionary. Make one row for each event with its label, trigger threshold, recorded time, distance or odometer, ignition field and the length of the saved window. Mark fields reported once for the download separately from those stored for each event.

The federal light-vehicle EDR standard distinguishes ignition cycle at the crash from ignition cycle at download. Its application is limited to specified vehicles. For a heavy truck's engine module, use that model's report and definitions to determine which fields it provides and how it sampled them. [NHTSA's EDR rule and field definitions](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-12-18/html/2024-29862.htm)

## Use the trigger definitions before lining up the traces

An NTSB report on a Detroit Diesel DDEC IV download distinguished the hard-brake records from the last-stop record. Its described hard-brake trigger used a configured deceleration threshold. The last-stop trigger used a transition from motion to a stop or ignition shutoff under the recorder's conditions. In that file, the most recent hard-brake entry and the last-stop entry were only seconds apart. The labels and recorded windows make the difference important. [NTSB event data factual report](https://data.ntsb.gov/Docket/Document/docBLOB?FileExtension=.PDF&FileName=Event+Data+Group+Chairman%27s+Factual+Report-Master.PDF&ID=40317971)

In another NTSB download of a DDEC IV, two hard-brake records were retained from a date months before the accident under investigation. That is a reason to ask which stored events belong to the crash being reviewed. [NTSB electronic control module factual report](https://data.ntsb.gov/Docket/Document/docBLOB?FileExtension=.PDF&FileName=Vehicle+Recorders+-+Electronic+Control+Module+-+Specialist%27s+Factual+Report-Master.PDF&ID=40355953)

## Ask for the sequence the data can support

If both counters were actually sampled at the trigger and the manufacturer confirms how the count increments, the matching numbers may help place both events within the same ignition cycle. Establish the order and any relationship to an impact using timestamps, event windows, vehicle motion and another source. Flag an uncertain clock setting. Use the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) to keep the module and external sources distinct.

For a companion record from a camera, see [how to compare a dashcam clock with dispatch time](/articles/dashcam-clock-different-from-911-call-time). If someone has supplied only an exported clip, see [how to verify a working copy while preserving the original](/articles/verify-dashcam-copy-preserve-memory-card).

title: The Slip-and-Fall Log Shows an Aisle Check Before the Spill
excerpt: Match the inspection entry to the exact aisle and compare it with the earliest evidence of the spill and the fall.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Slip-and-Fall Log Shows an Aisle Check Before the Spill
metaDescription: Match the inspection entry to the exact aisle and compare it with the earliest evidence of the spill and the fall.
content:
A store's log shows an inspection at 2:00 p.m. You fell at 2:17. The useful question is what the check covered and what happened during those 17 minutes. A signed entry describes a check. A camera, witness or incident note may tell you when the spill appeared or was first reported.

## Confirm what the inspection covered

Request the incident report and the inspection entries surrounding the fall, including any route, department or zone identifiers the store uses. Identify the exact shelf, aisle entrance or display. Compare a record for the whole department with one that specifies the affected patch of floor. Ask whether the logged time is when an employee reached the area or when the route was signed off.

Seek footage and statements for the interval before and after the event. Keep the timestamps and their sources. A witness may have seen an employee pass the area without seeing what the employee checked. A camera may show a spill begin in one place and spread into a walking path later. Record the difference.

## Compare the chronology against the notice issue

Consider two example timelines. In the first, the 2:00 check covers the exact location and the spill is visible for the first time at 2:16. In the second, the 2:00 entry covers a different aisle and footage shows the substance at 1:48. The second record creates a different question about how long the condition was discoverable and what the store knew.

The California Supreme Court's *Ortega v. Kmart* opinion considered whether a failure to inspect within a reasonable time could support an inference about notice. It recognized that the inference can be drawn from the evidence in the circumstances. California's civil jury instructions discuss whether a dangerous condition existed long enough that reasonable care would have discovered it. [California Supreme Court opinion in Ortega](https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/ortega-v-kmart-corp-32244/) · [California civil jury instructions, CACI No. 1011](https://www.justia.com/trials-litigation/docs/caci/1000/1011/)

## Put each time beside its source

Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to track inspection, spill onset, first report and fall as separate events. For an event you cannot place precisely, record the earliest and latest plausible times from your records. A short timeline with the original log and any video is easier to review than a single assertion that the store checked the aisle.

When two recordings use different clocks, [align shared events before comparing the times](/articles/dashcam-clock-different-from-911-call-time). For a separate example of what an older inspection record establishes, read [the rented boom lift delivery guide](/articles/rented-boom-lift-maintenance-tag-delivery-inspection).

title: The Rented Boom Lift's Maintenance Tag Predates Delivery
excerpt: Match the tag to the lift's serial number and compare the shop service, delivery condition and pre-use check after a worksite injury.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Rented Boom Lift's Maintenance Tag Predates Delivery
metaDescription: Match the tag to the lift's serial number and compare the shop service, delivery condition and pre-use check after a worksite injury.
content:
A rented boom lift arrives on Monday with a service sticker dated Friday. A Tuesday incident raises a question about the lift's condition when it reached the site. Work backward from the serial number. The Friday sticker may document service at the rental yard. Delivery and daily checks describe later moments.

## Separate service, handover and operation

Save the rental agreement and identify the make, model, serial number, hour meter and attachment configuration. Request the maintenance work order behind the sticker, including what was inspected, repaired or left open. Compare those records with the rental company's outbound condition sheet and the delivery ticket or receiving photos. Ask whether the same machine number appears on every document.

Collect the operator's pre-use or shift inspection record and any reported defect, swap or repair at the site. If a form says only that the equipment was received, record what it actually certifies. An operator's notes, delivery photos or the rental firm's service calls may provide separate evidence of the condition of a control, guard or other specific component.

## Check which rule and procedure apply to the lift

For aerial lifts covered by OSHA's construction rule, lift controls must be tested each day before use. OSHA's aerial-lift guidance also describes pre-start inspection and following manufacturer recommendations. Look up the actual equipment type and applicable standard and compare the manufacturer checklist with what was recorded. A mechanic's service tag and a daily control test serve different purposes. [OSHA construction aerial lift rule](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1926/1926.453) · [OSHA aerial lift inspection guidance](https://www.osha.gov/etools/scaffolding/aerial-lifts)

Suppose a tag lists hydraulic service on Friday, the Monday ticket logs delivery at 7:42 a.m. and the Tuesday sheet marks “controls checked” without naming the machine. Ask which serial number the Tuesday check covered and whether it included the control involved. If a defect was first reported after delivery, date that report and identify who saw it.

## Ask for records by serial number

Use the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) to name the work order, handover documents, daily inspection and defect communications. Keep the earliest photos with the time, position and source. If the lift was returned or repaired, ask what records document its condition at pickup and before the repair.

For the separate question of reporting an injury to an employer, see [how to document an undated California DWC-1](/articles/california-dwc-1-employer-did-not-date-form). For a different example of testing the scope of a signed inspection, see [how to compare a store's aisle log with the time of a spill](/articles/slip-and-fall-aisle-inspection-before-spill).

title: A Medical Record Addendum Was Entered Weeks After Your Visit
excerpt: Identify what the addendum changes, who entered it, and which date belongs to the visit versus the later medical record entry.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Medical Record Addendum Was Entered Weeks After Your Visit
metaDescription: Identify what the addendum changes, who entered it, and which date belongs to the visit versus the later medical record entry.
content:
A visit note is dated May 4. A paragraph attached to it is dated May 27 and changes a detail about how your injury occurred. Keep both. The date care took place, the date a clinician entered information and the date you downloaded the chart are separate facts.

## Request the record that shows the relationship

Ask the provider for the encounter note and related addenda or corrections, with the available author, signature and entry dates. Identify the exact visit and the statement you are trying to reconcile. If a portal view shows only the newest text, ask the records office how it labels an original note and a later entry and what versions it can provide. Preserve the files as received.

CMS's Medicare review manual discusses amendments, corrections and delayed entries. It expects the change to be identifiable and its date and author to be clear. Those instructions apply to Medicare record review. The same fields can help you understand the chronology of an injury chart. [CMS Program Integrity Manual, section 3.3.2.5](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/downloads/pim83c03.pdf)

## Put the changed detail next to its source

For example, the initial note says left wrist pain began “yesterday.” The addendum says “three days ago” based on a later conversation. Record what each note says and the date of the conversation the addendum describes, if shown. Ask the provider whether the addendum corrects the original statement, adds a later history or refers to a separate encounter. The way it answers that question can affect how you explain the difference to an insurer.

If you believe the record contains an inaccurate or incomplete statement, ask the provider for its amendment process. HHS explains the HIPAA right to request a change and the option to submit a statement of disagreement if the covered provider or health plan denies the request. Identify the entry and supply any relevant documentation through its approved channel. [HHS guidance on medical record corrections](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-individuals/medical-records/index.html)

## Keep later care changes in their own column

Use the [Medical Records Gap Organizer](/tools/care-record-gap-view) to track the original note, the addendum and any requested clarification. If the insurer has the earlier copy, identify the newer version by date and author so a reviewer can see what changed. For a different kind of later change, see [how to update a therapy cost estimate after the plan moves to home exercises](/articles/future-physical-therapy-estimate-home-program). If the disputed date appears on the bill rather than the chart, read [how to reconcile repeated service dates after an overnight stay](/articles/medical-bill-repeated-service-dates-overnight-stay).

title: Your Hospital Bill Repeats a Service Date After an Overnight Stay
excerpt: Compare the encounter period, line date, units and provider before treating two entries from an overnight hospital visit as duplicates.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Hospital Bill Repeats a Service Date After an Overnight Stay
metaDescription: Compare the encounter period, line date, units and provider before treating two entries from an overnight hospital visit as duplicates.
content:
A visit starts late Tuesday and ends Wednesday morning. The statement lists the same service date on several lines, and two descriptions look alike. Check which date the bill is showing and whether the entries represent distinct services, units or providers. Matching dates are a cue to ask for the detail behind the charges.

## Identify which date is on the statement

Request an itemized bill and write down the account number, admission or arrival date and discharge date. For the lines in question, ask for the line date, description, billing code where available, units, billing entity and any adjustment or reversal. Note whether the display repeats an encounter date or shows a date for each service. CMS's sample medical bill guide explains the role of service dates, charges and insurance payments on a bill. [CMS guide to reading your medical bill](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/how-read-your-bill)

CMS's institutional billing instructions distinguish the line-item date of service and apply specific reporting rules to Medicare outpatient bills and inpatient Part B bills. Use your provider's explanation of the bill and claim type to see which reporting convention applies. [CMS institutional billing instructions for line dates](https://www.cms.gov/outreach-and-education/mln/wbt/mln7388180-mln-wbt-1450/1450/lesson05/16/index.html)

## Match the lines by more than date

Suppose two $48 lines share the description “medication” and show Tuesday as the date. Ask the hospital whether the charge detail reflects different administrations, different products or a reversal and replacement. The code, units and administration time may clarify them. If the two entries are both active and the billing office ties them to the same administration, ask for a corrected itemization.

An overnight encounter can also generate separate facility and professional bills. An imaging line from the hospital and another from the group that read the images may concern the same scan while reflecting separate billed components. Compare the billing entity, service description and payer's explanation of benefits for each.

When appointments share one invoice, [match each therapy date and receipt to its claim line](/articles/reconcile-therapy-invoice-multiple-service-dates). If an existing copay was assigned to the wrong visit, [ask the office to trace the posting](/articles/copay-credited-wrong-service-date).

## Ask the billing office to reconcile a specific pair

Provide the account number and the two line references, and ask which service, time and units each line represents. Request a dated updated statement or a written explanation of why both entries belong. Use the [Duplicate Medical Bill Finder](/tools/medical-bill-duplicate-finder) to flag similar lines for review. Compare any revised statement with [the current EOB and the payments already posted](/articles/medical-bill-balance-after-revised-eob).

If the second bill comes from a separate imaging provider you expected to see on a self-pay estimate, use [the good faith estimate guide](/articles/good-faith-estimate-missing-imaging-provider). If the same line reappeared on a Medicare recovery demand, see [how to match it to the earlier removal](/articles/medicare-recovery-demand-includes-removed-service).

title: The Good Faith Estimate Left Out a Separate Imaging Provider
excerpt: Identify who billed for the scan and the reading, compare each provider's written estimate, and check the self-pay dispute process.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Good Faith Estimate Left Out a Separate Imaging Provider
metaDescription: Identify who billed for the scan and the reading, compare each provider's written estimate, and check the self-pay dispute process.
content:
You scheduled care as a self-pay patient. The clinic gave you an estimate, then a separate radiology group billed for reading the images. Ask who billed each component and which entity's charges your estimate listed. The estimate and bill need to correspond to the same provider or facility before you compare the amounts.

## Find the billing entity for each charge

Keep the dated estimate and the initial bills from the clinic and the imaging group. Write down the provider or facility name, service date, description and account reference for each line. Ask the scheduling office whether imaging was part of the arranged care and whether the scan and interpretation were expected to be billed separately. Ask the imaging group whether it issued its own written estimate and for a copy if it did.

CMS's current consumer guide explains that an estimate may cover a single provider or facility even when several participate in scheduled care. Federal guidance describes enforcement discretion for some estimates that omit co-provider or co-facility charges while further rulemaking is pending. These sources apply to the uninsured or self-pay estimate process. [CMS guide to good faith estimates](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/what-good-faith-estimate) · [HHS co-provider guidance](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/good-faith-estimate-uninsured-self-pay-part-3.pdf)

If both the imaging center and radiologist sent claims, [match the radiology bill to the right EOB](/articles/match-radiology-bill-eob-claim-number). When a billing service sends the statement under its own name, [confirm which provider and claim it represents](/articles/eob-no-provider-name-billing-company-statement).

## Compare each bill with its own estimate

For an example, the facility estimates $900 and bills $930. A radiology group then bills $520 for the interpretation. The facility's difference is $30. The radiology charge needs to be compared with the group's written estimate if one exists. Combining both bills and subtracting the facility's $900 estimate would mix two providers.

CMS says the federal patient-provider dispute process may be available if a provider or facility bills at least $400 more than its good faith estimate and the other requirements are met. The initial bill must be within the applicable 120-calendar-day filing window. If you have no written estimate from the billing provider, CMS explains how to submit a complaint and ask about other options. [CMS patient-provider dispute instructions](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/dispute-bill)

## Ask for a written reconciliation

Ask both billing offices to confirm the roles, itemized amounts and any estimate they sent. Use the [Claim Expense and Receipt Tracker](/tools/receipt-coverage-map) to separate the clinic, imaging facility and interpreting group's entries. If repeated dates are part of the confusion, see [how to compare lines on an overnight hospital bill](/articles/medical-bill-repeated-service-dates-overnight-stay). For care billed to a health plan rather than self-pay, [check the insurer's processing and the provider's current balance](/articles/medical-bill-balance-after-revised-eob).

title: A Removed Service Reappeared on Your Medicare Recovery Demand
excerpt: Match the disputed service across the conditional payment history and the demand, then use the appeal instructions for the named debtor.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Removed Service Reappeared on Your Medicare Recovery Demand
metaDescription: Match the disputed service across the conditional payment history and the demand, then use the appeal instructions for the named debtor.
content:
You received a revised Medicare conditional payment list after disputing an unrelated service. The final demand now appears to include it again. Compare the line identifiers before comparing totals. A later demand may reflect a new claims search, and two entries with the same provider and date can represent different services or adjustments.

## Assemble the record in issue order

Keep the original Conditional Payment Letter or detail, your relatedness dispute, the written result or updated detail showing the removal, and the final demand with its attachment. Note the case identifier, date each version was issued and who is named as debtor. CMS explains the role of conditional payment information, how beneficiaries can dispute unrelated items and when the recovery demand follows. [CMS beneficiary recovery process](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process)

Create a row with the service date, provider, paid amount, billing or claim identifier where shown, and the reason it was removed. Then match it against the demand detail. If you see a $180 payment from the same office on the same day, look for the procedure and reference number before assuming it is the removed $180 line. A reversal or reprocessed claim can change identifiers. Ask the recovery contractor to explain any apparent replacement.

If you're still waiting on a formal demand, [compare two interim repayment estimates](/articles/compare-repayment-estimates-pending-demand). If the closing statement already uses one of those numbers, [ask whether it is a reserve or a projection](/articles/settlement-statement-lists-estimated-lien).

## Use the procedure on the actual demand

If the demand is directed to you and you dispute the amount or the existence of the debt, CMS describes appeal rights for the named debtor. Its guidance states that the appeal must be filed within 120 days of receipt of the demand. Follow the notice for the filing method and include the demand identifier, matched lines and the earlier determination. CMS also explains that interest may accrue during an appeal, so review the payment and appeal instructions together. [CMS reimbursement and appeal guidance](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/overview/reimbursing)

A concise request can say which item was removed, show where it appears now, and ask for the basis for including it. Save the submission confirmation and any later decision. Use the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner) to record receipt of the demand and the deadline you verified.

If two services are difficult to distinguish on the provider's bill, see [how to read repeated line dates](/articles/medical-bill-repeated-service-dates-overnight-stay). If the Medicare item appears twice on a closing statement, see [how to reconcile a possible duplicate settlement deduction](/articles/duplicate-lien-settlement-statement).

title: What an Injury-Claim Photo Can Show About Activity Duration
excerpt: Document the start, stop, breaks and assistance around a photographed activity so the image has an accurate time context.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: What an Injury-Claim Photo Can Show About Activity Duration
metaDescription: Document the start, stop, breaks and assistance around a photographed activity so the image has an accurate time context.
content:
A photo shows you standing on a trail after a crash. The picture captures a moment of standing. To describe the activity accurately, document how long you walked, how often you stopped, what help you used and what happened afterward. Start with the original file and keep your explanation separate from the image.

## Distinguish capture time from activity time

Preserve the photo as received or taken, including the surrounding files if they are available. Record who captured it, when and how you obtained it. Save any original metadata and compare capture time, posting time and the time shown by a second record. If you make a marked-up version, identify it as a working copy. NIST's evidence guidance discusses keeping digital material intact and documenting its handling. [NIST digital evidence preservation guidance](https://www.nist.gov/publications/digital-evidence-preservation-considerations-evidence-handlers)

Build a short activity record. Use confirmed start and stop times where you have them, any stops or assistance, and the source for each detail. If you estimate a duration from a text or a witness's recollection, label it as an estimate. A sequence of photos can provide more context than an individual image, particularly when combined with a route, entry receipt or message.

## Show the parts of the activity the photo leaves open

In a hypothetical example, a picture at 11:12 a.m. shows a person standing at an overlook. A parking receipt and a companion's messages place the outing between 10:58 and 11:30. The person walked for roughly six minutes, rested twice and accepted a ride back. Put the documented period, walking estimate and observed assistance in separate fields. If the symptoms changed later that afternoon, keep a contemporaneous note with its own time.

In *Forman v. Henkin*, New York's Court of Appeals addressed requests for social media material in an injury case and tied the scope of disclosure to relevance and the issues being litigated. The court discussed the kinds of information images and metadata could reveal. Review the scope of any actual discovery request with counsel and preserve the original material. [New York Court of Appeals opinion in Forman](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2018/2018_01015.htm)

## Record the context while it is fresh

Use the [Daily Function Journal](/tools/daily-function-journal) to record duration, breaks, help and recovery time. Keep the note factual and tie it to the corresponding date. For social media data needed in discovery, see [what to collect when an account was deleted or deactivated](/articles/injury-discovery-deleted-social-media-account-export). If a revised therapy plan also documents activity restrictions, see [how to separate past care from the current home program](/articles/future-physical-therapy-estimate-home-program).

title: How to Calculate a Shift Differential Lost During an Injury Absence
excerpt: Use the assigned shifts and payroll rate to calculate missed premium pay separately from base wages and overtime.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Calculate a Shift Differential Lost During an Injury Absence
metaDescription: Use the assigned shifts and payroll rate to calculate missed premium pay separately from base wages and overtime.
content:
Before your injury, you were scheduled to work nights. When you returned, the employer assigned day shifts at the same base rate. To measure what changed, use the actual schedule and payroll rules for the night premium. Track full missed shifts separately from shifts you worked at a different rate.

## Confirm which hours qualified for the premium

Collect the posted schedule, time cards, wage statements and the employer's pay policy or applicable agreement. Ask payroll to identify the premium amount, eligible hours and any conditions. Some policies apply a premium to certain hours within a shift. Others pay a different rate for the full shift. Match the applicable rule to each work date.

Compare the schedule made before the injury with what was worked or paid. If your shifts changed from week to week, use a representative set of actual schedules and explain why they are comparable. Ask the employer to confirm any known staffing or schedule change that would have affected the assignment regardless of your injury.

## Calculate the premium and the base amounts separately

Suppose two eight-hour night shifts were assigned, the base rate was $22 and the differential was $2.50 per eligible hour. If all 16 hours qualified, the premium was $40 and the base pay was $352. If both shifts were unpaid because they were missed, those two components total $392 before any other payroll item. If you worked the same 16 hours on days at the base rate, the difference in this example is the $40 premium.

Overtime requires its own comparison. The federal overtime regulation includes shift differentials in the regular rate for overtime under the FLSA. Ask payroll for its actual calculation if overtime would have applied. Keep any paid leave or replacement payment in a separate column and identify what period it covers. [29 CFR § 778.207 on shift premiums and overtime](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/778.207)

## Send an itemization a reviewer can recalculate

Use the [Hourly Lost Work Calculator](/tools/hourly-lost-work-calculator) for the base hours and an attached line for each shift premium or overtime item. The California civil instruction on past earnings illustrates the need to support the amount actually lost. Applicable damages rules depend on the case. [California civil jury instruction on lost earnings, CACI No. 3903C](https://www.justia.com/trials-litigation/docs/caci/3900/3903c/)

If payroll kept your salary but deducted leave for a phased return, see [how to compare half days with salary and leave records](/articles/salaried-employee-half-days-after-injury-lost-pay). If the disputed pay was an app incentive, see [how to document a missed rideshare bonus](/articles/missed-rideshare-weekly-bonus-after-crash).

title: Your California Employer Gave You a DWC-1 Without a Date
excerpt: Record when you received the claim form, prove when you returned it, and ask for the employer's completed dated copy.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your California Employer Gave You a DWC-1 Without a Date
metaDescription: Record when you received the claim form, prove when you returned it, and ask for the employer's completed dated copy.
content:
The employer hands you a workers' compensation form with its date fields blank. Write down when you received it and complete the employee portion with the facts you can verify. The date the form was provided and the date the completed form reached the employer are separate entries on California's DWC-1.

## Match each date to what happened

Get the current form from California's Division of Workers' Compensation. The employer section distinguishes when the employer first knew about the injury, when it provided the form and when it received the completed form. Keep a copy of what you received, including any email, envelope or other delivery record. Enter your own injury and signature information in the employee section. Ask the employer to fill its own section. [California DWC-1 claim form and instructions](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dwc/DWCForm1.pdf)

Return the completed employee portion using the process in the DWC's instructions and keep proof of delivery or receipt. The DWC recommends keeping a copy and describes certified mail with a return receipt if you submit by mail. If you hand it in, note the date, person and location and ask for written acknowledgment. [California DWC claim filing guide](https://www.dir.ca.gov/dwc/FileAClaim.htm)

## Ask for the dated copy after return

California's regulation requires the employer to date the form and provide a dated copy to the employee and claims administrator within one working day after receiving the completed claim form. For example, if the form was handed out Monday and delivered back on Wednesday, record both dates and ask for the copy reflecting Wednesday's receipt. Save your receipt confirmation with the form. [California Code of Regulations, title 8, § 10140](https://www.dir.ca.gov/t8/10140.html)

If the copy has the wrong date or you did not receive one, send a short written request identifying the injury and when you returned the form. Attach your receipt record and ask for the completed copy and claims administrator contact. California DWC's filing guide explains where to get assistance if you need help with the process.

## Keep the filing timeline with the injury records

Use the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner) to track notice of injury, receipt of the blank form, return and receipt of the dated copy. If the injury involved rented equipment, see [what to request from the equipment supplier and site](/articles/rented-boom-lift-maintenance-tag-delivery-inspection). If you went back on a limited schedule, preserve the restrictions, work hours and pay records using [the half-day return guide](/articles/salaried-employee-half-days-after-injury-lost-pay).

title: Which Appointment Date Starts a New York Wrongful Death Notice Period?
excerpt: Find the estate representative's appointment record and track municipal notice, service and lawsuit dates on separate lines.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Which Appointment Date Starts a New York Wrongful Death Notice Period?
metaDescription: Find the estate representative's appointment record and track municipal notice, service and lawsuit dates on separate lines.
content:
A family has a death certificate, a petition for administration and later letters appointing the estate's representative. For a New York wrongful death claim subject to the municipal notice requirement, the appointment record matters. Identify the date the court appointed the representative and the public entity to be served.

## Use the court record for the appointment date

Collect the signed appointment order or decree, issued letters and court docket information. Keep the petition date and death date alongside them. If an order and the letters appear to show different dates, ask counsel or the court clerk to clarify the appointment record before calculating the deadline. Preserve any restriction or later amendment to the letters.

New York General Municipal Law § 50-e generally requires notice within 90 days of the claim arising where the statute applies. For wrongful death actions it measures the 90 days from appointment of the estate representative. The section also addresses who must be served and how. Check the rule for the particular public entity involved. [New York General Municipal Law § 50-e](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GMU/50-E)

## Track service and commencement independently

In *Ramos v. New York City Transit Authority*, an Appellate Division opinion identifies September 26, 2005 as the date letters of administration were granted. The court explained that a summons and complaint served within 90 days of appointment did not serve as the required wrongful death notice, and it permitted an amendment to a previously timely notice on the facts before it. That case illustrates why you should identify the document served, its recipient and its date. [Appellate Division opinion in Ramos](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2009/2009_01912.htm)

Section 50-i separately sets a two-year period from death for wrongful death actions against the municipal entities it covers, subject to the applicable law. A claim for the decedent's own injuries can involve a different clock. Verify each claim, entity and deadline while you gather the records. [New York General Municipal Law § 50-i](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GMU/50-I)

## Keep proof of the specific document served

Record the notice version, service method, recipient, address and proof of service. Store it with the appointment documents. Use the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner) for dates checked against the applicable rule. If the entity is uncertain or the clock may be running, ask a New York lawyer promptly about the specific records and service options.

For the broader claim documents, see [the wrongful death guide](/articles/wrongful-death-lawsuits-in-2026-a-familys-complete-guide-to-seeking-justice). For a separate example of how proper receipt can matter when the wrong office gets a claim, see [California's government vehicle claim guide](/articles/california-government-vehicle-claim-wrong-agency).

title: You Sent a California Government Vehicle Claim to the Wrong Agency
excerpt: Identify the public entity and its designated recipient, then determine whether the claim actually reached the proper office in time.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: You Sent a California Government Vehicle Claim to the Wrong Agency
metaDescription: Identify the public entity and its designated recipient, then determine whether the claim actually reached the proper office in time.
content:
After a crash with a government vehicle, you mailed the claim to the department on the door. The agency's insurer says another office handles claims. Identify the legal public entity and the statutory recipient. The department that operates a vehicle and the office authorized to receive a claim may be different.

## Confirm which public entity the documents identify

Keep the crash report, agency vehicle identifiers, registration information if available and any letter naming the employer, operator or claims administrator. Ask the department to confirm the legal name of the entity responsible for receiving claims. A city, county and the State of California can have separate routes. California Courts' guide distinguishes the state claims process from filing with a local agency. It describes the usual six-month presentation deadline for injury or property damage claims. [California Courts government claim guide](https://selfhelp.courts.ca.gov/civil-lawsuit/government-claim)

## Trace where the first submission actually went

Keep the signed claim, envelopes or delivery records, and any acknowledgment from the office that received it. Ask if it forwarded the exact claim, to whom and when. Request the receiving office's proof of receipt. California Government Code § 915 sets out presentation methods. It also has an actual-receipt provision that can apply when the proper recipient receives the claim within the prescribed time. The listed recipient depends on the entity. [California Government Code § 915](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-gov/title-1/division-3-6/part-3/chapter-2/article-2/section-915/)

For example, a local department acknowledges a letter on Monday and sends it to the public entity's clerk on Thursday. Confirm when the clerk actually received the claim, the version that arrived and the deadline for the claim. The department's Monday acknowledgment and the clerk's receipt document different facts.

## Address any remaining time while checking receipt

If the usual period is still open, confirm the proper form and presentation method for the entity promptly. If it may have expired, get advice about whether a late-claim application under § 911.4 or another route applies. That section has its own requirements and time limits. Keep a record of any rejection or late-claim notice and the date you received it. [California Government Code § 911.4](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-gov/title-1/division-3-6/part-3/chapter-2/article-1/section-911-4/)

Use the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner) to record each dispatch, receipt and verified deadline. For a distinct illustration of how the filing clock depends on the governing rule, read [the New York wrongful death appointment and notice guide](/articles/new-york-wrongful-death-notice-appointment-date). If the crash report itself omits a contact, see [how to identify a missing impact and request a supplement](/articles/police-crash-report-missing-second-impact).

title: Your Draft Settlement Release Lists the Wrong Crash Date
excerpt: Match the draft release to the claim, incident and agreed payment. Request a corrected version and verify its scope before signing.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Draft Settlement Release Lists the Wrong Crash Date
metaDescription: Match the draft release to the claim, incident and agreed payment. Request a corrected version and verify its scope before signing.
content:
You agreed on an amount after a June 8 crash, but the draft release says June 18. Ask for a corrected document and check where else the date appears. The date can help identify the incident and define the claims the release would resolve. Review it alongside the rest of the agreement.

## Identify the incident from independent records

Compare the police report or other contemporaneous record, your insurer's acknowledgment and the written offer. Confirm the date, location, claim number, parties and vehicle. A claim number can identify the file even when the document also carries the wrong date. If there were two accidents or two claims involving the same car, check both references.

Read the definition of the occurrence, description of the released claims and list of released parties. Check each attachment, signature packet and proposed payment schedule for the same identifiers. California Civil Code § 1641 illustrates the principle of reading a contract as a whole and giving effect to its parts where possible. The applicable rule depends on the agreement and jurisdiction. [California Civil Code § 1641](https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-civ/division-3/part-2/title-3/section-1641/)

## Ask for a corrected draft with the same agreed terms

A message can identify the draft version and paragraph, state the date supported by the records and request an updated draft and a list of changes. Ask the preparer to confirm which claims and parties the agreement covers. Compare the new version with the offer, including the amount, payment conditions and any separate provision on unknown claims or other losses.

In *Pastrana-Ortiz v. Wemple*, a New York appellate court addressed a signed release following a rear-end crash and found factual issues about the parties' understanding of injuries and the circumstances of signing. The dispute concerned the signed agreement. Correcting a draft before execution is a practical way to keep the intended incident clear. [New York Appellate Division opinion in Pastrana-Ortiz](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2025/2025_03425.htm)

If you have only discussed the offer on the phone, [record its terms and ask for the complete proposed release](/articles/record-spoken-settlement-offer-before-release). If the offer letter omits the expiration date, [get the exact cutoff in writing](/articles/insurance-offer-expires-no-date-in-letter).

## Keep the versions with the settlement file

Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to match the corrected date and other identifiers with the supporting documents. If a version was already signed, save it as executed and ask qualified counsel how to address the discrepancy under the applicable law.

If the agreement promises installments, compare the release against [the first-payment schedule and any funding conditions](/articles/structured-settlement-schedule-missing-first-payment-date). If an earlier insurance payment is affected by a separate fee document, see [how to check which recovery the fee addendum covers](/articles/contingency-fee-addendum-after-insurance-payment).

title: Injury Discovery Asks for an Export From a Deleted Social Media Account
excerpt: Document the account's status, preserve available archives and identify what can be recovered within the scope of the discovery request.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Injury Discovery Asks for an Export From a Deleted Social Media Account
metaDescription: Document the account's status, preserve available archives and identify what can be recovered within the scope of the discovery request.
content:
A discovery request asks for a social media export from an account you no longer use. First identify what happened to the account and when. An account that was deactivated, an account you requested to delete and an account you simply cannot access present different record problems. Keep any confirmation emails or messages showing the actual status.

## Identify the accounts, dates and materials requested

Give the request and any court order to the lawyer handling the claim. List the platform, account identifier, relevant period and categories requested. Record the last time you could access the account and any deletion, deactivation or lockout notices. Preserve the files you already have, including older downloads, device copies, attachments and existing screenshots. Keep their source and date.

For an account you can access, see which export categories, dates and formats are available. Meta describes its account-center tools for downloading information across its apps. Platform capabilities vary. Keep the original archive and a record of what you requested and received. If access is unavailable, document what the service confirms and ask counsel how to address gaps or seek records through the appropriate process. [Meta's information-access tools](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/10/manage-your-information-across-apps/)

## Tie the response to the scope and preservation rules

In *Forman v. Henkin*, the New York Court of Appeals considered discovery from a deactivated Facebook account and linked the scope of discovery to relevance and the issues in the case. A particular request can be limited by date, content and purpose. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) addresses electronically stored information that should have been preserved for litigation, was lost because of a failure to take reasonable preservation steps, and is unrecoverable through additional discovery. Check the rules and order in your own case. [New York Court of Appeals opinion in Forman](https://www.nycourts.gov/Reporter/3dseries/2018/2018_01015.htm) · [U.S. Courts Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule 37(e)](https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/current-rules-practice-procedure/federal-rules-civil-procedure)

## Make a record of what you can provide

Keep a source list separating an actual platform archive, locally saved copies and items you know only from a notice or recollection. Record unsuccessful access or export attempts with dates and relevant responses. Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to track categories and sources without pasting private messages into a shared file.

For the context behind a photo, see [how to record the length and limits of the activity it shows](/articles/document-activity-duration-photo-injury-claim). For a technical comparison of preserved and working files, see [how to use a checksum for a dashcam copy](/articles/verify-dashcam-copy-preserve-memory-card).

title: Your Future Physical Therapy Estimate Changed to a Home Program
excerpt: Compare the dated care plans and recalculate the remaining appointments, equipment and follow-ups using the current recommendation.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Future Physical Therapy Estimate Changed to a Home Program
metaDescription: Compare the dated care plans and recalculate the remaining appointments, equipment and follow-ups using the current recommendation.
content:
An early estimate assumes weekly physical therapy for three months. Your clinician later recommends a home program with a check-in. Update the future-cost calculation using the current plan. Keep care already received, recommended future care and possible care if symptoms change on separate lines.

## Find the written change and the remaining services

Request the earlier and current plan or discharge note. Record when the change was made, what supervised visits remain, what follow-up is recommended, and which equipment or instruction is part of the new plan. Ask whether the check-in is scheduled, contingent on progress or already included in another visit. Collect written prices from the appropriate provider or supplier.

The Medicare Benefit Policy Manual discusses recording therapy type, amount, frequency and duration and documenting changes to the plan. That is Medicare guidance. The dated clinical record provides the basis for describing the care recommended in your own case. [CMS Medicare Benefit Policy Manual, chapter 15, § 220.1.2](https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/bp102c15.pdf)

## Reprice the remaining plan line by line

Suppose the earlier projection listed 12 visits at $110 each, for $1,320. The updated plan specifies two $110 follow-ups and a $45 piece of equipment. The updated future total for those items is $265. Keep the cost of any visits already attended in the past-care record. If the therapist recommends more appointments only if function worsens, list the trigger and the source as a separate scenario.

State whether a figure is a provider estimate, an insurance copayment or another expected out-of-pocket amount. Use comparable price types when totaling a scenario. California's civil jury instruction on future medical expenses illustrates the distinction between reasonably necessary future care and its reasonable cost. The applicable damages rules depend on the jurisdiction and record. [California civil jury instruction on medical expenses, CACI No. 3903A](https://www.justia.com/trials-litigation/docs/caci/3900/3903a/)

## Tie every cost to the current plan

Use the [Future Care Cost Planner](/tools/care-cost-scenario-planner) for the dated current recommendation and its unit prices. Attach the old estimate for comparison and note which items changed. For details on when the change was entered in the chart, read [the medical record addendum guide](/articles/medical-record-addendum-entered-weeks-after-visit). If you need to document how long you can perform the exercises or another daily activity, see [how to record duration, breaks and assistance](/articles/document-activity-duration-photo-injury-claim).

title: You Returned to Salaried Work for Half Days After an Injury
excerpt: Compare gross salary, hours and leave balances by pay period to show whether reduced hours caused lost pay or used paid leave.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: You Returned to Salaried Work for Half Days After an Injury
metaDescription: Compare gross salary, hours and leave balances by pay period to show whether reduced hours caused lost pay or used paid leave.
content:
A medical restriction limits your return to four hours a day. Your salary may stay the same while you use accrued leave, or the pay statement may show unpaid time. Compare what was scheduled, what you worked, what you were paid and which leave account changed. Keep those measures separate in the claim record.

## Ask payroll to explain the affected pay periods

Collect the written restriction, return-to-work schedule, gross pay stubs and leave statements before, during and after the half days. Ask the employer to confirm your usual hours, hours worked, paid leave used, unpaid leave and any changes to base salary or recurring compensation. Use gross amounts consistently and flag a benefit or withholding change if it alters your take-home comparison.

For employees covered by the federal salary-basis exemption rules, federal regulations specify when salary deductions may be made, including an exception for unpaid FMLA leave. The FMLA regulations separately address how reduced-schedule leave is counted when applicable. Whether a deduction was permitted depends on the worker's classification, leave and governing law. [29 CFR § 541.602 on the salary basis](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/541.602) · [29 CFR § 825.205 on reduced-schedule FMLA leave](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/825.205)

## Compare pay and leave as separate amounts

In an example, usual gross pay is $1,200 per week. You work half days for two weeks and receive $2,400 total. Payroll records 40 hours of paid leave used. The pay comparison shows no reduction in gross salary in that period. The leave ledger shows 40 hours used. Ask the reviewer how the applicable claim treats used leave and preserve the employer's balance records.

If gross pay actually fell, compare the amount paid with the documented usual amount for the same period. Show any paid leave or wage-replacement benefit on its own line and record the dates it covers. A change in net deposit can also reflect withholding, so explain discrepancies using the detailed pay record.

## Keep a dated record of each phase

Use the [Phased Return-to-Work Planner](/tools/phased-return-work-planner) to record restrictions, hours and changes in schedule. If the reduction also changed shift premiums, see [how to calculate the missed differential separately](/articles/calculate-lost-shift-differential-injury). If your return followed a California work injury, keep the schedule with [the record of when the DWC-1 was returned](/articles/california-dwc-1-employer-did-not-date-form).

title: A Contingency Fee Addendum Came After One Insurance Payment
excerpt: Compare the original fee agreement and later addendum against the date, coverage and amount of each insurance payment.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Contingency Fee Addendum Came After One Insurance Payment
metaDescription: Compare the original fee agreement and later addendum against the date, coverage and amount of each insurance payment.
content:
One insurer paid a claim under one coverage. Later you signed an addendum changing the contingency fee for your matter. Ask which recoveries each document covers and when the change took effect. The date of a payment and the description of the legal work covered by the agreement both matter to the accounting.

## Collect the signed versions and the payment record

Save the original agreement, the full signed addendum and any correspondence explaining its effective date. Identify each payment by insurer, coverage, check or transfer date, amount and payee. Note whether it was deposited into a trust account or already disbursed. Ask for the existing settlement statement and any fee or cost entries tied to that payment.

California's State Bar describes contingency fees and the role of the fee agreement in determining what you pay. California Business and Professions Code § 6147 requires specified information for covered contingency agreements, including the rate and how costs and disbursements affect the fee and recovery. Check which jurisdiction and contract terms apply to your representation. [State Bar of California fees and billing guide](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/public/legal-resources/working-attorney/what-expect-regarding-fees-and-billing) · [California State Bar Act, § 6147](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-09/State_Bar_Act.pdf)

If your agreement applies a fee to only one recovery, [calculate the fee on that specific coverage payment](/articles/calculate-settlement-fee-one-coverage-payment). If you paid a case cost early, [track it separately from the amount withheld at closing](/articles/calculate-settlement-net-costs-already-paid).

## Ask for the calculation for each recovery

For an illustration, the first carrier paid $15,000 before the addendum and a second paid $35,000 after it. Applying 25% to the first and 33% to the second produces fees of $3,750 and $11,550 before considering costs. Applying 33% to both produces a different total. Ask the lawyer to identify which signed provision supports each rate, what amount it applies to and how any costs enter the computation.

If the addendum says it covers further work or a different coverage, ask how the statement reflects that language. If it uses a date or trigger that could include the earlier payment, ask for the firm's written explanation and compare it with the signed copies. For an unresolved dispute, consult the applicable bar's fee dispute information or independent counsel.

## Request an itemized statement

Use the [Net Settlement Comparison Tool](/tools/offer-net-comparison) to compare the fee calculations and costs you were given. Keep different treatments as clearly labeled scenarios until the parties confirm the governing terms. If the release lists the wrong incident, see [how to reconcile the draft with the offer](/articles/settlement-release-wrong-crash-date). For a later installment payment, see [which schedule establishes when it begins](/articles/structured-settlement-schedule-missing-first-payment-date).

title: Your Structured Settlement Schedule Has No First Payment Date
excerpt: Compare the release, assignment, annuity schedule and any approval order to identify the first due date and who will confirm it.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Structured Settlement Schedule Has No First Payment Date
metaDescription: Compare the release, assignment, annuity schedule and any approval order to identify the first due date and who will confirm it.
content:
Your structured settlement lists monthly payments but leaves the start date blank. Get the actual schedule before budgeting around it. A proposed illustration, signed settlement agreement, assignment and annuity schedule can describe different stages. Find the controlling documents and compare their amounts and timing.

## Identify the signed payment obligation

Ask for the signed agreement or release and its payment exhibit, any qualified assignment, the issued annuity schedule if available, and any approval order required in the case. Look for the payee, amount, payment interval, first payment date and any event that starts the schedule. Separate an up-front cash payment from recurring payments and any future lump sums.

For a qualified assignment under federal tax law, 26 U.S.C. § 130 defines conditions including periodic payments fixed and determinable as to amount and timing. The statute also describes the relationship between a qualifying funding asset and the periodic payments. Read the actual agreement and assignment to determine how your schedule is set. [26 U.S.C. § 130](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-136/t26/s130/)

## Ask for a written start date from the responsible party

Some records identify an obligor or assignee and an annuity issuer. Record which entity confirms the payment obligation and which handles delivery. New York's structured settlement definitions, in a law governing transfers of payment rights, distinguish the obligor, annuity issuer and documents that describe the arrangement. Your agreement identifies the roles for your case. [New York General Obligations Law § 5-1701](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GOB/5-1701)

In an example, the signed exhibit says the first $750 payment is due January 15, while a preliminary estimate leaves the date blank.
