Compare the final documents and ask for confirmation that they agree. If the agreement instead ties commencement to funding or approval, request proof of the triggering event and the resulting calendar date. Record when the payment is due and how and when it is expected to arrive.

## Use the confirmed schedule for planning

Enter the dates confirmed from your documents in the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner). Keep any missing or conflicting date open for written resolution before relying on it. If a date or incident in the release itself differs from the agreed terms, see [how to reconcile the draft release](/articles/settlement-release-wrong-crash-date). If the distribution also includes a contingency fee deduction, read [how to trace the signed fee terms to each payment](/articles/contingency-fee-addendum-after-insurance-payment).

title: Your Medical Bill Still Shows a Balance After a Revised EOB
excerpt: Match the revised insurance statement to your earlier payment and ask the provider for a line-by-line account reconciliation.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Medical Bill Still Shows a Balance After a Revised EOB
metaDescription: Match the revised insurance statement to your earlier payment and ask the provider for a line-by-line account reconciliation.
content:
A revised explanation of benefits (EOB) can change the amount your health plan assigns to you while the hospital still displays an old balance. Reconcile those two records with your payment receipt before treating the number on either screen as the amount still due. The insurer explains how it processed the claim. The provider's ledger shows what it actually charged and collected. [CMS guide to reading an EOB](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits)

## Find the version the provider posted

Open the original and revised EOBs together. Find the service date, provider, claim reference and service line. Look for a replacement or adjustment indicator and record the date the plan processed the revision. If the plan issued a new reference number, ask it to identify which earlier claim that number replaces.

Now ask the provider for the current itemized bill and the existing payment history for that encounter. A balance-only screen hides the useful columns. You want the dates and amounts of patient payments, insurer payments, adjustments and any reversal or transfer between accounts. HHS identifies billing, payment and claims records as examples of records that can be accessible under HIPAA when the rule applies. [HHS guidance on access to billing records](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/faq/what-personal-health-information-do-individuals/index.html)

## Follow the money through one example

Suppose you paid $150 at check-in. The first EOB assigned you $340, and the provider sent a bill for $190 after crediting the deposit. The revised EOB assigns you $220. If the provider posts the revision and the $150 remains credited to that same encounter, the remaining amount in this example is $70. If the portal shows $220, check where the deposit went. If it still shows $190, ask whether the provider has posted the revised insurer remittance.

A single visit can produce separate hospital and physician bills. Match the receipt to the same billing entity before subtracting a payment. Enter the insurer's current patient responsibility and the payment actually credited to the account in the [Medical Bill and EOB Reconciler](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler).

If your statement combines services from two notices, [match one provider bill to both EOBs](/articles/reconcile-one-provider-bill-two-eobs). If both notices have the same claim number, [identify which version the plan still uses](/articles/two-revised-eobs-same-claim-number).

## Ask for the corrected balance in writing

> I paid $150 on May 4. The revised EOB for the May 4 encounter assigns $220 to me. Please confirm the revised claim was posted, identify the ledger entry for my payment and send an itemized statement showing the current balance.

Send it through the provider's secure channel. If billing or collection notices continue while the provider researches the payment, ask for written confirmation of the account's status and keep the notices. For a balance involving an auto-insurance payment, see [how to trace MedPay through a hospital ledger](/articles/medpay-hospital-payment-before-health-insurance-reprocessing). If the health plan actually denied a service, start with [the imaging authorization guide](/articles/health-plan-denied-imaging-after-facility-change).

title: The Adjuster Says Your Portal Upload Is Missing
excerpt: Use the upload receipt, file names and claim number to locate an insurance submission and document what the adjuster can open.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Adjuster Says Your Portal Upload Is Missing
metaDescription: Use the upload receipt, file names and claim number to locate an insurance submission and document what the adjuster can open.
content:
A portal's confirmation is useful evidence of the submission you attempted. The practical problem is whether the correct documents reached the adjuster's view of the right claim. Solve that with a file-level inventory and a written acknowledgment. Re-uploading every attachment without a list makes it harder to tell whether the original packet was found.

## Separate the upload from the attachment

Save the full confirmation screen or email, including its time, any submission ID and the claim number shown. Save the originals in the form you sent them. Build a short inventory with the exact file names, page counts and descriptions. If the receipt shows only one batch number, keep your inventory labeled as your own record of what you sent.

Consider an upload containing three PDFs. The receipt shows batch 8841 and the adjuster sees two PDFs. The difference could be one rejected file, a document assigned to a different claim activity, or a receipt that never identified its contents. Ask the adjuster to name the two readable attachments so you can isolate the third. If the company asks for a new copy, reference batch 8841 in the message and preserve both confirmations.

## Ask for a readable copy check

> Please confirm which documents from submission 8841 are visible and readable on claim 1234. My inventory shows estimate-v2.pdf (four pages), tow-receipt.pdf (one page) and photos-index.pdf (two pages). If a file is missing, please send the approved way to resend it and tell me which claim contact should receive it.

Use the [Insurance Claim Follow-Up Email Builder](/tools/claim-follow-up-composer) to turn those details into a short message. Keep sensitive attachments inside the carrier's approved channel. If an active deadline is near, check it on the policy or notice and confirm the insurer's designated way to submit the material.

If the request comes from a new adjuster, [share the original receipt and file list](/articles/new-adjuster-asks-for-already-submitted-records). For repeated requests, [log each upload and confirm whether the attachment opens](/articles/track-repeated-insurer-attachment-requests).

## When the missing record matters to a decision

Ask for the written decision and identify the document the insurer says it lacked. In Washington, the current claim-file rule requires enough detail to reconstruct pertinent events and permits insureds to request portions of a first-party claim file at reasonable intervals, subject to specified limits. That provides a way to ask for the carrier's record of the submission. It gives no assurance that a particular portal log exists. [Washington claim-file documentation rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-340)

If the dispute stays unresolved, retain the receipt, inventory, messages and response as a single packet. The Washington insurance regulator explains its consumer complaint process and what it reviews. [Washington Office of the Insurance Commissioner's complaint process](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/complaints-appeals-fraud/complaints/understanding-complaint-process)

For a denial that cites a different reason on review, compare both letters using [the guide to changed denial reasons](/articles/insurer-changed-denial-reason-complaint). For proof of which policy dates apply, see [how to assemble a renewal record](/articles/auto-claim-denied-wrong-policy-renewal-date).

title: The Same Lien Appears Twice on Your Settlement Statement
excerpt: Trace duplicate-looking medical bill and reimbursement entries to their payees and reconcile the net amount before disbursement.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Same Lien Appears Twice on Your Settlement Statement
metaDescription: Trace duplicate-looking medical bill and reimbursement entries to their payees and reconcile the net amount before disbursement.
content:
A closing statement might list $2,400 under medical bills and another $2,400 under reimbursement. Identical numbers deserve a question. The entries could represent the same obligation, distinct obligations, or a reserve shown beside a payment. The way to tell is to follow each proposed deduction to the person being paid and the record that authorizes it.

## Compare the payee, account and status

Take the two lines from the settlement statement and ask for the current document behind each. For a provider balance, match the billing entity, service dates and latest ledger. For a health-plan recovery demand, identify the plan or recovery administrator, its claim reference and the service lines in the demand. For a trust-account hold, identify the amount still being held and whether it has already reduced the amount payable to you.

An old lien notice and an updated payoff from the same creditor can describe one debt at different stages. Likewise, a provider balance and an insurer's demand can concern the same treatment while representing different amounts and different payees. Keep both on the worksheet until you can distinguish them. The [Duplicate Settlement Deduction Checker](/tools/deduction-overlap-checker) can flag repeated labels and amounts for follow-up.

## Reconcile the example to the dollar

Imagine a $30,000 settlement. The statement lists $10,000 in fees, $700 in costs, $2,400 as a hospital payment and $2,400 as a hospital reserve. Counting both entries leaves $14,500 for the client. Counting a single $2,400 deduction leaves $16,900. Ask the preparer to show whether the reserve is an additional amount to withhold or a note describing the same hospital item. A useful answer will identify who receives each dollar and which line belongs in the net calculation.

The question changes if a demand comes from Medicare. CMS distinguishes conditional payment information from the formal demand and describes a process for disputing charges unrelated to the case. Match the current demand and its underlying claims before treating a preliminary figure as the amount to disburse. [CMS guide to Medicare recovery](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process)

If a vendor invoice appears twice, [trace it across the cost and lien entries](/articles/duplicate-vendor-fees-settlement-statement). When a disputed amount remains held, [match the partial disbursement and the reserve](/articles/disputed-lien-held-in-trust-partial-disbursement).

## Request a statement that shows what happened

Ask for a revised statement identifying each amount paid, still held or released. If you have counsel, ask which funds remain disputed and what document will resolve each line. As one state example, California's Rule 1.15 addresses accounting for client funds and keeping disputed funds separate until the dispute is resolved. The rule that applies to your lawyer depends on the jurisdiction. [State Bar of California, Rule 1.15](https://www.calbar.ca.gov/legal-professionals/rules/rules-professional-conduct/current-rules-professional-conduct/chapter-1-lawyer-client-relationship)

For a bill that changed after health insurance reprocessed it, check [the revised EOB workflow](/articles/medical-bill-balance-after-revised-eob). When the payee is an employer health plan, trace the legal basis using [the guide to dated plan amendments](/articles/employer-health-plan-reimbursement-amendment-effective-date).

When the fee agreement changed during the claim, [match the fee version to each payment](/articles/contingency-fee-addendum-after-insurance-payment). For a structured settlement, [obtain a confirmed first payment date](/articles/structured-settlement-schedule-missing-first-payment-date).

title: A Total-Loss Check Went to Your Old Lender After a Refinance
excerpt: Reconcile the lender on your title, the payoff on your old loan and the insurer's check before requesting a corrected payment.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Total-Loss Check Went to Your Old Lender After a Refinance
metaDescription: Reconcile the lender on your title, the payoff on your old loan and the insurer's check before requesting a corrected payment.
content:
The insurer's check names the bank you paid off last month. Your new lender still shows the full loan balance. Start with the path the money actually took. A stale payee in the insurer's file, a release still in transit and a check already deposited by the old lender require different follow-up.

California's insurance department explains that a physical damage claim check may name the insured and a lienholder. The exact payees and title steps depend on the policy, the settlement and the title record. [California Department of Insurance's auto claims guide](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/105-type/95-guides/01-auto/upload/Accident-What-Next-w-05-27-21-Web-Only.pdf)

## Line up three records by VIN

1. **Old lender.** Obtain the payoff posting, account closure or balance confirmation and lien release. Ask whether the bank received the insurance check, returned it or deposited it. If deposited, ask where it posted.
2. **New lender.** Ask for its current payoff statement, the exact legal payee name and its lien filing or title status. The payoff can have a validity date. Record it with the amount.
3. **Insurer.** Ask for the check number, issue date, payee line and payment status. Ask which lender or title record it relied on and how its correction process works.

State title records can differ from an insurer's customer profile. For example, New York DMV describes filing a new lien and showing original proof of satisfaction to remove an old one from a title. Check the process with the state that issued yours. [New York DMV lienholder instructions](https://dmv.ny.gov/titles/add-or-remove-a-lienholder)

## Treat a pending check differently from a cleared one

If the old lender returned the check uncashed, provide the insurer with the documentation it asks for to void and reissue it. Ask it to confirm both steps in writing. If the check cleared, ask the insurer and the old lender to trace the proceeds before assuming a replacement check can be issued. Use a single timeline so each party sees when the refinance, loss, title filing and check processing occurred. [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder)

In an illustrative example, an insurer values a totaled car at $17,800 and the new lender quotes a $19,200 payoff. The $1,400 difference is separate from the payee error. Correcting the check does not change those two figures. If you bought GAP, read its terms and contact the provider about the documentation it needs. [CFPB guide to Guaranteed Asset Protection](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-guaranteed-asset-protection-gap-insurance-en-797/)

Keep the lender payoff date and scheduled payments visible while the correction is in progress. If the settlement figure itself looks wrong, separate that issue from check routing and follow [how to check a total-loss valuation date](/articles/appraisal-award-valuation-date-total-loss) or [how to document missing adaptive equipment](/articles/total-loss-valuation-missing-adaptive-equipment).

If a rental authorization is ending while a check is being traced, ask for the payment dispatch date and the benefit remaining. [How to check the rental cutoff after a total-loss offer](/articles/total-loss-rental-before-settlement-check).

title: A Repair Supplement Was Denied for a Missing Pre-Repair Scan Invoice
excerpt: Build a record tying the diagnostic scan to the damaged vehicle, the repair order and the exact supplement line the insurer declined.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Repair Supplement Was Denied for a Missing Pre-Repair Scan Invoice
metaDescription: Build a record tying the diagnostic scan to the damaged vehicle, the repair order and the exact supplement line the insurer declined.
content:
The shop says it scanned the car. The insurer says the supplement arrived without the invoice. Before debating the price, find out whether the missing record is the scan report, the invoice for a subcontracted scan or an in-house labor line on the shop's final bill. Those documents answer different questions.

## Match proof of the work to proof of the charge

Ask for the estimate version and disputed line number. Then request the scan printout or electronic report with the VIN, scan time and results. Ask for the corresponding itemized charge and repair order. For an outsourced scan, identify the vendor invoice the shop received. For an in-house scan, ask the shop to point to its own documentation and billing line. A scan report can show that diagnostics ran. It may not identify the amount charged for that operation.

California's repair regulations describe authorization for extra work and what belongs on an invoice for shops governed by those rules. Use the records to show which charge the shop documented. Payment still depends on the coverage and the insurer's review of the charge. [California's additional repair authorization rule](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/16-CCR-3354) · [California's repair invoice rule](https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/16-CCR-3356)

## Link the operation to the vehicle's procedure

American Honda's collision position statement specifies a preliminary diagnostic scan during estimating and a scan after repair for vehicles within its scope. For a specific repair, match the manufacturer's guidance to the vehicle and the damage involved. Attach the relevant procedure or page with the corresponding scan report. [American Honda's scan requirements, reproduced by CCC](https://go.cccis.com/honda-position-statement)

Consider an example where a supplement lists a $125 pre-scan and a $160 post-scan. The insurer acknowledges the post-scan invoice and leaves the pre-scan blank. Submit the earlier time-stamped report and the pre-scan charge together. Label the two operations separately so the reviewer can match each charge to its own report. The [Auto Repair Estimate Comparison](/tools/repair-quote-comparator) tool can help align the lines across versions.

If the shop sent a revised estimate and is still waiting for a decision, [follow up on the specific repair supplement](/articles/follow-up-no-response-repair-supplement). If the reviewer needs visual proof, [ask which photos support the original estimate](/articles/photos-insurer-used-for-damage-estimate).

## Ask the insurer to classify the decision

Request a short written answer identifying whether the line is pending documentation or declined after the carrier reviewed the documentation. If the denial is about rate, necessity, coverage or duplicate billing, ask for that reason and the record the reviewer used. Save the dated supplement and the response together.

If the carrier cannot locate the attachments, use [the portal receipt workflow](/articles/insurance-claim-portal-upload-missing). If it issues a new reason after receiving them, preserve both decisions using [the denial comparison guide](/articles/insurer-changed-denial-reason-complaint).

title: Your Auto Claim Denial Uses the Wrong Policy Renewal Date
excerpt: Identify which policy term applied at the moment of a crash and send the insurer a documented correction of the date it used.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Your Auto Claim Denial Uses the Wrong Policy Renewal Date
metaDescription: Identify which policy term applied at the moment of a crash and send the insurer a documented correction of the date it used.
content:
A denial letter puts the crash on the wrong side of a renewal. The useful response is a comparison of the term the adjuster used and the term you believe was in force. Include the covered vehicle and coverage type. A renewal date by itself cannot establish whether the particular coverage survived the change.

## Put the loss inside a policy term

Collect the declarations from both sides of the renewal, any binder or endorsement, the renewal offer and its acceptance record, premium receipts, and any cancellation or nonrenewal notices. Write down the loss date, clock time and time zone from the best contemporaneous record you have. Read the policy's effective-time language. A calendar date can represent different intervals depending on how the policy states the hour and location.

In an illustrative case, a crash occurred at 8:40 p.m. on June 30. The denial relies on declarations beginning July 1 and says the term had not begun. A declaration for the preceding term, together with any later changes to it, is the place to look. If the carrier actually meant that the old term ended early for nonpayment, ask for the cancellation notice and the premium history that support that position.

A card, an automatic bank debit and a declarations page answer different questions. The card identifies a policy. The debit records a transaction. Ask the carrier to show how the money was applied and which declarations, endorsements or notices controlled the coverage on the loss date.

## State the discrepancy in two sentences

> Your letter dated August 12 applies the term beginning July 1. The crash report records the loss on June 30 at 8:40 p.m., and the enclosed declarations show a preceding term for the same VIN. Please identify the term and provision applied at that time and reconsider the decision based on the enclosed records.

In Texas, the insurance department describes cancellation as ending a policy before its stated end and nonrenewal as declining to continue it at expiration. Its consumer guide explains state-specific notice and complaint rules. Look up the rule for the state in which the policy was issued. [Texas Department of Insurance auto guide](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/pubs/consumer/cb020.html)

## Preserve the original denial and the response deadline

Keep each letter as issued and record when you received it. Washington, for example, requires an insurer relying on a specific policy provision, condition or exclusion to reference it in the written denial under its claim-settlement rule. [Washington insurance settlement standards](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-380)

Use the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner) to record dates taken from the actual notice and policy. If the original evidence is missing from the carrier's file, follow [the upload receipt procedure](/articles/insurance-claim-portal-upload-missing). If the company replaces the date issue with a different ground, [compare the two written denial reasons](/articles/insurer-changed-denial-reason-complaint).

title: MedPay Paid the Hospital Before Health Insurance Reprocessed the Bill
excerpt: Trace the auto insurer's payment and the health plan's revised decision to see which credits the hospital actually posted.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: MedPay Paid the Hospital Before Health Insurance Reprocessed the Bill
metaDescription: Trace the auto insurer's payment and the health plan's revised decision to see which credits the hospital actually posted.
content:
An auto insurer sends the hospital a MedPay check. Weeks later, your health plan reprocesses the same visit and a new patient balance appears. The transaction you need to trace is the auto payment on the hospital's ledger. It might still be posted, have moved to a different account, or have been returned. The new EOB alone rarely answers which happened.

California's insurance department describes medical payments coverage as limited coverage for certain crash-related medical expenses regardless of fault. Policy language and the applicable coordination rules determine how your coverage works. [California auto insurance guide](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/105-type/95-guides/01-auto/auto101.cfm)

## Give each organization a question it can answer

- **Auto insurer.** Ask for the payment amount, date, payee, check or electronic trace number, and invoice or encounter reference. Ask whether a refund was received or requested.
- **Health plan.** Ask which claim version is current, why it was reprocessed and what other insurance or prior payment the plan accounted for in assigning patient responsibility.
- **Hospital.** Ask where the MedPay payment posted, which adjustment followed the reprocessing, and whether any money was transferred, refunded or left unapplied. Request the existing ledger and current itemized bill.

Use the [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) for the response from each organization. Record the reference numbers next to the dollars. A payment date without an account number can leave you trying to reconcile two bills from the same visit.

When the hospital is still waiting on a plan that says it finished processing, [ask which decision reached the hospital's ledger](/articles/hospital-insurance-pending-eob-processed). If the plan paid you directly, [verify the payee and the provider's remaining balance](/articles/eob-payment-to-patient-provider-balance).

## Check the ledger before doing the subtraction

Suppose a new EOB assigns $650 to the patient, and the auto insurer confirms that it sent $500. If the hospital kept and applied the $500 to that same responsibility, a simplified balance is $150. If the hospital returned the $500 or it already formed part of the health plan's calculation, subtracting it again produces a misleading result. Ask the plan and provider to reconcile their records before assigning a credit.

CMS explains that an EOB does not tell you whether you already paid the displayed patient amount. For Medicare beneficiaries, separate Medicare Secondary Payer rules can apply to liability and no-fault insurance. CMS includes medical payments coverage among its examples of no-fault insurance. [CMS EOB guide](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/guides-resources/read-explanation-benefits) · [CMS guidance on liability and no-fault reporting](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/liability-no-fault-workers-compensation-reporting)

Get the corrected balance and the status of any refund in writing. For a payment made out of your own pocket, use [the revised EOB reconciliation guide](/articles/medical-bill-balance-after-revised-eob). If the same charge later appears on a settlement accounting, [follow the payee and ledger behind each deduction](/articles/duplicate-lien-settlement-statement).

title: The Total-Loss Valuation Omitted Dealer-Installed Adaptive Equipment
excerpt: Document a vehicle's mobility conversion, identify the coverage that applies and request a valuation that accounts for it.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Total-Loss Valuation Omitted Dealer-Installed Adaptive Equipment
metaDescription: Document a vehicle's mobility conversion, identify the coverage that applies and request a valuation that accounts for it.
content:
A valuation report matches your van's VIN and mileage and compares it with ordinary vans on dealer lots. Your van has a lowered floor, a powered ramp and wheelchair securement points. The disagreement starts with the vehicle description. Ask the insurer to identify the modifications it recognized and how it valued each covered item.

## Describe the equipment in terms an appraiser can match

Start with the conversion invoice and the vehicle VIN. Separate structural conversion work, permanently installed controls or lifts, and removable equipment. Include the conversion manufacturer, model and installation date, with labeled photographs and available maintenance records. A mobility dealer can help identify equipment from its markings and distinguish an integrated conversion from a removable device.

NHTSA's guide discusses vehicle modifications ranging from swivel seating to hand controls, along with the role of a qualified mobility dealer. Use the actual conversion and installation records to describe what was on your vehicle before the loss. [NHTSA guide to adapting vehicles for people with disabilities](https://www.nhtsa.gov/document/adapting-motor-vehicles-people-disabilities)

## Find where the policy places the conversion

Ask whether the carrier considers the item part of the vehicle valuation, subject to a separate equipment endorsement, limited by a sublimit, or excluded by a particular term. Request that distinction in writing. An invoice shows what was installed and what it cost when purchased. An endorsement helps explain which costs may be covered. Current comparable vehicles help estimate what the equipped vehicle was worth.

Washington's total-loss regulation offers a specific example of why features matter. Its settlement rules call for appropriate adjustments for options, mileage or condition when determining comparability, and its valuation-report rule describes the information to include. Whether a particular modification falls within a policy's coverage is a separate question. [WAC 284-30-391](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-391) · [WAC 284-30-392](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-392)

## Submit comparable vans with the conversion described

In a sample request, two same-year vans list at $24,000. The first has a standard floor. The second has a ramp but a different conversion and a different mileage. A used mobility van priced at $32,500 can be informative if it matches the conversion, location and relevant date. Explain what is alike and what still needs an adjustment. Keep dealer details, the listing date and the equipment configuration with each lead.

Use the [Claim Expense and Receipt Tracker](/tools/receipt-coverage-map) to map invoice lines to the equipment shown in the photos. Ask for an itemized revised report or an explanation of the treatment of each item. If the report uses a later market date, [check which date the appraiser actually valued](/articles/appraisal-award-valuation-date-total-loss). If a refinance has also complicated the payment, [trace the check and lien separately](/articles/total-loss-check-old-lienholder-after-refinance).

title: When an Insurer Changes Its Reason for Denial in Writing
excerpt: Put two denial letters side by side and prepare a focused insurance complaint about the reason the carrier now relies on.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: When an Insurer Changes Its Reason for Denial in Writing
metaDescription: Put two denial letters side by side and prepare a focused insurance complaint about the reason the carrier now relies on.
content:
The first letter says a requested document never arrived. The second acknowledges the document and cites a policy exclusion. Save both decisions. A regulator or reviewer needs to see what changed, when it changed and which records the insurer used for the new position.

## Build a two-letter comparison

For each version, capture the letter date, receipt date, signer, claim number, coverage section, stated ground and cited policy text. Attach the relevant page from the policy in effect at the loss. If the second letter says it supplements the first, ask whether both grounds remain in force. If it says it supersedes the first, identify the active deadline and ask the carrier to confirm it.

Describe the change as the documents show it. “The July 6 letter denied the claim because the repair order was absent. The July 20 letter confirms receipt and cites an exclusion on page 18. Please identify the facts and the policy edition supporting the July 20 decision.” Keep your conclusions separate from the quotations.

## Ask the reviewer to examine the specific change

Washington's claim-settlement rule requires a written denial to identify the provision, condition or exclusion when the insurer relies on it under the rule. Its Office of the Insurance Commissioner also describes how it reviews complaints, contacts insurers and explains the limits of its role. The rules and complaint process for your state may differ. [Washington settlement standards](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-380) · [Washington insurance complaint process](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/complaints-appeals-fraud/complaints/understanding-complaint-process)

Use the [Insurance Complaint Organizer](/tools/insurance-complaint-packet) to assemble the two letters, a short chronology and your requested outcome. An example outcome is a written decision that identifies the operative policy provision and addresses the attached proof of submission. The [NAIC's state insurance complaint guide](https://content.naic.org/consumer/how-to-file-complaint) explains where consumers can start.

If you've heard the decision only by phone, [ask for the dated denial even if the portal shows the claim as open](/articles/adjuster-verbal-denial-claim-portal-open). For a disagreement about the crash, [ask the insurer to name the disputed fact](/articles/ask-insurer-disputed-accident-facts).

## Keep the complaint and the claim deadline on separate tracks

Record the date of the complaint and each appeal, suit or policy deadline shown by your actual documents. Verify the effect of a complaint on those dates with the applicable rule or qualified counsel. A regulator's acknowledgment identifies the complaint you filed. Your calendar should also show what remains to be done under the policy or denial letter.

If the dispute started with an attachment, [match the receipt to the adjuster's visible file list](/articles/insurance-claim-portal-upload-missing). If the letters use different policy terms, [reconstruct the renewal and loss dates](/articles/auto-claim-denied-wrong-policy-renewal-date). For a carrier that changed its response to a repair invoice, see [the pre-repair scan supplement workflow](/articles/repair-supplement-denied-missing-pre-repair-scan-invoice).

title: The Appraisal Award Uses a Different Date From the Total Loss
excerpt: Distinguish a vehicle appraisal's signature date from its valuation date and verify the market data used in a total-loss award.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Appraisal Award Uses a Different Date From the Total Loss
metaDescription: Distinguish a vehicle appraisal's signature date from its valuation date and verify the market data used in a total-loss award.
content:
An award dated August 18 can value a vehicle as of a May 2 loss. Those dates answer different questions. Before challenging an award, identify the effective valuation date in the appraiser's instructions or report. Then check the dates of the comparables used to reach that number.

## Separate four dates on one page

Record the loss date, the date the appraiser was asked to value the vehicle, the date each comparable was available and the day the award was signed. A report may also contain a print date or the date a vendor retrieved its data. If the report says only “as of August 18,” ask the appraiser whether that refers to the effective date, the market snapshot or the document's preparation.

A May 2 collision, a June 5 appraisal demand, three listings dated May 8 through May 21 and an award signed August 18 are compatible with a May valuation. Replace those listings with August-only observations and the sourcing question changes. Ask the appraiser to show how those observations relate to the loss date under the governing policy and rules.

## Compare the award with its underlying valuation

Washington's total-loss rule allows appraisal for a first-party dispute over actual cash value when the policy contains an appraisal provision. It directs the insurer to advise its appraiser of the state's total-loss calculations and sets requirements for the timing of comparable vehicles used in settlement offers. The rule permits certain comparables within a window around the loss, so a listing after the crash can still be relevant. [Washington total-loss rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-391)

Texas's insurance department separately describes appraisal as a way to resolve disagreement over how much a covered loss is worth. Read your own clause for the scope of the award and the procedure for a dispute. [Texas insurance department guide to total-loss valuation disputes](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/blog/my-totaled-car-is-worth-more-than-insurance-wants-to-pay.html)

## Send a narrow request for the missing date

> Please confirm the effective valuation date used for my vehicle, the dates the comparable vehicles were available, and whether the August 18 date reflects the award signature or the market date. If the effective date was different from May 2, please identify the instruction or policy language used.

Use the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) to specify the award, appraisers' valuation reports and comparable sheets. Keep the exact policy and award with the request. If the discrepancy could affect a final award, confirm any deadlines for disputing it under the applicable law before waiting on an informal answer.

If the records also omit installed features, see [the adaptive equipment valuation guide](/articles/total-loss-valuation-missing-adaptive-equipment). If the amount is settled and only the lender on the check is wrong, [separate the payment problem from the appraisal](/articles/total-loss-check-old-lienholder-after-refinance).

For a vehicle that was already sold, document its actual availability and the price the vendor used. [How to check a historical comparable in a total-loss report](/articles/total-loss-comparable-car-sold-before-valuation).

title: A Crash Cost You a Weekly Rideshare Bonus. How Do You Show It?
excerpt: Use the actual promotion terms, completed trips and comparable workweeks to document a missed rideshare bonus after a crash.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Crash Cost You a Weekly Rideshare Bonus. How Do You Show It?
metaDescription: Use the actual promotion terms, completed trips and comparable workweeks to document a missed rideshare bonus after a crash.
content:
A weekly payout can drop after a crash in two ways. You can lose trip income during the missed shifts, and those missing trips can leave you short of a promotion threshold. Show the two amounts separately. The trip shortfall is a record. The bonus you might have earned is a conditional part of your estimate.

## Save the offer for that specific week

Take a dated copy of the promotion with its start and end times, target trip count, amount, geographic limits and eligibility conditions. Save any enrollment or progress screen, then download the trip and payout records for that period. Uber describes Quest as a promotion that can pay for reaching a trip target within a defined period, with availability and terms that vary. Use your offer and its actual rules for the calculation. [Uber's description of Driver app promotions](https://help.uber.com/driving-and-delivering/article/earn-extra-with-quest?nodeId=2d5ba130-4944-4a18-bc99-dd2adad19c32)

Show the last eligible trip before the crash and the number still needed. Then record the dates you were unable to work and the documents that explain the interruption, such as a repair intake, vehicle release or documented medical restriction. Preserve the matching platform records when you returned to driving.

## Show one week with and without the bonus

Suppose you completed 27 of the required 30 eligible trips before a crash and missed a Saturday shift. In four of five comparable weeks, you made at least three eligible trips on Saturday. Save all five weeks, including the one in which you did not reach the threshold. Explain whether those shifts were in the same area and during comparable hours. Keep the unpaid bonus labeled as a scenario.

If comparable trip receipts averaged $700 with $140 in relevant operating costs and the crash week recorded $470 with $90 in costs, the illustrative net trip difference is $180. A separate $90 bonus would make the difference $270 if the records support including it. Confirm that the baseline receipts excluded incentives before adding one. IRS recordkeeping guidance explains why contemporaneous income and expense records matter for a business. It does not supply a damages formula. [IRS recordkeeping guidance](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/recordkeeping)

## Make the workweek auditable

Use the [Gig Worker Income Loss Calculator](/tools/gig-net-income-comparison) for the receipts and cost comparison. Attach a separate page for the promotion, its progress and the reason the missed shift would likely have qualified. Describe which costs stopped when you did not drive and which continued. Keep the raw statements so a reviewer can recalculate either scenario.

For coverage questions during different app stages, read [which insurance can apply to Uber and Lyft crashes](/articles/uber-and-lyft-accidents-who-actually-pays-for-your-injuries-in-2026). If the insurer cannot find the promotion screenshots, [use a file-level submission inventory](/articles/insurance-claim-portal-upload-missing).

title: How to Check a Seat Belt Part Number Against a Recall After a Used Car Crash
excerpt: Match the vehicle, installed assembly and recall campaign. Keep the recall status and the component's service history separate.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: How to Check a Seat Belt Part Number Against a Recall After a Used Car Crash
metaDescription: Match the vehicle, installed assembly and recall campaign. Keep the recall status and the component's service history separate.
content:
A VIN search is the quickest way to look for an open recall. A used car's seat belt may have been replaced earlier, and a campaign may describe a pretensioner or buckle in a particular seating position. To identify the part that was present at the crash, connect the VIN to the installed assembly and its repair history.

## Save the vehicle result with the date you ran it

Record the VIN from the vehicle and compare it with the VIN on the title or repair order. Save the dated search result, including the campaign number and any remedy information. NHTSA explains that the VIN search has limits, including recalls already repaired and some recently announced recalls for which affected VINs are still being identified. Its site also offers searches for recalls by vehicle and equipment. [NHTSA recall lookup and search limitations](https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls)

Ask the dealer or manufacturer for available campaign and service records for that VIN. If the records show an inspection or replacement, note the service date, seating position and part number on the repair order. A work order that just says “seat belt” leaves the particular component unresolved.

## Read the part section of the actual campaign

Honda's November 2023 Part 573 report for campaign 23V-782 identifies affected vehicle populations and several front seat belt pretensioner part numbers. The remedy described in that report involved a dealer inspection and replacement where necessary. The published campaign shows why it matters to match the specific component and affected population rather than relying on a general description of a belt. [Honda's Part 573 recall report filed with NHTSA](https://static.nhtsa.gov/odi/rcl/2023/RCLRPT-23V782-1271.PDF)

Ask a qualified technician to document any accessible label, installed position and condition of the assembly without disturbing it. Keep photos of the visible area and any previous replacement invoice. Avoid disconnecting or removing a restraint component yourself. If the vehicle is at a tow yard, [request the custody and intake records first](/articles/tow-yard-intake-photos-vehicle-transfer).

## Record what the search actually established

A useful evidence note can read, “VIN lookup performed May 10. Manufacturer campaign shown as repaired in 2024. Repair order requested to confirm which assembly was inspected or installed.” That distinguishes a campaign status from a confirmed part identity. Keep any unclear serial, model or production-range information marked for verification. The recall report establishes the manufacturer's reported defect and remedy, and a vehicle inspection is needed to investigate what occurred in the particular crash.

Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to map the VIN search, dealer work order and inspection photographs to those separate questions. For original condition photos, see [how to document a car before and after storage](/articles/pre-tow-photos-rain-storage-vehicle-damage).

title: Requesting Crosswalk Signal Timing Records After a Pedestrian Crash
excerpt: Ask the agency for the timing plan, phase map and available event logs for the crossing and time involved in a pedestrian collision.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Requesting Crosswalk Signal Timing Records After a Pedestrian Crash
metaDescription: Ask the agency for the timing plan, phase map and available event logs for the crossing and time involved in a pedestrian collision.
content:
After a pedestrian crash, “send the traffic light timing” can get you a settings sheet for the entire intersection. That may tell you what the controller was configured to do. To examine what a particular crosswalk displayed, ask for the exact leg of the crossing and the records that tie an indication to the incident time.

## Name the corner and the movement

Identify both streets, the side of the intersection, the pedestrian's direction and the vehicle movement involved. Describe the hour in local time with the date and a window that brackets the event. Include the agency's signal ID if available. A pedestrian walking east across the north leg and a driver turning right from a different approach may be governed by separate indications.

The federal MUTCD's traffic-signal provisions distinguish vehicle and pedestrian indications. The physical signal faces and phase assignments at the particular intersection determine which records you need to match. [FHWA's current MUTCD edition and Part 4](https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/kno_11th_Editionr1.htm)

## Request the settings and the recorded events

Ask for the plan and phase diagram effective on the date, time-of-day schedules, pedestrian intervals for that crossing, and any logs showing controller events or unusual operation within your window. If the intersection uses a system with high-resolution logs, request the timestamps, phase or event codes and any data dictionary needed to read them. FHWA describes controllers that record timed inputs and outputs as part of automated traffic signal performance measurement systems. Confirm whether that capability was installed and whether the logs still exist. [FHWA explanation of traffic signal performance data](https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/fhwahop20002/ch2.htm)

A weekday timing sheet might show a seven-second walk setting. That number alone leaves open when the walk interval actually began during the relevant cycle, whether a push button placed a call and whether the controller was operating on the expected plan. Keep the plan, logs and observations distinct in your notes.

## Ask the records office for existing documents

> Please provide the active timing plan and phase diagram for the north-leg crosswalk at Oak Street and First Avenue on May 4, and any available controller event logs from 4:10 to 4:30 p.m. local time. Please include code definitions or related controller configuration records for interpreting that export.

Identify the road owner before sending the request. For example, New York City DOT's FOIL instructions ask for a specified intersection and date range and direct requesters to ask for records. Other agencies use their own channels. [NYC DOT public records instructions](https://home4.nyc.gov/html/dot/html/about/foil.shtml)

Use the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) to adapt the request. To compare the records with recorded images, see [how to request a native video export](/articles/request-native-crash-video-frame-timing). If the key witness saw a signal across the intersection, [map which signal the witness actually observed](/articles/witness-saw-opposite-red-light).

title: A Carrier's Safety Rating Changed After a Freight Broker Tendered a Load
excerpt: Build a timeline of the tender, carrier notices and federal safety records before drawing conclusions from a current SAFER snapshot.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Carrier's Safety Rating Changed After a Freight Broker Tendered a Load
metaDescription: Build a timeline of the tender, carrier notices and federal safety records before drawing conclusions from a current SAFER snapshot.
content:
A SAFER report pulled after a truck crash shows a carrier's current rating. To examine what information was available when a broker selected the carrier, use the carrier's USDOT number and preserve dated records. The tender, any later reassignment, the agency notice and the rating's effect can occur on different days.

## Start with the carrier on the shipment

Compare the USDOT number on the broker's carrier agreement or onboarding record with the carrier shown on the tender, dispatch records and bill of lading. A similar name on a current search result is weak evidence of identity. If a load changed hands, mark the time and source of each change. The federal broker records rule describes transaction records kept by brokers and provides review access to parties to a brokered transaction. Whether a person can obtain other records depends on the requester and applicable process. [Federal broker transaction records rule](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-371/subpart-A/section-371.3)

## Put each safety record at the right point in time

Keep a copy of the rating result and the date you retrieved it. Separate a proposed safety determination, the agency's notice and any final or effective status. Federal regulations address notice and the effect of an unsatisfactory rating, including timing rules that can differ by carrier type. The actual notices, any changes to them and applicable orders matter to the timeline. [Federal motor-carrier safety fitness rules](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/cfr/49/385?link-type=pdf&year=mostrecent)

The Safety Measurement System is a separate FMCSA source. A prioritization indicator or inspection history is a different record from a formal safety rating. Note which dataset supplied each observation and how current it was. [FMCSA SAFER Company Snapshot](https://safer.fmcsa.dot.gov/CompanySnapshot.aspx) · [FMCSA Safety Measurement System explanation](https://ai.fmcsa.dot.gov/SMS)

## Compare what was known at tender and before pickup

In a hypothetical file, the broker tenders a load on Monday. The carrier receives a proposed rating notice on Wednesday, collects the load on Friday and has an updated public rating the next month. Friday's question is whether any new notice or status reached the relevant parties before pickup. Monday's question is what they could see or had received when making the initial assignment. A copy pulled the next month cannot answer either on its own.

Ask for the dated onboarding checks, rechecks, tender acceptance, any substitution records and any notice that was sent before dispatch. Use the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) to attach each observation to its record and retrieval time. For the liability context, read [the freight broker case study](/articles/can-a-freight-broker-be-sued-after-a-truck-crash). If the chronology also uses recorded footage, [check the video clock separately](/articles/request-native-crash-video-frame-timing).

title: A Diminished Value Estimate Compares Your Trade-In to Dealer Retail
excerpt: Separate retail asking prices from trade-in offers and measure how much of the gap can be traced to the accident history.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Diminished Value Estimate Compares Your Trade-In to Dealer Retail
metaDescription: Separate retail asking prices from trade-in offers and measure how much of the gap can be traced to the accident history.
content:
A dealer lists a clean-history car at $23,000 and offers $18,000 for your repaired car. The $5,000 difference contains more than the crash history. The first number is a retail asking price. The second is a proposed acquisition price and may be tied to a purchase transaction. To estimate a history-related difference, compare figures from the same side of the market.

## Label each number by what it buys

Record whether each figure is a listing, completed sale, standalone purchase offer or trade allowance in a package deal. Include mileage, trim, region, condition and date. Get the offer in writing and ask whether it depends on financing or buying another vehicle. The FTC advises car shoppers to keep the purchase price and trade-in negotiations distinct enough to see when one figure offsets another. The same discipline helps identify what a trade-in quote can show. [FTC guide to financing or leasing a car](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/financing-or-leasing-car)

## Build two comparisons that can be checked

In one illustration, a buyer offers $18,000 for the repaired car and $19,400 for a genuinely comparable clean-history car under the same purchase terms. The $1,400 difference is a lead to investigate. Separately, similar cars list at $23,000 with clean history and $21,800 with disclosed comparable repairs. The $1,200 retail asking-price difference provides a second observation. Neither set establishes a final valuation without checking condition, date and the evidence behind the prices.

Ask the appraiser how they adjusted for prior damage, differences in mileage and repair quality, how they sourced the history descriptions and whether either comparison used actual sale data. Do not count outstanding repair defects as a history-only discount without identifying them. Put each comparable's source and limitations next to its price.

## Check which kind of claim you have

In *State Farm v. Mabry*, the Georgia Supreme Court interpreted the policy at issue to include diminution in value within the loss assessment even after repair. That ruling is tied to the policy and law considered there. The Georgia insurance regulator's auto claim guidance is a starting point for the state process. [Georgia Supreme Court opinion in Mabry](https://law.justia.com/cases/georgia/supreme-court/2001/s01a0982-1.html) · [Georgia insurance regulator's auto claim tips](https://oci.georgia.gov/insurance-resources/auto/auto-claim-tips)

The [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) can pair each value claim with the underlying offer, listing, repair record or appraisal. For a closely related issue involving adjustment of a vehicle's pre-loss condition, read [the total-loss condition adjustment case study](/articles/what-the-condition-adjustment-does-to-a-total-loss-offer). If the appraiser used market data from a different date, see [how to read an appraisal's valuation date](/articles/appraisal-award-valuation-date-total-loss).

title: The Police Crash Report Leaves Out a Second Impact
excerpt: Compare the report narrative, diagram and vehicle event fields. Then send the reporting agency a precise request backed by evidence.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Police Crash Report Leaves Out a Second Impact
metaDescription: Compare the report narrative, diagram and vehicle event fields. Then send the reporting agency a precise request backed by evidence.
content:
A report describes one rear-end strike. You remember a second impact, perhaps when your car was pushed into another vehicle. Start by locating the exact omission. A second contact can appear in the unit-level event fields even when the narrative summarizes the crash in one sentence.

## Read the report as a set of records

Obtain the report with its continuation pages and any available supplement. Match each unit number to the vehicles involved. Check the written narrative, diagram and event codes separately. An entry labeled first harmful event identifies the first injury- or damage-producing event within the reporting framework. Other fields can capture later events. Use your agency's code sheet. The federal MMUCC provides voluntary crash-reporting guidance, and the local form controls what a particular field means. [NHTSA's Model Minimum Uniform Crash Criteria](https://www.nhtsa.gov/traffic-records/model-minimum-uniform-crash-criteria)

## Show exactly which contact is missing

Write one line per reported contact. For example, “Impact A: Unit 3 struck the rear of Unit 2. Impact B: Unit 2 contacted the rear of Unit 1 after being pushed forward.” Mark the source for each statement. Identify what you personally felt, what a witness saw, what a video shows and which damage photos are merely consistent with a contact.

If you have two short clips, keep the original exports and identify the clock used by each. Two images of the same damage can show condition while leaving the order unresolved. For timing evidence, see [how to ask for native crash footage](/articles/request-native-crash-video-frame-timing). If a witness saw only the first collision, preserve the limits of that observation.

## Send the request to the agency that wrote the report

Ask how the investigator accepts supplemental evidence. Include the report number, unit numbers, disputed passage, a short factual chronology and the best supporting record. Request the procedure and, if a supplement is issued, a copy. Texas's CR-100 manual gives a concrete example. It instructs investigators to use a supplemental report when they need to amend a report already sent to TxDOT or provide additional information. Local procedures vary. [TxDOT crash-report instructions, Section 5](https://www.txdot.gov/content/dam/docs/division/trf/crash-records/cr100-v29.pdf)

> In report 1234, Unit 2's event sequence ends with the rear impact. Please review the attached original video and the still indexed at 14:08:16 showing Unit 2 contacting Unit 1. Please tell me how I can submit this for the investigator's review.

Use the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) to format the request. Keep the original report with any supplement and give the insurer both versions, with a dated note identifying the change. If the second driver left and the file depends on proof gathered later, see [how to use tow records in a hit-and-run claim](/articles/hit-and-run-claim-tow-receipt-no-scene-photos).

title: Request Tow Yard Intake Photos After Your Car Moved Between Lots
excerpt: Trace the vehicle through each facility and request the original intake, transfer and arrival records tied to the same VIN.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Request Tow Yard Intake Photos After Your Car Moved Between Lots
metaDescription: Trace the vehicle through each facility and request the original intake, transfer and arrival records tied to the same VIN.
content:
The lot that holds your car today may only have photos taken after a transfer. Find the facility that first accepted it, then use the transfer record to match the same vehicle at the second lot. Those two sets of photos answer questions about condition at different moments.

## Start with the first tow ticket

Pull the VIN, tow ticket number, pickup time and destination from the first record. Ask the tower whether it delivered the vehicle to that address or to a different facility. Ask each facility for its intake identifier, date and time, original photos if available, and the condition or inventory sheet associated with that arrival. Give a date range if their intake was overnight.

Texas's licensing department describes records a licensed vehicle storage facility must keep, including the date and destination of a vehicle transfer and identifying information for the tower. Its guidance also covers how an owner or authorized person can access a vehicle. Ask for copies of existing images and clarify the facility's release procedure. The Texas recordkeeping rule does not assure that intake photographs were taken. [Texas TDLR storage records guidance](https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/towing/compliance/vsf/record-keeping.htm) · [Texas TDLR vehicle access guidance](https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/towing/compliance/vsf/vehicle-access.htm)

## Identify the missing point in the chain

In one example, a vehicle arrives at Lot A at 9:15 p.m., leaves the next morning and arrives at Lot B before noon. A photograph from Lot B showing a damaged mirror documents its condition after arrival there. Look for Lot A's arrival photos, the pickup record for the transfer, and Lot B's first condition entry before trying to place the damage at a specific point. Record the source of each timestamp and flag gaps.

Ask the transfer operator for dispatch, pickup and delivery records and any photos taken while loading or unloading. If there are no pictures, invoices, a condition notation or a release receipt may still narrow the window. Ask whether relevant footage exists and whether it can be preserved, since its availability can change.

## Request a record package by VIN and event

> Please provide any intake photos and the condition or inventory sheet for VIN ending 4821 on May 4, plus the May 5 release and transfer record naming the receiving facility. Please include the time shown in the original record and identify the lot where it was made.

Use the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) for separate requests to each facility. Keep originals in separate folders so the date, lot and source stay clear. If rain changed the car's appearance, compare [pre-tow and later storage photos](/articles/pre-tow-photos-rain-storage-vehicle-damage). If the first tow ticket is also your strongest contemporaneous record of the crash, see [the hit-and-run documentation workflow](/articles/hit-and-run-claim-tow-receipt-no-scene-photos).

title: Photograph Crash Damage Before Rain and Tow Yard Storage Change It
excerpt: Preserve the earliest safe views of the vehicle and separate what was visible at pickup from what appears after outdoor storage.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Photograph Crash Damage Before Rain and Tow Yard Storage Change It
metaDescription: Preserve the earliest safe views of the vehicle and separate what was visible at pickup from what appears after outdoor storage.
content:
A wet fender can look different from the same fender under a dry shop light. Later photos may also show surface changes, dirt or a different position. For an insurance file, organize images by when and where they were taken so a reviewer can compare the same area across conditions.

## Get a baseline when it is safe

Leave traffic lanes and follow the instructions of emergency responders. If you can photograph the car from a safe position before it is moved, start with a wide image showing the vehicle and its location. Then capture an angle that shows where the damaged panel sits and a closer view of what is visible. Note which areas you could not safely see. If the first safe view is at the tow destination, record that as the first image rather than describing it as a scene photo. [California insurance department's accident guide](https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/105-type/95-guides/01-auto/upload/Accident-What-Next-w-05-27-21-Web-Only.pdf)

Use the [Accident Photo Checklist](/tools/photo-documentation-planner) to track the sides and details you captured. Keep the camera originals and use copies for markup, cropping or sharing. Preserve the source and date of each file. NIST's digital evidence guidance describes preserving data and documenting its handling so that later users can identify the material they received. [NIST digital evidence preservation guidance](https://www.nist.gov/publications/digital-evidence-preservation-considerations-evidence-handlers)

## Match the same panel across the two sets

For example, your earliest image shows the left rear quarter panel at pickup. A later image after rain and storage shows a mark beside the wheel arch that is hard to see in the first shot. Match seams, trim or another fixed feature to confirm you are looking at the same spot. Note angle, lighting, wetness and any obstruction. The comparison is stronger when both views actually show the area being discussed.

If weather is part of the dispute, note the yard address and period outdoors. NOAA's Local Climatological Data can show precipitation observations for reporting stations. Record which station you used and how far it is from the lot. Station data provide context for the region and period. The condition of the car comes from its own records. [NOAA Local Climatological Data](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/local-climatological-data)

## Keep condition and custody separate

Label each set by event, such as scene, pickup, first lot, transfer or inspection. Add the name of the person or business that provided it. If you can only establish that a mark was visible at the last inspection, state that directly and identify what earlier view would help. For records created when the car changed lots, use [the tow intake and transfer guide](/articles/tow-yard-intake-photos-vehicle-transfer). For photos intended to identify a specific safety component, read [how to match the component to a recall record](/articles/used-car-crash-seat-belt-recall-part-number).

title: Ask for the Native Crash Video Before You Measure Frame Timing
excerpt: Request the recorder's original-format export, timing information and playback instructions before calculating the interval between two crash events.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Ask for the Native Crash Video Before You Measure Frame Timing
metaDescription: Request the recorder's original-format export, timing information and playback instructions before calculating the interval between two crash events.
content:
A shop emails a short MP4 labeled “30 fps.” You need to know how much time passed between two visible events. Ask for the closest available export to what the recorder stored, along with information about its clock and export settings. A frame rate reported for a shared copy may describe that copy's playback.

## Send the camera owner a request they can act on

Identify the camera location, direction and a time window in local time. Ask the owner to preserve and export the native or original-quality recording for that window, with its normal player or instructions if the format requires one. Ask whether the export was converted, trimmed or screen-recorded and whether an on-screen time is generated by the recorder or the export software. Request any existing time zone or clock-offset information.

SWGDE's video analysis guidance describes obtaining the best available original data and documenting processing. If a conventional playable copy is the only version immediately available, keep it and record how it was provided while following up for the source export. [SWGDE best practices for digital forensic video analysis](https://www.swgde.org/documents/published-complete-listing/18-v-001-2-0/)

## Distinguish playback rate from the time between frames

Consider an illustrative file. The displayed timing metadata reports one frame at 18.410 seconds and another at 18.760 seconds. Their reported separation is 0.350 seconds. Counting 15 frame intervals at an assumed 30 frames per second would instead yield 0.500 seconds. Which timing represents the source recording depends on how the camera recorded and how the file was created.

For supported ISO base media formats, SWGDE explains how presentation timestamps can describe intervals between specific displayed frames. It also discusses limitations introduced by some exports and the role of an external timing reference. A camera's visible wall-clock overlay is another record that may need alignment. [SWGDE guidance on frame timing in ISO base media formats](https://www.swgde.org/documents/published-complete-listing/19-v-005-swgde-best-practice-for-frame-timing-analysis-of-video-stored-in-iso-base-media-file-formats/)

## Keep a record of the exact file you received

Save the original filenames, how and when each file arrived, the camera identity and the sender's export notes. Calculate a checksum of the preserved file if you need to match an analysis copy against it. The [SHA-256 File Checksum Tool](/tools/evidence-file-fingerprints) helps compare the bytes of two copies. The file source and clock accuracy still depend on the underlying evidence.

When the footage will be compared with traffic-controller events, use [the crosswalk timing records guide](/articles/crosswalk-signal-timing-records-pedestrian-crash). For a recording that could help place a dog and delivery worker at a particular moment, see [the New York gate-latch evidence guide](/articles/new-york-dog-bite-delivery-gate-latch-evidence).

If the disagreement is between the camera clock and a dispatch record, [use a shared event to estimate the offset](/articles/dashcam-clock-different-from-911-call-time). If you have the card, [verify a working copy and preserve the original medium](/articles/verify-dashcam-copy-preserve-memory-card).

title: A Crash Witness Saw Red From the Opposite Side. Which Signal Was It?
excerpt: Record the witness's vantage point and identify the signal face, lane and movement they actually saw at the intersection.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Crash Witness Saw Red From the Opposite Side. Which Signal Was It?
metaDescription: Record the witness's vantage point and identify the signal face, lane and movement they actually saw at the intersection.
content:
“I saw red” is useful once the observation has a location and an object. At an intersection with multiple approaches and turn indications, a person standing across the road can see a signal that governs a different lane. Before turning the statement into a conclusion about a driver, identify the face the person remembers.

## Draw the view before discussing fault

Ask the witness to mark their position on a neutral sketch, the direction they faced and where they first noticed the vehicle. Let them point to the remembered signal on a photo or drawing, and record whether they could see the front of that signal or only a reflection or side view. Ask whether they saw a circular light, an arrow or a pedestrian indication. Preserve uncertainty in their words.

The federal MUTCD differentiates vehicle indications such as circular red and red arrows, and separately describes pedestrian indications. For a particular intersection, check which movement the indicated face governed using the signal plan or a clear contemporaneous image. [FHWA's current MUTCD, Part 4](https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/kno_11th_Editionr1.htm)

## Tie the red indication to a moment

A witness may remember red when they looked up after hearing the crash. Ask for the sequence in their own words. Did they see the light before the car entered the intersection, as it crossed the stop line, at impact or after they heard a sound? Record any interruption in their view and any timing source they actually used.

The U.S. Department of Justice's eyewitness guidance recommends starting with open-ended prompts and documenting what the witness recalls. Adapt that interview principle to a traffic observation. An invitation such as “Show me which light you saw and tell me what happened before you looked at it” leaves room for a more useful answer. [NIJ guide to eyewitness evidence](https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/nij/178240.pdf)

## Check whether a second record can identify the face

A photo of the northbound lanes may show two heads aligned from the witness's location. A dated phase map and lane diagram can help establish which one applied to the northbound turn lane. If a recording exists, compare the visible scene and the camera time with the witness's sequence. Keep observations about placement, color and timing distinct in the file.

Use [Accident Witness Questions](/tools/witness-interview-planner) to prepare neutral prompts. For the agency records that can clarify what a crosswalk or lane displayed, see [how to request signal timing and event logs](/articles/crosswalk-signal-timing-records-pedestrian-crash). If the police report compresses a multi-impact collision, follow [the guide to documenting a missing second impact](/articles/police-crash-report-missing-second-impact).

title: Documenting Damaged Aftermarket Panniers in a Motorcycle Claim
excerpt: Match the panniers, mounting hardware and receipts to your motorcycle policy's physical damage or accessory coverage.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Documenting Damaged Aftermarket Panniers in a Motorcycle Claim
metaDescription: Match the panniers, mounting hardware and receipts to your motorcycle policy's physical damage or accessory coverage.
content:
A motorcycle repair estimate may include a cracked rack and leave the cases off the sheet. Panniers, racks and the belongings inside them are separate things to document. Ask which policy section the insurer is applying to each, then show the reviewer exactly what was mounted on the bike and damaged in the crash.

## Identify the case and hardware individually

List the left and right cases, lids or locks, mounting plate, rack and any hardware the shop says must be replaced. Note the part number, purchase date, finish and mounting system. Photograph damaged surfaces and the points where the cases attach to the motorcycle. If the cases came with a used bike and you have no separate invoice, ask for the seller's listing, bill of sale, dealership accessory records or another dated image that shows the same items installed.

Have the shop say whether a case, its lid or a mounting component can be replaced separately. If the repair estimate uses a kit price, ask which parts the kit includes so the same bracket is not included a second time. Save a written parts quote identifying the specific models. Enter the items and supporting documents in the [Claim Expense and Receipt Tracker](/tools/receipt-coverage-map).

## Ask how the policy values each item

Washington's insurance regulator distinguishes liability for damage to others from physical damage coverage such as collision. As a carrier-specific example, Progressive's motorcycle accessory guide lists saddlebags among items that accessory coverage can include. Read the declaration and endorsement for your own bike to identify eligible equipment, the limit, any deductible and the value basis. Ask which provisions apply to gear or contents that were inside the cases. [Washington insurance regulator's auto coverage guide](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/insurance-resources/auto-insurance/how-auto-insurance-works/learn-how-auto-insurance-works) · [Progressive's motorcycle accessory coverage description](https://www.progressive.com/answers/motorcycle-accessory-coverage/)

Consider a hypothetical damaged right case costing $310 to replace, a $65 bracket and an intact left case. The parts request starts with the two damaged components. If only a complete pair is available, attach the supplier's response and ask how the carrier handles the set. A pair's price is useful when it explains the parts constraint and why a standalone replacement cannot be sourced.

## Send one list with an answerable question

Ask the adjuster to identify which items appear in the bike estimate, which are considered under accessory coverage and which need more documentation. If the motorcycle is a total loss, ask whether covered accessories are already in the vehicle valuation. Keep a dated copy of the inventory and any written decisions.

If the shop added a separate operation after the first estimate, follow [how to document a missing supplement invoice](/articles/repair-supplement-denied-missing-pre-repair-scan-invoice). If weather or storage changed the appearance of the gear, see [how to compare the first and later condition photos](/articles/pre-tow-photos-rain-storage-vehicle-damage). For the coverage background, see [the motorcycle claims guide](/articles/motorcycle-accident-claims-in-2026-how-to-maximize-your-settlement-and-protect-your-rights).

title: Filing a Hit-and-Run Claim With a Tow Receipt and No Scene Photos
excerpt: Use the tow receipt to anchor time and location, then look for records that corroborate the crash and the unidentified vehicle.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Filing a Hit-and-Run Claim With a Tow Receipt and No Scene Photos
metaDescription: Use the tow receipt to anchor time and location, then look for records that corroborate the crash and the unidentified vehicle.
content:
A tow receipt can put your car at a pickup location near the time you remember. The same ticket may record why the tow was requested or what the operator saw. Build the claim around the details the ticket actually contains, then look for independent records that speak to the collision itself.

## Turn the tow ticket into a timeline

Copy the ticket number, VIN, pickup location, dispatch and pickup times, destination, and any damage notes. Clarify whether a printed time is when the operator arrived, when the vehicle was picked up or when the charge was entered. Ask the company for available dispatch or arrival records and original loading photos. Ask the receiving lot for its earliest images or condition record. [Tow yard intake and transfer records guide](/articles/tow-yard-intake-photos-vehicle-transfer)

Use the police incident number to request the full available report and any supplement. If you remember the other vehicle, write down what you actually saw, including direction, color and any partial plate. Ask promptly about available footage from cameras pointed at the scene or the route away from it. Preserve witness contact details and record when you asked each source. Washington's insurance regulator gives guidance on reporting and working with the insurer after a crash with an uninsured or underinsured driver. [Washington Office of the Insurance Commissioner's guide](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/insurance-resources/auto-insurance/auto-insurance-claims/what-do-if-youre-hit-uninsured-or-underinsured-driver)

## Separate a contact crash from a no-contact allegation

In Washington, the statutory definition of a phantom vehicle addresses crashes without physical contact. It requires corroboration from evidence other than testimony by the insured or a person with a resulting underinsured motorist claim, and reporting to the appropriate law-enforcement agency within 72 hours. The requirements for your state, policy and coverage may differ. Confirm the claim type and reporting requirements that apply to the facts you describe.
