[Washington RCW 48.22.030(8)](https://app.leg.wa.gov/RCW/default.aspx?Cite=48.22.030)

A ticket showing your vehicle was towed from an intersection at 7:42 p.m. helps establish a place and approximate time. A dispatch call describing another vehicle leaving, a neutral witness's observation or footage can address a different part of the story. Give each record its own role instead of asking the tow ticket to establish the entire sequence.

## Tell the insurer what the packet establishes

Use the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to group records under time, location, contact, identity and damage. Send a short note explaining that you have the tow ticket and identify the police, facility or camera records still pending. Ask how the carrier will review those records under the coverage you are claiming.

If the police narrative leaves out another contact, read [how to ask about a crash-report supplement](/articles/police-crash-report-missing-second-impact). For the broader reporting and coverage questions, see [the hit-and-run claims guide](/articles/hit-and-run-accident-what-to-do-who-pays-and-how-to-protect-your-rights-in-2026).

title: A Delivery Worker Was Bitten at a New York Gate. What Can the Latch Show?
excerpt: Reconstruct how the dog reached the delivery route and preserve evidence about the latch, the route and prior problems with the gate.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: A Delivery Worker Was Bitten at a New York Gate. What Can the Latch Show?
metaDescription: Reconstruct how the dog reached the delivery route and preserve evidence about the latch, the route and prior problems with the gate.
content:
A package is marked delivered and a dog reaches the worker on the way out. One person remembers the gate closing. Another says the latch had been sticking. To make the condition of the gate useful in a claim, connect its operation and repair history to the route people were expected to take.

## A New York delivery case puts restraint in focus

In *Flanders v. Goodfellow*, a postal carrier was delivering a package when the owners' dog escaped past a person through an open front door and bit her. The case concerned a doorway. Its reasoning makes it useful to a different entrance dispute involving a gate. New York's Court of Appeals recognized that an owner can face a common-law negligence claim and reinstated both negligence and strict-liability claims on the record before it. The court sent the case back for further proceedings. [New York Court of Appeals opinion in Flanders](https://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2025/2025_02261.htm)

Strict liability and negligence present distinct proof questions. The opinion discusses the owner's actual or constructive knowledge of dangerous propensities for the strict-liability theory. An inquiry about a defective latch instead asks who controlled the restraint, what they knew about its operation and how the dog reached the worker. New York's dangerous-dog statute also addresses medical costs in specified circumstances. [New York Agriculture and Markets Law § 123](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/AGM/123)

## Photograph the route and preserve the condition

From a place you are authorized to be, document the delivery path, gate swing, latch, keeper plate, warning signs and visible wear. If a camera captured the delivery, ask its custodian for a copy around the time shown in the delivery scan. A single photo of a gate resting closed may leave open whether it latched and how it opened. Keep any later repair or adjustment date with the corresponding photos.

Ask who owns or maintains the gate and who usually uses it. A dated complaint that the latch failed to catch can answer a different question from a report about prior lunging or escape. Save the delivery instructions, scanner time, route note and available witness statements. For an employee injured during a delivery, preserve the incident and employer reports alongside the property records.

## Label what each record can establish

A latch invoice can identify the part and repair date. A witness can place the dog and worker on either side of the gate. A time-stamped video may show when the gate swung and whether anyone handled it. Enter those separate questions in the [Claim Evidence Organizer](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) and add the record that answers each.

If you need footage from a doorbell or exterior camera, use [the native video request checklist](/articles/request-native-crash-video-frame-timing). If a witness saw the approach from across the street, adapt [the vantage-point questions for a crash witness](/articles/witness-saw-opposite-red-light). See also [the site's overview of dog bite claims](/articles/dog-bite-laws-in-2026-your-complete-guide-to-victim-rights-and-compensation).

title: The Employer Health Plan's Repayment Demand Relies on an Undated Amendment
excerpt: Ask the plan administrator to identify the reimbursement language, its effective date and the document that adopted it.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Employer Health Plan's Repayment Demand Relies on an Undated Amendment
metaDescription: Ask the plan administrator to identify the reimbursement language, its effective date and the document that adopted it.
content:
A recovery letter quotes an employer health plan's right to reimbursement and attaches a page labeled “amended.” The page has no date. Ask for the dated, complete instrument that supplies the language and the plan's explanation of why it applies to the benefits or settlement at issue. A new booklet may describe the plan today while leaving an earlier period unresolved.

## Direct the request to the plan administrator

Identify the plan name, plan year and named administrator. A recovery vendor can explain the demand it sent. The administrator is the point of contact for formal plan documents. For plans subject to the relevant ERISA provision, 29 U.S.C. § 1024(b)(4) requires furnishing specified instruments and the latest updated summary plan description on written request by a participant or beneficiary. Ask for the operative version for your case and identify the disputed language. [29 U.S.C. § 1024(b)(4)](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/t29/s1024/)

Request the complete governing instrument, the amendment that added or changed the reimbursement term, its adoption and effective dates, and any transition provision that the administrator says applies. Ask for the calculation and list of payments the vendor included. If the response quotes a summary, ask how it relates to the plan instrument. Preserve the exact copies and the date each arrived.

## Mark the dates separately

Consider a hypothetical crash in March, health benefits paid in May and a settlement in December. The demand cites a provision marked effective July 1. Lay out all four dates, then ask the plan which event triggers the provision and how the effective-date or transition text treats earlier payments. The crash date, treatment date, payment date and date of recovery can answer different questions.

In *Curtiss-Wright v. Schoonejongen*, the U.S. Supreme Court examined ERISA's requirement for a plan amendment procedure. It upheld the procedure at issue and left compliance with it for further proceedings. The dispute concerned retiree health benefits. For a repayment demand, the practical lesson is to distinguish the existence of a procedure from proof of how and when the cited text was adopted. [U.S. Supreme Court opinion in Curtiss-Wright](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-514/pdf/USREPORTS-514-73.pdf)

## Match the claim amount to the plan text

Ask for a table tying each payment to a service date and the claim reference, and for the provision the plan uses to calculate reimbursement. A narrow request makes it easier to see whether the remaining question is the version, the expense list or the amount. The [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) can organize the document names and date ranges. If counsel handles the settlement, send the demand and the dated versions for review before the allocation of funds.

For the recovery context, see [how an employer health plan pursued a settlement in Montanile](/articles/can-an-employer-health-plan-claim-your-injury-settlement). If the closing statement also shows a provider balance, read [how to reconcile possible duplicate deductions](/articles/duplicate-lien-settlement-statement).

title: The Health Plan Denied Imaging After the Facility Changed
excerpt: Compare the authorization, the facility that performed the scan and the submitted claim before asking for a correction or appeal.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: The Health Plan Denied Imaging After the Facility Changed
metaDescription: Compare the authorization, the facility that performed the scan and the submitted claim before asking for a correction or appeal.
content:
Your scan was approved at one location. The appointment moved, and the EOB now says authorization was absent or invalid. Compare the approval and the actual claim before concluding the plan rejected the scan itself. The facility, billing entity, procedure code or dates may differ between records.

## Compare the order, approval and claim

Ask the ordering office for the written authorization, number, approved service, date range and approved location if listed. Ask the facility that performed the imaging for the claim details and denial notice, including the billing entity, service date, procedure code and the relevant identifier for the site or provider. Confirm what changed when you rescheduled and whether the change was submitted before service.

One example of a plan-specific workflow comes from EmblemHealth's radiology and cardiology FAQ for HIP members. It describes an authorization lookup that lists the site name and location as well as the authorization number and dates. Check your own plan's notice and the fields used in its authorization process. [EviCore provider FAQ for EmblemHealth's HIP plans](https://www.evicore.com/sites/default/files/resources/2026-04/Emblem%20HIP%20Radiology%20and%20Cardiology-%20FAQ%20March%202026.pdf)

## Ask whether the problem is a claim field or a coverage decision

Suppose the same provider group operates two locations. The approval lists an outpatient imaging center. The scan was performed at the hospital, and the claim names the hospital facility. Ask the health plan which field triggered the denial and whether it will accept a correction, requires additional authorization documentation or treats the case as an appeal of a coverage decision. Ask the ordering office to confirm what updates it requested and keep any response.

If a coding or routing error occurred, ask the facility to explain its corrected-claim process and confirm when it submits the correction. If the carrier maintains the denial, follow the appeal instructions on the notice. CMS explains internal appeals and when independent review may be available for eligible disputes. Verify the applicable deadline while a facility correction is pending. [CMS action plan for a denied health claim](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights/get-help/find-action-plan/health-insurance-plan-denied-claim) · [HealthCare.gov guide to internal appeals](https://www.healthcare.gov/appeal-insurance-company-decision/internal-appeals/)

## Send a short record of the change

> Authorization 123 named Site A. The ordering office moved the appointment to Site B and the scan took place there on May 4. Please identify the field and rule behind the denial and confirm how the provider or member can have the claim reviewed.

Keep the request in the plan's secure channel. Use the [Insurance Claim Date and Reminder Planner](/tools/important-date-planner) for dates shown on the notice and the [Records Request Letter Builder](/tools/records-request-composer) to list the records you need. If an approval leads to a revised EOB, [reconcile it with the current provider balance](/articles/medical-bill-balance-after-revised-eob). If auto medical payments were sent first, [trace them through the hospital's payment ledger](/articles/medpay-hospital-payment-before-health-insurance-reprocessing).

title: Can a Freight Broker Be Sued After a Truck Crash?
content:
The name on a tractor door identifies only one link in a shipment. When a truck hauling plastic pots struck a tractor-trailer stopped beside an Illinois road, the injured driver asked a question that went further upstream. Who picked the company hauling the load, and what did it know when it picked that company? [U.S. Supreme Court opinion in Montgomery](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1238_1b7d.pdf)

That question reached the U.S. Supreme Court in *Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC*. On May 14, 2026, the Court unanimously held that a state-law negligent hiring claim against a freight broker for selecting a motor carrier falls within the federal motor vehicle safety exception at issue. The ruling sends the dispute back for further proceedings. Whether the broker actually made a negligent selection remains a separate issue. [Supreme Court opinion, slip opinion pp. 1–4, 9–10](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1238_1b7d.pdf)

## The decision that happened before the collision

Caribe Transport II was the motor carrier. Its driver was hauling the shipment when his truck struck Shawn Montgomery's stopped rig. C.H. Robinson had arranged the shipment as a broker. Montgomery sued the driver, carrier, broker, and related entities. His claim against the broker focused on its selection of the carrier. [U.S. Supreme Court opinion in Montgomery](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1238_1b7d.pdf)

Montgomery alleged that the carrier had a **conditional federal safety rating** when selected. The Supreme Court described the allegation as part of the claim it was reviewing. To decide whether the selection was negligent, a court would still need evidence about the rating, the time at which it applied, and the broker's conduct under the applicable state law. [Supreme Court opinion, slip opinion pp. 3–4](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1238_1b7d.pdf)

That distinction matters when reading the docket. A court can describe an allegation in enough detail to decide whether the law permits a claim to proceed without treating the allegation as a proven finding. The strongest factual sentence to write from this record is that Montgomery **alleged** a conditional rating at the time of selection.

## Why federal trucking law was the first hurdle

The Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act limits state regulation relating to a broker's prices, routes, or services. Section 14501(c)(2)(A) preserves state safety authority with respect to motor vehicles. The lower courts held that the federal law barred Montgomery's claim. The Supreme Court held that the safety exception covered the negligent hiring claim before it. It assumed for that analysis that the general preemption provision would otherwise apply. [49 U.S.C. § 14501(c)](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-120/t49/s14501/)

Think of the appeal as a question about the door to the courthouse. Behind that door are different questions. What duty did the broker owe under state law? What would a reasonable selection process have shown? Could an alleged lapse in selecting the carrier be connected to this crash and these injuries? The Supreme Court resolved the federal statutory issue. Those other questions turn on the case record and the applicable law.

## Follow the load through three records

- **Dispatch records connect a driver and vehicle to a particular trip.** A tractor registration or a photo of a logo can help identify the equipment. A dispatch record can put that tractor and driver on the actual shipment.
- **Shipment records identify the parties and their roles.** A bill of lading, load confirmation, and broker-carrier agreement can help establish who moved the goods and who arranged the movement. Compare legal names and identifiers across the documents, especially where a brand name appears on more than one company's paperwork.
- **Selection records address the decision challenged in the lawsuit.** An onboarding file, dated safety check, or approval log may show what the selector knew or checked before assigning the load. A record created after the crash should be labeled with its actual date.

The carrier's USDOT number is a useful link between records. The public FMCSA Company Snapshot can confirm the company you are looking at and show the latest safety information available there. The agency explains that the public snapshot does not maintain a historical safety-rating archive. Save the date of any lookup and keep it separate from evidence about the date the load was booked. [FMCSA SAFER FAQ](https://safer.fmcsa.dot.gov/faq.aspx) · [FMCSA Company Snapshot](https://safer.fmcsa.dot.gov/CompanySnapShot.aspx)

## A small difference in dates changes the question

Consider an illustration unrelated to the parties in *Montgomery*. A shipment confirmation is dated March 3. A public carrier lookup from April 20 shows a conditional rating. The difference is 48 days. The April printout can identify a question about the March decision. Establishing the March rating requires a record for that earlier date.

The useful next entries in the file are the exact carrier name and USDOT number, the original assignment timestamp, the date any rating took effect, and the document that establishes each fact. Separate the question of what the regulator's records showed from the question of what the broker actually reviewed. A dated screening report can help answer the latter.

## Start a record of the two timelines

One timeline covers the shipment, including broker assignment, carrier acceptance, and dispatch. The second covers the collision, including the vehicle locations, time, and witnesses. Give each entry a document reference. Keeping the timelines separate makes it easier to see whether an alleged earlier choice has a supported connection to what happened on the road.

Use the [Evidence-to-Fact Map](/tools/evidence-to-fact-map) to label the document behind each assertion. Start with the identity of the carrier and the date it accepted the load.

## Ask what the broker could see at the selection date

Request a record that identifies the carrier by USDOT number and shows when the broker chose it for that shipment. Then compare that timestamp with the effective date of any safety rating and with the version of the carrier information someone actually consulted. FMCSA's public records can help locate a carrier. A current snapshot and a contemporaneous selection record answer different questions. [FMCSA company safety records](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/safety/company-safety-records)

The [truck accident evidence guide](/articles/truck-accident-claims-why-18-wheeler-crashes-are-fundamentally-different-in-2026) explains which documents may show who arranged, dispatched, and operated the trip. The [Swanton event-data case](/articles/why-time-zero-matters-in-a-truck-crash-black-box-report) shows why the same discipline applies to the collision timeline. Put each decision and its supporting record in the [Insurance Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) so the selection date stays separate from the crash and later investigation.

If the public rating changed after the shipment was assigned, compare the broker's dated tender and recheck records with the carrier's notice and effective rating. [How to trace a safety rating change after a tender](/articles/carrier-safety-rating-change-after-freight-tender).

## Read the record

- [U.S. Supreme Court, *Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC*, No. 24-1238, May 14, 2026](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1238_1b7d.pdf)
- [Supreme Court docket and filings](https://www.supremecourt.gov/docket/docketfiles/html/public/24-1238.html)
- [Federal transportation statute, 49 U.S.C. § 14501](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-120/t49/s14501/)
- [FMCSA, public company safety records](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/safety/company-safety-records)
excerpt: A shipment of plastic pots led to a Supreme Court ruling on freight brokers. Follow the documents that connect a carrier selection to the crash.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Freight Broker Liability After a Truck Crash in 2026
metaDescription: The 2026 Montgomery ruling lets a truck crash claim over carrier selection proceed past a federal hurdle. Learn which records show who picked the carrier.

title: Can Your Auto Policy Cover a Crash in a Work Car?
content:
A Pennsylvania detective was seriously injured when two drivers crashed into his unmarked police car. The other drivers' insurers and his employer's auto insurer paid their limits. He and his wife also paid for stacked underinsured motorist coverage on their personal vehicles. The question was whether those personal policies covered him in the city-owned car he regularly drove for work. [Pennsylvania Supreme Court opinion in Rush](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/SUPREME/out/J-28-2023mo%20-%20105815114253376462.pdf)

In *Rush v. Erie Insurance Exchange*, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court held that the regular-use exclusion in the policies at issue was consistent with the state's motor vehicle insurance statute as applied in the case. The outcome turns on a distinction easy to miss on a declarations page. A policy's limit tells you how much coverage is available for a covered claim. The definitions and exclusions determine whether that coverage applies to the trip in the first place. [Pennsylvania Supreme Court opinion, pp. 1–4 and conclusion](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/SUPREME/out/J-28-2023mo%20-%20105815114253376462.pdf)

## The three layers that paid or declined

Matthew Rush was driving the City of Easton's Ford Fusion on November 28, 2015. The city's fleet policy provided $35,000 in underinsured motorist coverage. The household had three vehicles on two Erie policies, each with a $250,000 UIM limit per covered vehicle according to the court's description. They had elected stacked coverage. The city car was outside both personal policies' vehicle lists, and the parties agreed Rush used it regularly. [Pennsylvania Supreme Court opinion in Rush](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/SUPREME/out/J-28-2023mo%20-%20105815114253376462.pdf)

After the available payments from the other drivers and the city's insurer, the couple sought benefits from Erie. Erie relied on identical exclusions addressing regular use of a non-owned vehicle that the personal policy did not cover for UM or UIM. The trial court and Superior Court sided with the insureds on the statutory question. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed. [*Rush*, pp. 1–5](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/SUPREME/out/J-28-2023mo%20-%20105815114253376462.pdf)

## Underinsured motorist coverage and the regular-use clause

Underinsured motorist coverage, usually abbreviated UIM, addresses injuries for which an at-fault driver has insufficient liability coverage, subject to the governing policy and law. Pennsylvania requires insurers to offer UIM on the policies described in § 1731, and the purchase is optional. That statutory starting point and a purchased limit tell only part of the story. [Pennsylvania Consolidated Statutes, 75 Pa.C.S. § 1731](https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/LI/CT/HTM/75/00.017.031.000..HTM)

In *Rush*, **regular use** and **stacking** addressed different questions. The exclusion concerned whether there was coverage for injury while using the particular non-owned vehicle. Stacking concerns how qualifying limits combine where applicable. You can read the stacking selection correctly and still have an unresolved question about the covered vehicle or trip.

An employer's fleet policy might name the business as the insured and extend particular coverage to drivers, occupants, or vehicles under its own terms. The household policy might use different definitions. Place the two contracts side by side. A reference to “you,” “resident,” “non-owned auto,” or “regular use” can point to a definition somewhere other than the page with the exclusion.

## Reconstruct the coverage questions in order

1. **Identify the vehicle and date.** Note the owner, VIN, trip purpose, and which policy versions were effective on the crash date. A renewal after the accident may contain different wording.
2. **Identify the available liability coverage.** Log each carrier's coverage position and any payment or tender. Record whose policy it was and which claim it addressed.
3. **Get the employer or fleet policy wording.** The declarations page and relevant coverage forms and endorsements answer different questions. Look for the UIM section and any conditions that apply to the driver or occupied vehicle.
4. **Read the personal policies for eligibility and exclusions.** Save the exact page cited in a coverage letter and the definition it cross-references. Document how often the vehicle was available to the person and how it was actually used. The parties in *Rush* agreed regular use was present. A disputed-use case needs its own facts.
5. **Then examine limit and priority questions.** Confirm the stacking election, any priority rules, payments already made, and how those matters fit the coverage that applies.

## A useful contrast within the same work fleet

Imagine two employees injured in separate crashes in the same company car. One was assigned the vehicle most days and kept the keys. The other drove it once while a colleague was away. They can share the same fleet declarations page and have materially different evidence of their access and use. The policy language and governing law are the next facts to examine in each case.

Practical records can be simple. Keep the vehicle assignment schedule, a dated employer description of the arrangement, the fleet policy, the personal endorsements, and the insurer's letter together. A useful written question for a coverage review is, “Which policy version, provision, and facts about my use of the vehicle support your position?”

## Does this apply outside Pennsylvania?

*Rush* interprets Pennsylvania's statute in the context of particular contracts and agreed facts. Work-vehicle claims in other states require a separate review of the policy and state law. In any jurisdiction, the file is easier to assess when it separates the use of the vehicle, the coverage trigger, the exclusion, and the size of the limit.

Keep responses from the fleet and personal insurers in one [Claim Contact Ledger](/tools/claim-contact-ledger), using a separate entry for each policy.

## Keep the policy clauses beside the vehicle assignment

In a coverage worksheet, give each policy its own row. Record who issued it, the effective dates, the insured vehicle or person, the UIM clause, and the exact exclusion the insurer invoked. Attach the vehicle assignment, trip purpose, and dates of use. A declaration showing the limit answers a different question from a clause defining whether the accident qualifies. That distinction is central to the Pennsylvania court's analysis. [Pennsylvania Supreme Court opinion in Rush](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/SUPREME/out/J-28-2023mo%20-%20105815114253376462.pdf)

The [rideshare insurance guide](/articles/uber-and-lyft-accidents-who-actually-pays-for-your-injuries-in-2026) applies the same method to driver status and trip timestamps. If a carrier denies a layer of coverage, the [coverage denial guide](/articles/how-to-fight-a-denied-insurance-claim-and-win) explains how to request the written reason and identify the clause under review. Use the [Insurance Claim Follow-Up Email Builder](/tools/claim-follow-up-composer) to draft one question per disputed policy.

## Read the record

- [Pennsylvania Supreme Court, *Rush v. Erie Insurance Exchange*, No. 77 MAP 2022, January 29, 2024](https://www.pacourts.us/assets/opinions/SUPREME/out/J-28-2023mo%20-%20105815114253376462.pdf)
- [75 Pa.C.S. § 1731, availability, scope, and amount of UM and UIM coverage](https://www.legis.state.pa.us/WU01/LI/LI/CT/HTM/75/00.017.031.000..HTM)

For a rotating fleet assignment, [compare on-call access with the regular-use language](/articles/regular-use-exclusion-on-call-fleet-car). Once coverage is established, [match any UIM credits to the actual liability payments](/articles/underinsured-motorist-credit-two-driver-payments).
excerpt: A Pennsylvania detective had UIM coverage at work and at home. A clause about the city car he regularly drove decided whether his personal policies applied.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Pennsylvania UIM Coverage for a Crash in a Work Car
metaDescription: The Rush decision explains a regular-use exclusion for a city car crash. Learn to compare Pennsylvania fleet and personal UIM policies before counting limits.

title: What the Condition Adjustment Does to a Total Loss Offer
content:
A total loss estimate can start with familiar numbers. The report lists cars like yours, their prices, and a value that seems to follow from those prices. Then a line called **condition adjustment** moves the number before the deductible even appears. The question is what that line actually compares. [Ninth Circuit opinion in Lara](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/02/11/21-35126.pdf)

Two Washington policyholders challenged a recurring condition deduction in *Lara v. First National Insurance Company of America*. The Ninth Circuit's 2022 decision explains why a shared line in a computer-generated report did not establish that a class of owners had all been underpaid. Washington's October 2026 claims-handling update gives owners additional grounds to ask for the evidence behind certain condition deductions. [Ninth Circuit opinion, pp. 5–11](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/02/11/21-35126.pdf) · [Washington Office of the Insurance Commissioner, R 2025-05](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/laws-rules/legislation-and-rulemaking/rulemaking/clarifying-and-updating-minimum-standards-claims-handling-r-2025-05)

## One adjustment, two comparisons

The court described a process in which CCC assembled comparable vehicles for the insurer and adjusted for differences. A dealer car can be presented in better condition than a typical privately owned car. A downward adjustment accounted for that assumed difference. The condition of the owner's specific vehicle could then affect the amount in the other direction. [Ninth Circuit opinion in Lara](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/02/11/21-35126.pdf)

Lara and another owner alleged that the way the standard deduction was presented failed to meet Washington's requirements. The court affirmed denial of class certification. Deciding injury in their proposed class would require individual work about vehicle value and the payment actually received. The ruling answers that class certification question. For the owner of a single car, the records still matter because they show whether a particular comparison and adjustment fit the vehicle. [*Lara*, pp. 6–12](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/02/11/21-35126.pdf)

## What the Washington report should show

Start with the report for **your loss vehicle**. The current text of WAC 284-30-392 calls for information collected during the initial inspection about its condition, equipment, and mileage, and the information the insurer used to value it. The comparable vehicles are to be listed with details such as the source, date, asking price, and sold price if available. Where the computerized-source provisions apply, weighting of vehicles used in an average must be explained. [WAC 284-30-392](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-392)

The updated rule separates two types of supporting records under its computerized-source provisions:

- **A comparable vehicle's condition reduced the payment.** Ask the insurer for the photographs and documentation it used to determine that comparable's condition. The rule calls for providing that support upon request.
- **The insurer deducted value for the condition of the loss vehicle.** The rule calls for providing supporting photographs and documentation for that condition determination.

Washington also requires explanations and dollar itemization for additions or deductions from actual cash value under its total loss settlement standards. Read the applicable version with the dates of your claim in mind. The amendments adopted under R 2025-05 took effect on October 18, 2026. [WAC 284-30-391](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-391) · [Adopted rule and effective date](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/laws-rules/legislation-and-rulemaking/rulemaking/clarifying-and-updating-minimum-standards-claims-handling-r-2025-05)

## A worked example with made-up numbers

Suppose a valuation report starts with an adjusted comparison average of $18,200. It lists a $900 deduction connected to the comparable vehicles' condition and another $350 for damage to your vehicle's interior that predated the crash. The resulting estimate is $16,950 before any deductible, taxes, or fees. A $500 policy deductible would put this simplified example at $16,450 before other applicable amounts.

Two different requests follow from those two deductions. For the $900 line, ask which vehicles it reflects and how their observed condition produced that amount. For the $350 line, ask which pre-loss condition the insurer documented and how it priced it. A dated photo showing the interior before the loss addresses the second line. A dealer listing and its photographs help check the first.

The arithmetic is simple. The value of the exercise is naming what would verify each input. If the report also has an adjustment for the same interior wear in a separate place, ask how the two entries relate. Seeing both lines is a reason to ask for an explanation. Whether they duplicate each other depends on what each one measures.

## Review the report before comparing checks

First, confirm the loss vehicle's trim, drivetrain, major options, mileage, and pre-loss condition. Next, verify the date, configuration, location, and listing details of each comparable. Then copy the price adjustments into a short list with the amount, the vehicle it affects, and the insurer's explanation.

Keep **valuation**, **deductible**, **taxes and fees**, **salvage**, and **loan payoff** on separate lines when they appear. A lower amount sent to the owner can reflect a difference in valuation, a policy deduction, a payment to a lender, or some combination. A line-by-line comparison shows which part is actually disputed.

For qualifying first-party physical damage policies issued or renewed effective on or after January 1, 2026, Washington law requires a clause providing a right to appraisal for disputes over actual cash value and amount of loss. Read the clause before deciding how to challenge a valuation. Its process and costs are a separate consideration from asking for a corrected report. [RCW 48.18.620](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=48.18.620)

The [Deduction Overlap Checker](/tools/deduction-overlap-checker) can organize repeated references in the amounts you enter. Bring the underlying valuation report to any discussion about an adjustment.

## Match the deduction to the record it should have

When two adjustments both use the word “condition,” write down whether each describes the loss vehicle or a comparable. In Washington, the valuation-report rule identifies the information required for each and specifies support for certain condition reductions. For a quote from a comparable listing, save its date, options, and mileage so you can show exactly which fact you are checking. [Washington valuation report rule](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-392)

Use the [Deduction Question Builder](/tools/deduction-question-builder) to ask for the source behind a line rather than requesting a new offer without explanation. The [Texas towing case](/articles/what-a-texas-tow-company-lost-along-with-its-only-truck) illustrates a different issue: a vehicle's value and loss of use can have separate evidence. The [car accident settlement breakdown](/articles/how-much-is-my-car-accident-settlement-worth-in-2025-complete-guide) shows how to keep valuation, policy deductions, and other payments apart when you compare totals.

When the report leaves out a mobility conversion, start with [the adaptive equipment valuation guide](/articles/total-loss-valuation-missing-adaptive-equipment). If the disputed date comes from an appraisal award, [separate its signature from the effective valuation date](/articles/appraisal-award-valuation-date-total-loss). For a repaired vehicle, [compare diminished value using prices from the same side of the market](/articles/diminished-value-trade-in-versus-dealer-retail).

## Read the record

- [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, *Lara*, No. 21-35126, February 11, 2022](https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2022/02/11/21-35126.pdf)
- [Washington total loss settlement standards, WAC 284-30-391](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-391)
- [Washington valuation report requirements, WAC 284-30-392](https://app.leg.wa.gov/WAC/default.aspx?cite=284-30-392)
- [Washington Office of the Insurance Commissioner, October 2026 rule update](https://www.insurance.wa.gov/about-us/news/2026/quicker-responses-more-transparency-consumers-added-claims-process)
excerpt: A deduction can change a totaled car's value before the deductible. The Lara case and Washington's 2026 rules show what to look for in the valuation report.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Washington Total Loss Valuation Condition Adjustments
metaDescription: Review a condition deduction in a Washington total loss report. See what the Lara case decided and which photos and records the 2026 rules call for.

title: What a Texas Tow Company Lost Along With Its Only Truck
content:
When J&D Towing lost its only tow truck, its balance sheet took two hits. A Dodge 3500 disappeared from the business. So did the ability to take a call and send a truck. A check for the value of the Dodge could pay for a replacement. It could do little about the jobs the company had already missed. [Texas Supreme Court opinion in J&D Towing](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)

The Texas Supreme Court used that distinction to decide *J&D Towing, LLC v. American Alternative Insurance Corporation*. In 2016 it held that an owner of totally destroyed personal property can recover proven loss-of-use damages in addition to the property's fair market value under Texas law. The case illustrates the work that goes into proving the second loss. [Texas Supreme Court opinion, pp. 2–5, 28–32](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)

## The $25,000 payment covered two different things

The December 2011 collision destroyed the Huntsville company's only tow truck. The other driver's insurer eventually paid its $25,000 property damage limit. J&D used the money to buy another truck and resumed business in March 2012. It pursued the uncovered loss of use under its own underinsured motorist policy. That policy tied payment to damages the insured was legally entitled to recover. [Texas Supreme Court opinion in J&D Towing](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)

The jury found $28,000 in loss-of-use damages. The trial court valued the truck at $19,500, leaving $5,500 of the prior $25,000 payment attributable to loss of use. It credited that $5,500 against the jury's loss-of-use award. The insurer disputed whether Texas law allowed loss of use after total destruction. The state Supreme Court resolved that legal issue in J&D's favor and rendered judgment for the company. [*J&D Towing*, pp. 3–5 and 31–32](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)

The arithmetic answers a useful question. Once part of a previous payment covered downtime, how much downtime remained uncompensated in the trial court's calculation? Here the difference was $22,500. The policy, evidence, and credit drove that result. A property damage payment in another case may have a different allocation. [Texas Supreme Court opinion in J&D Towing](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)

## Proving downtime takes a different file from proving value

Comparable truck listings can support a pre-loss value. The downtime file needs evidence about what the business was equipped to earn, which expenses it avoided, and how long replacement reasonably took. Keep the two files connected by the same dates and vehicle identifier.

For a business vehicle, dispatch logs can establish how many eligible jobs arrived on particular dates. Invoices, payments, and prior work records can show the usual income from that kind of job. Fuel and trip expenses can show what the business would have spent to do the work. A rental inquiry may show whether a substitute was available and suitable for the work. 

The opinion describes measures that can fit different facts, including lost profits and the reasonable rental cost or value of a substitute. It also limits loss-of-use recovery to damage that can be reasonably tied to the loss and to a reasonable period for replacement, with the usual requirements of proof. A calendar that runs through every day until a check arrives can hide the difference between an unavoidable delay and time a workable substitute was available. [*J&D Towing*, discussion of loss-of-use limits](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)

## Count a missed job at its contribution

Take a hypothetical week in which a truck normally completes 12 tows at $150 each. Each completed job requires $35 in incremental fuel, dispatch, and other trip costs. Suppose the business can complete four of those jobs with another truck. The eight remaining jobs represent $1,200 in forgone sales and $280 in avoided trip costs, for **$920 in estimated lost contribution** in this simplified example.

Then test the assumption. Were those eight actual requests or a historical average? Could another operator have handled more of them? Does the $35 include any costs the business had to pay even while the truck sat? The answers can change the calculation materially. Keep recurring fixed costs separate and document how any profit estimate treats them.

If a rented truck covered a job, use the revenue and rental records for the same period. Counting the entire job as lost and including the expense of the substitute that performed it would count incompatible outcomes for that job.

## Give the replacement timeline a beginning and an end

Use the collision date as an anchor. Record when the total loss was confirmed, what substitutes were available, which listings you checked, what made a replacement suitable, and when the business actually resumed. A vehicle that requires special equipment or inspection may take more evidence to replace than a readily available passenger car.

Organize the claim as three reconciled amounts. The first is the value of the property. The second is the supported cost of lost use or of a substitute for the relevant interval. The third is what has already been paid for either loss. That last column explained the $5,500 credit in *J&D Towing*.

The [Gig Net Income Comparison](/tools/gig-net-income-comparison) can compare entered receipts and operating costs across periods. Keep the original dispatch and expense records with the calculation.

## Compare the substitute and downtime records by date

For each day the truck was unavailable, record what work was actually scheduled, what substitute equipment was available, and when a replacement could reasonably be obtained. A rental quote can help explain the cost of an alternative. Net receipts and avoided trip costs can help explain a missed business opportunity. The Texas court discussed different ways to measure proven loss of use and the need for a reasonable period tied to the loss. [Texas Supreme Court opinion in J&D Towing](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)

Use the [Gig Worker Income Loss Calculator](/tools/gig-net-income-comparison) to compare documented, similar-length periods of receipts and operating costs. Keep the [total-loss valuation case](/articles/what-the-condition-adjustment-does-to-a-total-loss-offer) next to the property file, and use the [car accident settlement breakdown](/articles/how-much-is-my-car-accident-settlement-worth-in-2025-complete-guide) to reconcile an earlier check with the specific losses it already covered.

## Read the record

- [Texas Supreme Court, *J&D Towing, LLC v. American Alternative Insurance Corporation*, No. 14-0574, January 8, 2016](https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1247477/140574.pdf)
- [Texas Supreme Court orders and judgment for January 8, 2016](https://www.txcourts.gov/supreme/orders-opinions/2016/january/january-8-2016/)
excerpt: A $25,000 total loss payment covered more than the tow truck itself. See how a Texas court separated vehicle value, lost use, and money already paid.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Texas Total Loss and Loss of Use for a Business Truck
metaDescription: J&D Towing lost its only truck. Follow the Texas Supreme Court case to understand how replacement time, lost profits, and prior payments fit together.

title: A $125,000 Crash Settlement and Medicare’s Repayment Demand
content:
Vernon Hadden settled an injury claim for $125,000. Then he had to account for a different number. Medicare had paid $82,036.17 for his care and sought $62,338.07 back after reducing its recovery for a share of his attorney fees. The gap between those amounts is a window into what happens between Medicare's payment of a medical claim and its final recovery demand. [Sixth Circuit opinion in Hadden](https://www.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/11a0293p-06.pdf)

In *Hadden v. United States*, a divided Sixth Circuit upheld that demand in a dispute over a Kentucky accident. A second driver had caused the truck that struck Hadden to swerve and was never identified. Hadden argued that the truck's owner accounted for only a small share of the fault, and that the share should reduce Medicare's reimbursement. The majority treated the scope of the claim resolved by the settlement, which included his medical expenses, as decisive in this case. [Sixth Circuit opinion, pp. 2–8](https://www.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/11a0293p-06.pdf)

## Why the number moves

Under the Medicare Secondary Payer framework, Medicare may make a conditional payment for care when a primary payer, such as a liability insurer, is expected to pay but cannot be expected to pay promptly. A later settlement, judgment, or other payment can trigger Medicare's right to recover eligible conditional payments. The payment history and the recovery demand are distinct records. [CMS, Medicare's recovery process](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process)

In Hadden's case, the $125,000 bought a full release of his claims against the company that owned the truck. His suit had sought all his medical expenses. The majority rejected the proposed 10 percent allocation on those facts. The dissent would have read the reimbursement statute differently in light of what a compromise settlement represents. This is a useful case to read when someone uses a fault percentage to estimate the net check, because the majority tied the outcome to the claim and release in the record.

## Match the document to its stage

**A conditional payment letter is an inventory at a particular date.** It lists charges Medicare's recovery contractor has associated with the incident and what Medicare has paid so far. An interim letter can be refreshed as more bills are paid. Review it for treatment connected to the accident and gather records for any line you dispute.

**A settlement creates a new set of inputs.** CMS asks for settlement information, including the amount and the fees and costs of obtaining it. Timing matters here because the agency can review payments through the date that applies under its process. Some eligible liability cases can use the Final Conditional Payment process through the Medicare Secondary Payer Recovery Portal before settlement. CMS explains the qualification and timing requirements separately. [CMS, demand calculation options](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/demand-calculation-options)

**A recovery demand states the amount CMS seeks.** It comes with information about the recovery and the relevant rights or deadlines. Save the actual letter, rather than relying on a number copied into an earlier settlement worksheet. [CMS, reimbursing Medicare](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/overview/reimbursing)

## Follow the fees through one example

Imagine a case with an $80,000 settlement, $24,000 in eligible costs of obtaining the recovery, and $30,000 in related Medicare payments. When the applicable conditions for the proportional calculation under 42 C.F.R. § 411.37(c) are met, the eligible costs represent 30 percent of the recovery. That proportion of the Medicare payments is $9,000. Subtracting it gives a modeled Medicare recovery of **$21,000**.

The regulation provides a different calculation when Medicare's payments equal or exceed the judgment or settlement and also addresses other circumstances. Compare the actual demand to the applicable subsection. In the example, the $24,000 is already a settlement expense. The $9,000 is a reduction in the Medicare recovery, rather than an additional expense. Keeping the two entries separate prevents the same cost from being subtracted twice. [42 C.F.R. § 411.37](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-411/subpart-B/section-411.37)

## Check one disputed charge from beginning to end

Pick the largest line you cannot explain. Record the service date, provider, item identifier if available, and amount Medicare paid. Match those fields to the medical record or billing statement that shows what the service was for. Compare the record with the incident date and the treatment the settlement claim addressed. A same-day provider visit may include multiple services, so a match on provider and date alone can leave an open question.

Keep the gross settlement, acquisition costs, related conditional payments, disputed charges, and final demand in distinct fields. The [Settlement Net Waterfall](/tools/settlement-net-waterfall) can help model those entries. For a private employer health plan's reimbursement claim, the plan documents and rules present a different inquiry from the Medicare recovery process.

## Give every recovery figure a document and a date

If a file contains a conditional payment amount, a correction request, and a final demand, create a line for each. Include the issue date, what charges it covers, and whether you have a written update. CMS describes how conditional payments are reviewed and how a demand follows settlement reporting. The regulation addresses the calculation of Medicare recovery when procurement costs apply. [CMS beneficiary recovery process](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process) · [42 C.F.R. § 411.37](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-411/subpart-B/section-411.37)

The [Net Settlement Calculator](/tools/settlement-net-waterfall) can compare the arithmetic under two written repayment figures while a line remains unresolved. The [employer health plan case](/articles/can-an-employer-health-plan-claim-your-injury-settlement) explains why a plan's recovery request may follow a different legal framework. Use the [settlement versus trial guide](/articles/settlement-vs-trial-which-path-to-choose-for-your-personal-injury-case-in-2026) to compare a release and the confirmed deductions together.

Once the demand amount is established, follow the corresponding payment or reserve through the settlement statement. [How to identify a possible duplicate lien deduction](/articles/duplicate-lien-settlement-statement).

If an item disappeared after a relatedness dispute and then reappeared, [reconcile the specific line on the final demand](/articles/medicare-recovery-demand-includes-removed-service).

## Read the record

- [U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, *Hadden v. United States*, No. 09-6072, November 21, 2011](https://www.ca6.uscourts.gov/opinions.pdf/11a0293p-06.pdf)
- [CMS, Medicare's recovery process for beneficiaries](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coordination-benefits-recovery/beneficiary-services/recovery-process)
- [42 C.F.R. § 411.37, amount of Medicare recovery after a judgment or settlement](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-B/part-411/subpart-B/section-411.37)
excerpt: Medicare sought $62,338.07 after a Kentucky crash settlement. The Hadden case shows why the payment list, legal costs, and final demand are different numbers.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: Medicare Repayment After a Car Accident Settlement
metaDescription: Follow Hadden's $125,000 crash settlement from conditional Medicare payments to a recovery demand, including a worked example of the fee reduction.

title: Can an Employer Health Plan Claim Your Injury Settlement?
content:
The most important number in Robert Montanile's case changed as his settlement moved from one place to another. His recovery was $500,000. About $240,000 remained after payments to his attorneys and repayment of money they had advanced. The health plan had paid at least $121,044.02 for his initial medical care. It wanted repayment from the recovery. [U.S. Supreme Court opinion in Montanile](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-577/pdf/USREPORTS-577-136.pdf)

By the time the plan sued, its claim depended on more than the amount it had paid. The U.S. Supreme Court asked whether the plan could identify settlement proceeds or property traceable to them, or whether it was trying to collect a debt from Montanile's general assets. That is the distinction at the heart of *Montanile v. Board of Trustees*, decided January 20, 2016. [U.S. Supreme Court opinion, 577 U.S. 136, pp. 138–141](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-577/pdf/USREPORTS-577-136.pdf)

## A recovery can lead to a second claim

Montanile was injured in a 2008 crash. His employer-related ERISA health plan paid for care under its benefit terms. The plan also had reimbursement language for recoveries from third parties, and Montanile signed a separate reimbursement agreement. After the settlement, the parties disputed the plan's claim. The attorney told the plan that money held for Montanile would be released unless the plan objected. The plan did not respond before the funds were distributed. It sued about six months later. [*Montanile*, pp. 139–141](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-577/pdf/USREPORTS-577-136.pdf)

The plan invoked ERISA § 502(a)(3), a federal provision authorizing specified parties to seek equitable relief. Its reimbursement provision gave it a claim against an identified fund. Enforcing a lien against identifiable proceeds or property acquired with them is different from collecting money from assets unrelated to the fund. The Court held that the provision would not allow the plan to reach general assets if the whole fund had been dissipated on nontraceable items. It sent the case back to determine whether and how much of the settlement could still be traced. [29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(3)](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-120/t29/s1132/) · [*Montanile*, pp. 142–151](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-577/pdf/USREPORTS-577-136.pdf)

## Start with the plan document and the payment ledger

A letter calling an amount a lien leaves several questions open. Which plan made the payments? Who is asserting the right on its behalf? What language was in effect on the relevant dates? Which services and amounts make up the claim?

Ask for the operative reimbursement language, applicable amendments, and an itemized payment ledger. Compare the governing plan terms with any benefits summary and separate agreement you signed. Make a note of which document specifies the type of recovery covered, the share sought, and the treatment of legal fees or expenses. Keep the actual terms attached to the calculation.

For fee allocation, another Supreme Court case is useful. In *US Airways, Inc. v. McCutchen*, the Court held that equitable rules cannot override the terms of the plan in this kind of equitable-lien claim. Where that plan was silent about allocating attorney fees, the Court applied the common-fund rule to fill the gap. This gives a reader two different questions to ask when checking a demand. What does the plan say about the recovery? What does it say about the cost of obtaining it? [*US Airways v. McCutchen*, 569 U.S. 88](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-569/pdf/USREPORTS-569-88.pdf)

## Walk a settlement statement through two scenarios

Consider a hypothetical settlement of $100,000 with $30,000 in attorney fees and case costs, and a $25,000 reimbursement demand. Entering all three numbers produces $45,000 after those two deductions. The $45,000 tells you what follows **if** the demand is paid at its stated amount.

Now suppose the itemization includes $4,000 in services the parties are still reviewing. Keep the $25,000 written demand in the first scenario. The second can show $49,000 after a hypothetical reduction, with the $4,000 explicitly marked as disputed. This makes the unresolved issue visible without treating either result as the negotiated distribution.

The reimbursement ledger should use the amount the plan actually paid when it claims repayment of benefits. An initial provider charge, a plan payment, and a patient balance are different entries. [Medical Bill–EOB Reconciler](/tools/medical-bill-eob-reconciler)

## Why the date of each letter belongs in the file

Log the first demand, responses, any dispute over itemization, and any agreement governing disbursement. Attach the settlement statement and correspondence showing where the funds were held. Resolve the reimbursement position before authorizing distribution with the people handling the claim. The litigation in *Montanile* concerned which remedy the plan could seek under a specific federal provision after money had moved.

This inquiry differs from Medicare recovery, Medicaid reimbursement, and provider liens. Identify the claimant and the source of its asserted right before applying a case or subtracting a figure from the settlement.

## Compare the document supporting the right with the record of payment

Put the plan's written reimbursement provision, the list of injury-related payments, and the settlement disbursement record in separate columns. Ask which version of the plan the demand relies on and which payments it includes. *McCutchen* and *Montanile* address different questions about plan terms and equitable relief. The terms of a claim and what can be traced to settlement proceeds each require their own evidence. [U.S. Supreme Court opinion in McCutchen](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-569/pdf/USREPORTS-569-88.pdf) · [U.S. Supreme Court opinion in Montanile](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-577/pdf/USREPORTS-577-136.pdf)

The [Duplicate Settlement Deduction Checker](/tools/deduction-overlap-checker) can flag repeated record references before you total the amounts. Compare the [Medicare recovery case](/articles/a-125000-crash-settlement-and-medicares-repayment-demand) to see how a different payer's statutory process works. For the complete settlement calculation, see [how to reconcile a written offer](/articles/how-much-is-my-car-accident-settlement-worth-in-2025-complete-guide).

## Read the record

- [U.S. Supreme Court, *Montanile v. Board of Trustees of the National Elevator Industry Health Benefit Plan*, 577 U.S. 136](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-577/pdf/USREPORTS-577-136.pdf)
- [U.S. Supreme Court, *US Airways, Inc. v. McCutchen*, 569 U.S. 88](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-569/pdf/USREPORTS-569-88.pdf)
- [29 U.S.C. § 1132, ERISA civil enforcement](https://uscode.house.gov/us/usc/119-120/t29/s1132/)
excerpt: A health plan paid more than $121,000 after a crash. The Montanile decision turned on whether it could trace the settlement money when it sued for repayment.
author: Atlantis Editorial
metaTitle: ERISA Reimbursement From a Personal Injury Settlement
metaDescription: Montanile shows how an ERISA health plan pursues repayment after a crash. Compare plan terms, payments, legal fees, and the record of settlement funds.

title: Why a Policy Limits Check Did Not End This Bad Faith Case
content:
GEICO sent a $100,000 policy limits check nine days after a fatal Florida crash. The estate later sent it back. A jury awarded $8.47 million in the resulting wrongful death case. In the separate bad faith lawsuit that followed, the insurer's early check was one event in a longer record of what it had done to protect its insured from a judgment above his coverage. [Florida Supreme Court opinion in Harvey](https://flcourts-media.flcourts.gov/content/download/425459/opinion/sc17-85.pdf)

The Florida Supreme Court's 2018 decision in *Harvey v. GEICO General Insurance Co.* makes the timeline unusually easy to see. Read it beside Florida's current bad faith statute. The case explains why communication mattered to the historical verdict. The current statute supplies a tender rule with its own trigger and conditions. [Florida Supreme Court opinion, pp. 2–7](https://flcourts-media.flcourts.gov/content/download/425459/opinion/sc17-85.pdf) · [2026 Florida Statutes, § 624.155](https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/624.155)

## What went missing between the request and the reply

- **August 8, 2006.** The crash happened. GEICO soon concluded that its insured, James Harvey, was at fault and recognized that the claim could exceed his policy limit.
- **August 14.** A representative of the estate's lawyer asked the adjuster for a statement from Harvey about other insurance, assets, and whether he was acting for his business. The adjuster did not immediately pass that request to him.
- **August 17.** GEICO tendered the full $100,000 with a release and a coverage affidavit.
- **August 31 and September 1.** Harvey learned of the request. He told the adjuster he was arranging to review his financial information with counsel and asked how to convey that he was working on the response. The adjuster did not pass that update to the estate's lawyer despite a supervisor's instruction.
- **September 13.** The estate returned the check and sued Harvey. The wrongful death verdict and excess judgment followed.

The Florida Supreme Court held that the record could support the bad faith jury's verdict in the later action brought by Harvey. It quashed the appellate decision and directed reinstatement of the judgment in the bad faith case. The court assessed the evidence under the standard for review of a directed verdict, with inferences drawn in favor of the party who had prevailed at trial. [*Harvey*, pp. 2–8, 11–18](https://flcourts-media.flcourts.gov/content/download/425459/opinion/sc17-85.pdf)

## Tender and settlement are different entries on the timeline

A tender is the insurer putting a payment forward. A completed settlement resolves the claims described in the agreement. In *Harvey*, the chronology had evidence of the first event and a dispute about why the second never happened. That difference is easy to lose in a file labeled “limits paid.”

The estate's request also had a purpose. Its lawyer was evaluating whether another policy, the business, or other sources might matter to the decision about settling. The trial record included evidence about what the estate might have done if the information had been provided. The case is worth reading for that causal question. A missed message matters to the analysis when the evidence links it to a lost chance to resolve the claim and to the resulting exposure. [Florida Supreme Court opinion in Harvey](https://flcourts-media.flcourts.gov/content/download/425459/opinion/sc17-85.pdf)

## The 90-day rule in current Florida law

Florida Statutes § 624.155(4)(a) provides a safe harbor for liability insurance bad faith claims, including those brought under common law. It applies when the insurer tenders the lesser of the policy limits and the amount demanded within 90 days after actual notice of a claim accompanied by sufficient evidence supporting the claimed amount. The facts about receipt, the supporting material, and the tender all matter to that provision.

Section 624.155(5) also states that negligence alone is insufficient for bad faith. It imposes a good faith duty on the insured, claimant, and their representatives in supplying information, setting deadlines, making demands, and attempting to settle. The factfinder may consider a failure to act in good faith when assessing damages. These provisions postdate the events in *Harvey*. The separate civil remedy notice provisions in subsection (3) answer a different procedural question. [2026 Florida Statutes, § 624.155(3)–(5)](https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/624.155)

## What to write down when dates are disputed

Imagine an insurer acknowledges an accident report on April 1 and receives a documented demand packet on April 11. Record both dates and preserve the receipt evidence and contents of both communications. Which event supplied actual notice with sufficient supporting evidence can matter under subsection (4). The crash date and the date typed on the demand letter are useful, but neither records what reached the insurer by itself.

A useful claim chronology has one line per event with the sender, recipient, date sent, date received if known, requested action, supporting documents, and response. Mark the proposed release and the tender as separate records. Where a party disputes that an event occurred, attach the evidence for the competing dates. The [Claim Timeline Builder](/tools/claim-timeline-builder) can keep those sources alongside the entries.

## Put proof of receipt beside the demand

Record the date a demand was sent, the date it reached the insurer, and which supporting records reached it at the same time. Keep the tender date and amount in a different row. This makes it possible to compare the actual evidence with Florida's liability bad-faith tender provision, which uses receipt of actual notice accompanied by sufficient supporting evidence. The terms of the offer and any release remain separate questions. [Florida Statutes § 624.155](https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/624.155)

The [Insurance Claim Contact Log](/tools/claim-contact-ledger) helps record receipt and unanswered questions. See the [claim-handling documentation guide](/articles/how-to-deal-with-insurance-bad-faith-your-complete-2026-action-guide) for how to organize the full correspondence, and [how to review a settlement offer](/articles/settlement-vs-trial-which-path-to-choose-for-your-personal-injury-case-in-2026) for the terms a tender or acceptance would need to resolve.

## Read the record

- [Florida Supreme Court, *Harvey v. GEICO General Insurance Co.*, No. SC17-85, September 20, 2018](https://flcourts-media.flcourts.gov/content/download/425459/opinion/sc17-85.pdf)
- [Florida Senate, current civil remedy statute, § 624.155](https://flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/624.155)
excerpt: GEICO tendered $100,000 nine days after a fatal crash. The Harvey record shows why a missed message mattered, and how Florida's current tender rule works.
